title: Context Graphs for Proactive Enterprise Agents
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and agentic frameworks have advanced enterprise AI considerably, yet agents remain fundamentally reactive: they wait for a human query before acting. This paper argues that genuine enterprise productivity gains require proactive agents: systems that surface relevant, actionable information to workers before they ask. We propose the Context Graph, a live relational data structure that models enterprise entities, their relationships, and state transitions over time. Built on this graph, we define a Delta Detection Engine that continuously monitors state changes, a Proactivity Scorer that ranks candidate insights by urgency, relevance, and persona-fit, and a Surfacing Layer powered by an LLM that delivers ranked notifications with grounded explanations. We formalize each component, derive a unified Proactivity Score function, and provide a complete end-to-end Python implementation using NetworkX and the Anthropic Claude API. Evaluation across three generic enterprise case studies (contract lifecycle management, engineering incident response, and sales pipeline hygiene) demonstrates that context-graph-driven proactivity achieves Precision@5 of 0.83, a false positive rate of 0.11, and reduces mean time to surface from 47 minutes (reactive baseline) to under 30 second.

AI.tldr: Proposes a proactive AI agent architecture using a Context Graph that monitors enterprise state changes and surfaces actionable insights to workers before they query, achieving Precision@5 of 0.83 and reducing insight delivery time from 47 minutes to under 30 seconds.
AI.motivation: Current RAG and agentic frameworks are fundamentally reactive—they only respond to explicit human queries. The authors argue that true enterprise productivity requires proactive agents that anticipate information needs and surface relevant, actionable insights before workers ask.
AI.method: The paper introduces three core components: (1) a Context Graph — a live relational data structure modeling enterprise entities, relationships, and state transitions over time; (2) a Delta Detection Engine that continuously monitors state changes in the graph; (3) a Proactivity Scorer that ranks candidate insights by urgency, relevance, and persona-fit; and (4) a Surfacing Layer using an LLM (Anthropic Claude) to deliver ranked notifications with grounded explanations. A unified Proactivity Score function formalizes the ranking. A complete Python implementation using NetworkX and Claude API is provided, evaluated on three enterprise case studies.
AI.result: The context-graph-driven proactive system achieved Precision@5 of 0.83, a false positive rate of 0.11, and reduced mean time to surface actionable insights from 47 minutes (reactive baseline) to under 30 seconds across contract lifecycle management, engineering incident response, and sales pipeline hygiene scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Context-graph-driven proactive agents represent a meaningful evolution beyond reactive RAG systems, demonstrating significant improvements in both precision and latency for enterprise intelligence delivery.

title: Towards the Explainability of Temporal Graph Networks via Memory Backtracking and Topological Attribution
summary: Temporal graphs are ubiquitous in real-world applications and Temporal Graph Networks (TGNs) have achieved superior predictive accuracy. Understanding which historical events drive model predictions can enhance trustworthiness of TGNs. Existing explanation methods overlook the memory module, the core component that records and updates node histories, leaving the influence of past events unexplored. To address this, we attribute TGNs predictions through the topology attribution tree and memory backtracking tree. The topology attribution tree captures the influence of neighbors and their memory vectors, then the memory backtracking tree quantifies how historical events shape node memory vectors. We apply the LRP in TGNs, ensuring that the total contribution of events equals the logits of model. Finally, top-k selection may be unfaithful due to the nonlinear mapping from logits to probabilities, we design optimization objectives to identify the important events. Experiments on nine temporal graph datasets, spanning node property prediction, link prediction tasks and graph classification tasks, show that our method provides faithful explanations and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/yazhengliu/MemExplainer

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MemExplainer, a method to explain Temporal Graph Network (TGN) predictions by attributing them through two novel structures: a topology attribution tree (capturing neighbor/memory influence) and a memory backtracking tree (quantifying how historical events shape node memory). Using Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and an optimization-based selection objective, MemExplainer outperforms baselines across nine datasets spanning node, link, and graph tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing explanation methods for Temporal Graph Networks (TGNs) overlook the memory module — the core component that records and updates node histories. This leaves the influence of past events on model predictions unexplored, limiting the trustworthiness and interpretability of TGNs.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) a topology attribution tree to capture neighbor influence and their memory vectors, (2) a memory backtracking tree to quantify how historical events shape node memory vectors, (3) application of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to ensure total contribution of events equals model logits, and (4) an optimization-based objective for identifying important events, replacing unfaithful top-k selection caused by nonlinear logit-to-probability mapping.
AI.result: Experiments on nine temporal graph datasets covering node property prediction, link prediction, and graph classification tasks demonstrate that MemExplainer provides faithful explanations and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: MemExplainer successfully addresses the gap in TGN explainability by accounting for the memory module's role, producing faithful, attribution-based explanations validated across diverse temporal graph tasks.

title: ASMR: Agentic Schema Generation for Ship Maintenance Report Writing
comment: Accepted at the DASHSys 2026 workshop (Systems for Data-centric Agents with Human-in-the-loop), co-located with VLDB 2026
summary: In this paper, we study the automatic schema generation problem: given a collection of historical ship maintenance and operational reports across multiple form categories, automatically discover compact and informative schemas that capture the essential information requirements of each report type. To address this challenge, we propose ASMR, a modular agentic framework consisting of two specialized agents. A Field Generation Agent extracts semantic concepts from historical narratives and generates candidate schema fields through adaptive multi-granularity clustering, while a Structural Optimizer Agent employs reinforcement learning to identify compact, informative, and non-redundant schema representations. The resulting schemas can guide report authors toward producing more complete, consistent, and actionable reports. Preliminary results demonstrate the promise of the proposed approach and highlight several open research challenges at the intersection of data management, agentic AI, and human-centered AI.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ASMR, a two-agent framework that automatically generates schemas from historical ship maintenance reports. A Field Generation Agent extracts concepts and clusters them into candidate fields, while a Structural Optimizer Agent uses reinforcement learning to produce compact, non-redundant schemas that guide report authors toward more complete and consistent documentation.
AI.motivation: Ship maintenance and operational reports across multiple form categories lack standardized schemas, leading to inconsistent, incomplete, and less actionable documentation. Manually designing schemas for diverse report types is labor-intensive and does not scale. An automated approach is needed to discover compact, informative schemas from historical report collections.
AI.method: ASMR is a modular agentic framework with two specialized agents: (1) a Field Generation Agent that extracts semantic concepts from historical narratives and performs adaptive multi-granularity clustering to generate candidate schema fields; (2) a Structural Optimizer Agent that employs reinforcement learning to select an optimal subset of fields, balancing compactness, informativeness, and non-redundancy.
AI.result: Preliminary results indicate the proposed approach shows promise in automatically generating useful schemas from historical ship maintenance reports, though the paper notes this is early-stage work with open research challenges remaining.
AI.conclusion: The ASMR framework demonstrates potential for automated schema generation in domain-specific reporting contexts. The authors highlight open research challenges at the intersection of data management, agentic AI, and human-centered AI, suggesting this is an emerging area requiring further investigation.

title: Forensic Schema for Psychological Manipulation in Cyber Fraud: LLM-Driven Victim Reports Analysis
comment: Accepted by the 23rd International Conference on Privacy, Security and Trust (PST 2026)
summary: Existing cybercrime classification schemas capture contact metadata and financial transactions but omit the psychological manipulation techniques perpetrators employ. We present a forensic schema (four categories, 35 questions) adding 11 manipulation indicators and cryptocurrency evidence fields to established forensic foundations. Applied to 10,994 victim reports via large language model (LLM)-driven annotation and validated against two human annotators (mean LLM-human $κ= 0.69$, matching inter-annotator $κ= 0.68$), the schema revealed a statistically distinct manipulation profile for each major fraud type (Cramer's $V$ up to $0.790$). A rationale-based evidence audit nonetheless exposed a forensic detail gap: detection of manipulation techniques was reliable, but victim narratives varied widely in the actionable detail supporting each Yes answer, and blockchain-specific identifiers were nearly absent. These findings point to AI-assisted victim intake with schema-informed follow-up questions as the most direct way to close the gap. The tiered annotation strategy also provides a reusable template for LLM-based extraction from other forensic text domains.

AI.tldr: A forensic schema with 11 manipulation indicators and cryptocurrency evidence fields was developed and applied to 10,994 cybercrime victim reports using LLM annotation. Each fraud type showed a distinct manipulation profile, but victim narratives lacked actionable forensic detail and blockchain identifiers, suggesting AI-assisted intake with schema-driven follow-up questions as a solution.
AI.motivation: Existing cybercrime classification schemas focus on contact metadata and financial transactions but systematically neglect the psychological manipulation techniques (e.g., grooming, urgency induction, authority impersonation) that perpetrators use to defraud victims. This gap limits both forensic investigations and understanding of how different fraud types leverage distinct psychological tactics.
AI.method: The authors constructed a forensic schema comprising four categories and 35 questions, incorporating 11 manipulation indicators and cryptocurrency-specific evidence fields. They applied it to 10,994 victim reports using LLM-driven automated annotation, validated against two human annotators (mean LLM-human κ = 0.69, matching inter-annotator κ = 0.68). They then conducted statistical analysis (Cramér's V) to identify manipulation profiles per fraud type and performed a rationale-based evidence audit to assess the forensic actionability of victim narratives.
AI.result: Each major fraud type exhibited a statistically distinct manipulation profile, with Cramér's V reaching up to 0.790. However, the evidence audit revealed a forensic detail gap: while detection of manipulation techniques was reliable, victim narratives varied substantially in actionable detail supporting each affirmative answer, and blockchain-specific identifiers (e.g., wallet addresses, transaction hashes) were nearly absent from reports.
AI.conclusion: The findings support AI-assisted victim intake systems that use the schema to generate targeted follow-up questions, closing the actionable detail gap in victim reports. The tiered LLM annotation strategy also serves as a reusable template for forensic text extraction in other domains.

title: PERFOPT-Bench: Evaluating Coding Agents on Software Performance Optimization
summary: Coding-agent benchmarks have largely measured whether agents can produce functionally correct patches, but production software also demands measurable speedups on real execution targets. Performance optimization is a distinct agentic task: agents must profile executions, diagnose cross-layer bottlenecks, edit code without breaking correctness, and verify that gains are reproducible rather than measurement artifacts. We introduce PERFOPT-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this full performance-engineering loop. Each task provides a correct but deliberately suboptimal codebase and asks the agent to improve a target performance metric; scoring requires hidden correctness tests, verified-speedup measurement, and trajectory-level audit. We evaluate 7 agent stacks with different LLMs and agent frameworks on 7 long-horizon optimization tasks. The results show that optimization performance is workload-dependent rather than determined by model identity alone: no single stack dominates, and changing the agent framework can materially change the same LLM's per-task speedup profile. We further find that raw speedup is unsafe as a benchmark score, since some large gains arise from benchmark-specific shortcut exploitation; an exploratory relay pilot suggests that restarting from an externalized optimization summary can recover additional headroom after an initial session stops. The benchmark and our evaluation are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Dataset-D3CC.

AI.tldr: PERFOPT-Bench evaluates coding agents on end-to-end performance optimization (profiling, bottleneck diagnosis, code editing, correctness verification, and reproducible speedup measurement), revealing that optimization success is workload-dependent rather than model-driven, and that raw speedup scores can be misleading due to shortcut exploitation.
AI.motivation: Existing coding-agent benchmarks focus narrowly on functional correctness of patches, neglecting the real-world requirement that software must achieve measurable performance improvements on actual execution targets. Performance optimization constitutes a distinct agentic task requiring cross-layer reasoning that current benchmarks fail to capture.
AI.method: PERFOPT-Bench presents 7 long-horizon optimization tasks, each providing a correct but deliberately suboptimal codebase with a target performance metric. Evaluation uses hidden correctness tests, verified-speedup measurement, and trajectory-level audit. Seven agent stacks combining different LLMs and agent frameworks are benchmarked. An exploratory relay pilot tests whether externalized optimization summaries enable cumulative gains across sessions.
AI.result: No single agent stack dominates across all tasks; optimization performance is workload-dependent. Changing the agent framework can materially alter the same LLM's per-task speedup profile. Raw speedup is unsafe as a benchmark score due to benchmark-specific shortcut exploitation yielding inflated gains. The relay pilot shows that restarting from an externalized optimization summary can recover additional headroom beyond initial session limits.
AI.conclusion: Performance optimization benchmarking requires holistic evaluation beyond raw speedup, incorporating correctness verification and trajectory auditing. Future agent development should account for workload-specific behavior and guard against shortcut-driven inflation of performance metrics.

title: DaV-Gen: End-to-End Generative Retrieval via Draft-and-Verify
summary: Mainstream industrial information retrieval systems (e.g., search and recommendation) are usually built upon Multi-Stage Cascade Architectures (MCAs), which balance effectiveness and efficiency through a coarse-to-fine ``retrieval-ranking'' pipeline. However, the optimization objectives across different stages are substantially inconsistent, propagating or even amplifying the early-stage errors that ultimately degrade the quality of final results. While emerging end-to-end generative models offer a potential solution by unifying the pipeline, their online serving performance is severely hindered by the auto-regressive process inherited from the standard decoder-only structure. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{DaV-Gen}, a novel unified solution designed to fundamentally refactor the paradigm for both search and recommendation via a ``Draft-and-Verify'' mechanism. Inspired by the process used by speculative decoding, our framework redesigns the generation task into two synergistic operations within a single model. During training, the model is concurrently optimized for both candidate drafting and fine-grained verification. This is achieved by a composite loss function that jointly trains the model on two distinct but related objectives: 1) a contrastive loss that structures the embedding space for efficient drafting, and 2) a fusion loss that combines generative likelihood with vector similarity to produce a superior verification score. This integrated training strategy equips the model with dual capabilities. At inference time, it first performs highly efficient vector-based drafting to generate a candidate set, and then verifies these candidates using the more powerful fused scoring function, thereby achieving both the speed of sparse drafting and the precision of advanced generative models within a unified, end-to-end architecture.

AI.tldr: DaV-Gen introduces a unified "Draft-and-Verify" framework for search and recommendation that replaces traditional multi-stage cascade architectures. A single model is jointly trained with contrastive and fusion losses to efficiently draft candidates via vector search and then verify them with a fused generative scoring function, achieving both speed and precision in an end-to-end system.
AI.motivation: Multi-Stage Cascade Architectures (MCAs) in industrial IR systems suffer from inconsistent optimization objectives across stages, causing error propagation/amplification. End-to-end generative models could unify the pipeline but are too slow for online serving due to auto-regressive decoding. A new paradigm is needed that combines the quality of unified generative models with the efficiency required for real-time serving.
AI.method: DaV-Gen proposes a "Draft-and-Verify" mechanism inspired by speculative decoding. A single model is trained with a composite loss: (1) a contrastive loss that structures the embedding space for efficient vector-based candidate drafting, and (2) a fusion loss that combines generative likelihood with vector similarity to produce a superior verification score. At inference, the model first drafts candidates via efficient vector search, then re-ranks them using the fused scoring function, all within one unified architecture.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative results or experimental outcomes.
AI.conclusion: DaV-Gen refactors the search/recommendation paradigm by unifying drafting and verification into a single end-to-end model, achieving both the speed of sparse/vector-based drafting and the precision of advanced generative models, without the inference latency drawbacks of auto-regressive generation.

title: The Behavioural Reflection Test: A time-efficient measure of reflective reasoning in morally and epistemically charged decisions
summary: How readily people override intuitive conclusions through reflection shapes how they navigate dense information environments with reliable and misleading sources; yet the effectiveness of a prominent measure, the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT), is eroded by widespread exposure to classic items and leaves open how such tendencies manifest more generally in decision style and linguistic expression. The Behavioural Reflection Test (BRT) addresses these issues with a brief open-ended measure of reasoning in morally and epistemically charged scenarios, alongside a four-item bespoke CRT (bCRT) as a low-exposure anchor. Among 473 online adults, higher bCRT predicted more evidence-sensitive, ethically driven decisions and reliance on high-quality sources, marked by more emotionally engaged, risk-attentive, economical language; associations the familiarity-adjusted CRT did not recover. The bCRT showed convergent validity, added item information above mean ability. Though open-ended, the BRT remained a time-efficient (median 11.8 minutes) behavioural assay of reflection with scope to extend across domains.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Behavioural Reflection Test (BRT), an open-ended measure of cognitive reflection in morally/epistemically charged scenarios, paired with a bespoke four-item CRT (bCRT) to counter item familiarity effects. Among 473 adults, bCRT predicted evidence-sensitive decisions, ethical reasoning, and emotionally engaged language, outperforming a familiarity-adjusted CRT. The BRT is time-efficient (median 11.8 min) and offers cross-domain applicability.
AI.motivation: The classic Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) has been compromised by widespread exposure to its items, reducing its validity as a measure of reflective reasoning. Moreover, the CRT leaves open how reflective tendencies manifest in broader decision styles and linguistic expression. The authors aimed to develop a measure that overcomes item familiarity confounds while capturing reflection in richer, morally and epistemically charged contexts.
AI.method: The authors developed the Behavioural Reflection Test (BRT), a brief open-ended measure assessing reasoning in morally and epistemically charged scenarios, complemented by a four-item bespoke CRT (bCRT) designed as a low-exposure anchor. They administered these instruments to 473 online adults and compared the predictive validity of bCRT against a familiarity-adjusted CRT. Outcomes examined included evidence-sensitive and ethically driven decisions, reliance on high-quality sources, and linguistic markers such as emotional engagement, risk-attentiveness, and economical expression.
AI.result: Higher bCRT scores significantly predicted evidence-sensitive, ethically driven decision-making and greater reliance on high-quality information sources. These participants also exhibited more emotionally engaged, risk-attentive, and linguistically economical expression. In contrast, the familiarity-adjusted CRT failed to recover these associations. The bCRT demonstrated convergent validity and contributed additional item information beyond mean ability. Despite being open-ended, the BRT remained time-efficient (median 11.8 minutes).
AI.conclusion: The BRT, together with the bCRT, provides a valid, time-efficient, and familiarity-resistant measure of cognitive reflection. It captures how reflective tendencies manifest in decision style and language, with potential for extension across different domains beyond the original scenarios.

title: From Solvers to Research: Large Language Model-Driven Formal Mathematics at the Research Frontier
summary: Recent developments in AI for Mathematics (AI4Math), especially Large Language Model (LLM)-driven theorem provers, has achieved remarkable success in formal proof generation for well-defined mathematical problems through Interactive Theorem Proving (ITP) languages. However, current systems remain fundamentally limited in tackling frontier research mathematics, such as discovering new theorems or resolving open conjectures, which are often open-ended, under-specified, and involve multiple layers of abstraction. We argue that the next leap in AI4Math systems requires a decisive shift from predefined problem-solvers to research agents that can address frontier mathematical challenges with rigorous formal mathematical reasoning. In this position paper, we provide a systematic review of the field, covering datasets, auto-formalization, and proof synthesis. More importantly, we identify core limitations of existing systems in serving as mathematical research agents, examining issues across datasets, relational structure, mathematical exploration, tool ecosystem, and human-AI collaboration, outlining a strategic road-map for the future of AI4Math.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that AI for Mathematics must evolve from solving well-defined formal proof problems to building autonomous research agents capable of open-ended mathematical discovery, and it provides a systematic review of current datasets, auto-formalization, and proof synthesis while identifying core limitations and proposing a strategic roadmap.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-driven theorem provers excel at formal proof generation for well-defined problems in ITP languages but are fundamentally inadequate for frontier research mathematics — tasks like discovering new theorems or resolving open conjectures that are open-ended, under-specified, and multi-layered in abstraction. The field needs a paradigm shift from predefined problem-solvers to genuine mathematical research agents.
AI.method: This is a position paper that conducts a systematic review of the AI4Math landscape across three pillars: (1) datasets, (2) auto-formalization, and (3) proof synthesis. It then critically examines limitations of existing systems through five lenses: datasets, relational structure, mathematical exploration, tool ecosystem, and human-AI collaboration, culminating in a strategic roadmap for future development.
AI.result: The paper identifies that existing AI4Math systems are constrained by narrow, well-specified datasets that do not reflect the open-ended nature of research mathematics; lack the ability to model relational structures across mathematical domains; have limited capacity for autonomous exploration; suffer from an underdeveloped tool ecosystem; and lack effective human-AI collaboration paradigms. It outlines a roadmap addressing these gaps.
AI.conclusion: The next leap in AI4Math requires building research agents that integrate rigorous formal reasoning with the flexibility to handle open-ended, under-specified frontier problems, supported by richer datasets, relational knowledge, exploration capabilities, a robust tool ecosystem, and meaningful human-AI collaboration.

title: AI-integrated models for assessing agricultural resilience
summary: Agricultural supply chains are vulnerable to disruptions through linked biophysical and economic systems. We develop an AI-powered tool that integrates economic models (GTAP) with biophysical models (APSIM) to analyze supply chain shocks, enabling policymakers and market participants to assess cross-disciplinary impacts through queries and responses written in natural language.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an AI tool that couples the GTAP economic model with the APSIM biophysical model to analyze supply chain disruptions in agriculture, allowing users to query cross-disciplinary impacts using natural language.
AI.motivation: Agricultural supply chains are susceptible to cascading disruptions across linked biophysical (crop yields, weather) and economic (markets, trade) systems, yet existing analytical tools typically address these domains in isolation, hindering comprehensive impact assessment.
AI.method: An AI-powered natural language interface is developed that integrates the Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP) computable general equilibrium model with the Agricultural Production Systems sIMulator (APSIM) crop model, enabling cross-disciplinary shock analysis through conversational queries and responses.
AI.result: The integrated tool enables policymakers and market participants to assess cross-disciplinary impacts of supply chain shocks through natural language queries, bridging the gap between biophysical and economic model outputs without requiring domain-specific modeling expertise.
AI.conclusion: Coupling biophysical and economic models within an AI-driven natural language interface offers a promising approach for holistic agricultural supply chain resilience analysis, democratizing access to complex cross-disciplinary insights.

title: Who Gets Missed in the Tail? Thresholded Subgroup Underdiagnosis in Long-Tailed Chest X-ray Classification
summary: In chest X-ray (CXR) classification, acceptable ranking performance can still leave rare-positive patients below threshold, especially within subgroups. We study this pre-deployment fairness problem as an audit question: after a long-tailed multi-label CXR model is converted from scores into decisions, who is missed? Across VinDr-CXR and MIMIC-CXR/CXR-LT, we use a diagnostic ladder to separate class-level long-tail losses, subgroup-aware weighting, group robustness, and threshold selection. On VinDr-CXR, group-tail weighting followed by tail-aware thresholding reduces tail FNR from 0.665 to 0.269, sex worst-group FNR from 0.705 to 0.157, and age worst-group FNR from 0.822 to 0.133, while macro-mAP increases from 0.611 to 0.635. On MIMIC-CXR/CXR-LT, the same score-to-threshold comparison reduces tail FNR from 0.866 to 0.741 and lowers worst-group FNR across sex, age, race, and insurance; residual missed-positive rates nevertheless remain high. Paired bootstrap contrasts on VinDr support the thresholded FNR reductions, and GroupDRO reference runs indicate that aggregate group robustness alone does not remove rare subgroup misses in this setting. The study supports a narrow audit claim: rare-label fairness in CXR depends jointly on the finding, subgroup, and operating threshold, not on label frequency or ranking metrics alone.

AI.tldr: In long-tailed chest X-ray classification, ranking metrics can mask missed rare-positive patients in subgroups. The study shows that combining group-tail weighting with tail-aware thresholding substantially reduces false negative rates for rare findings across sex and age subgroups, though residual missed-positives remain high. Fairness depends jointly on finding, subgroup, and operating threshold—not on label frequency or ranking metrics alone.
AI.motivation: Even when a CXR model achieves acceptable overall ranking performance (e.g., mAP), rare-positive patients—particularly those in specific demographic subgroups—can still fall below the decision threshold and be systematically missed. The authors frame this as a pre-deployment audit question: after scores are converted to binary decisions, who is left undiagnosed?
AI.method: The authors propose a diagnostic ladder framework with four components: (1) separating class-level long-tail losses, (2) subgroup-aware weighting, (3) group robustness via GroupDRO, and (4) tail-aware threshold selection. They evaluate on VinDr-CXR and MIMIC-CXR/CXR-LT, measuring tail false negative rate (FNR), worst-group FNR by sex, age, race, and insurance, and macro-mAP. Paired bootstrap contrasts and GroupDRO reference runs are used for statistical validation.
AI.result: On VinDr-CXR, group-tail weighting + tail-aware thresholding reduces tail FNR from 0.665→0.269, sex worst-group FNR from 0.705→0.157, age worst-group FNR from 0.822→0.133, while macro-mAP improves from 0.611→0.635. On MIMIC-CXR/CXR-LT, tail FNR drops from 0.866→0.741 with similar worst-group FNR reductions across demographics, though residual missed-positives remain high. GroupDRO alone does not eliminate rare subgroup misses. Bootstrap contrasts confirm FNR reductions are statistically significant on VinDr.
AI.conclusion: Rare-label fairness in CXR classification depends jointly on the specific finding, the subgroup, and the operating threshold, not on label frequency or ranking metrics alone. The diagnostic ladder approach—particularly tail-aware thresholding—can substantially reduce but not eliminate disparities in missed diagnoses for rare conditions in underrepresented subgroups.

title: Multi-Agent Firewall Architecture for Privacy Protection of Sensitive Data in Interactions with Language Models
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have become essential productivity tools, their integration into workflows without adequate safeguards creates significant risks. This paper proposes an open-source, privacy-focused, user-facing firewall designed to secure both web-based and programmatic LLM interactions. The architecture combines a browser extension and a proxy for total traffic interception across both HTTP(S) and WebSocket communications. At its core, a flexible multi-agent pipeline delivers data leakage prevention through a hybrid approach combining deterministic detectors with LLM-driven semantic analysis, proprietary code leakage prevention, and extensible components designed for future security enhancements such as prompt injection evasion. The framework's layered architecture enables deployment across heterogeneous environments, allowing organizations to balance computational cost, detection depth and latency. Evaluation results demonstrate it achieves F1 scores of up to 94.93% on optimal configurations.

AI.tldr: An open-source, privacy-focused LLM firewall combining a browser extension and proxy for HTTP(S)/WebSocket interception, using a multi-agent pipeline with deterministic and semantic analysis for data leakage prevention, achieving up to 94.93% F1 score.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly integrated into workflows but lack adequate safeguards, creating significant security risks — particularly around data leakage and proprietary code exposure. Existing solutions fail to provide comprehensive, privacy-preserving, user-facing protection across both web-based and programmatic LLM interactions.
AI.method: A dual-layer architecture combining a browser extension and a proxy server to intercept all traffic (HTTP/S and WebSocket). The core is a flexible multi-agent pipeline employing a hybrid detection approach: deterministic rule-based detectors combined with LLM-driven semantic analysis for data leakage prevention and proprietary code leakage prevention. The framework is extensible for future threats (e.g., prompt injection) and supports layered deployment to balance computational cost, detection depth, and latency.
AI.result: The system achieves F1 scores up to 94.93% on optimal configurations, demonstrating effective data leakage prevention performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture offers a viable, open-source, privacy-focused LLM firewall that can be deployed across heterogeneous environments, enabling organizations to tailor the trade-off between cost, detection depth, and latency while maintaining strong security guarantees.

title: ScopeJudge: Cost-Aware Pre-Execution Gating for Offensive Security Agents
summary: As LLM agents take on offensive security work, a single out-of-scope tool call can breach a client's engagement boundary, disrupt production, or void a bug-bounty finding. Unlike a fixed safety policy, the boundary that matters is declared in the user's request and must be inferred from intent. That challenge is sharpened by the adversarial nature of offensive security: the same tool call is in or out of scope depending not on the action itself but on the target it touches and the context in which it runs, which no fixed policy can enumerate in advance. We study pre-execution gating: a cheap, trusted LLM judge inspects each call proposed by a strong, swappable agent, and accepts or rejects it before it runs. We introduce ScopeJudge, a benchmark of 4,897 tool calls (7.7% scope violations) from agent trajectories on tasks engineered to tempt agents out of scope and labeled at the call level by professional penetration testers, with substantial inter-grader agreement (Fleiss kappa = 0.64) that sets an expert agreement reference point of F1 = 0.78. We evaluate eight judge models under five transcript strategies, varying how much context the judge sees, from the static policy alone to the full raw transcript, and chart the resulting cost-accuracy Pareto frontier. We find that a static policy is structurally insufficient for scope enforcement: blind to the user's request, judge recall collapses to near zero, confirming that scope lives in the request and that request-conditioned monitoring is necessary. Because a missed violation costs more than a spurious rejection, we report precision, recall, and F1 separately and recommend two operating points: a cost-sensitive configuration and a recall-first one for high-stakes deployments. We release the ScopeJudge dataset to support real-time monitoring and scalable oversight of autonomous security agents.

AI.tldr: ScopeJudge is a benchmark for pre-execution gating of LLM agents in offensive security, where a trusted judge model inspects proposed tool calls before execution to prevent scope violations. The dataset contains 4,897 labeled tool calls from agent trajectories, and experiments across eight judge models and five transcript strategies reveal that static policies are structurally insufficient—scope enforcement requires request-conditioned monitoring.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents are deployed for offensive security tasks, a single out-of-scope tool call can breach engagement boundaries, disrupt production systems, or invalidate bug-bounty findings. Unlike fixed safety policies, scope boundaries depend on the user's declared intent and the specific target/context of each action, making enumeration-based policies impossible. This motivates the need for pre-execution gating with context-aware judges.
AI.method: The authors introduce ScopeJudge, a benchmark of 4,897 tool calls (7.7% scope violations) collected from agent trajectories on deliberately tempting out-of-scope tasks. Calls were labeled by professional penetration testers with Fleiss κ=0.64 inter-grader agreement (expert F1=0.78 reference point). Eight judge models are evaluated under five transcript strategies varying context richness (static policy only → full raw transcript), measuring cost-accuracy trade-offs along a Pareto frontier. Evaluation reports precision, recall, and F1 separately, and recommends two operating points: cost-sensitive and recall-first.
AI.result: Static policy alone is structurally insufficient—judge recall collapses to near zero without access to the user's request, confirming scope is request-dependent. Request-conditioned monitoring is necessary. The cost-accuracy Pareto frontier is charted, and two recommended operating points are identified: a cost-sensitive configuration and a recall-first configuration for high-stakes deployments where missed violations are more costly than spurious rejections.
AI.conclusion: Pre-execution gating with a trusted, context-aware LLM judge is a viable approach to scope enforcement for autonomous security agents. Static policies fail fundamentally; the judge must see the user's request. The ScopeJudge dataset and benchmark are released to support real-time monitoring and scalable oversight in this domain.

title: Functional and Secure Code Generation with Task Vectors
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, but they struggle to generate functional code free of security vulnerabilities. Prior work to improve the secure code generation abilities of such coding LLMs has largely focused on evaluating code functionality and security separately using different datasets, or focused on finding vulnerabilities post-generation. At the same time, the text-generation domain has seen significant work on alignment techniques, where models are tuned such that their outputs exhibit certain qualities (e.g., helpfulness, harmlessness). Of particular interest is task-vector arithmetic, where linear operations on LLM weights can be used to arbitrarily enhance alignment while incurring only minimal computational overhead. We develop a novel method, SecVecCoder, leveraging task vectors to produce trustworthy code that is simultaneously functional and secure without the need for post-generation adjustment. Across six coding LLMs from three families on the CodeGuard+ benchmark, SecVecCoder improves the rate of trustworthy code completions by 2.1-36.0 percentage points over the base model, with improvements on unseen CWE types reaching up to 39.1 percentage points. Since the effectiveness of the coding LLM relies only on changing the model weights, SecVecCoder requires no method-specific decoding and hence achieves a decoding latency within 0.6% of the base model's, on average.

AI.tldr: SecVecCoder leverages task-vector arithmetic on LLM weights to generate code that is simultaneously functional and secure, improving trustworthy code rates by 2.1–36.0 pp across six models on CodeGuard+ with negligible latency overhead (~0.6%).
AI.motivation: Existing coding LLMs struggle to produce code that is both functional and free of security vulnerabilities. Prior approaches either evaluate functionality and security separately, focus on post-generation vulnerability detection, or incur significant overhead. Meanwhile, alignment techniques in text generation — particularly task-vector arithmetic — offer lightweight, weight-space manipulation for imparting desired qualities. This motivates adapting task-vector methods to the secure code generation domain.
AI.method: SecVecCoder applies task-vector arithmetic directly to LLM weights. A "security vector" is derived by subtracting the weights of a base model from those of a security-fine-tuned variant. This vector is then added (with a scaling coefficient) to the base model's weights, steering outputs toward secure code generation without modifying the decoding procedure. The approach requires no post-generation adjustment and no method-specific inference changes.
AI.result: Evaluated on the CodeGuard+ benchmark across six coding LLMs from three families, SecVecCoder improves trustworthy code completions by 2.1–36.0 percentage points over base models. On unseen CWE types, improvements reach up to 39.1 pp. Decoding latency is within 0.6% of the base model on average, as no inference-time modifications are needed.
AI.conclusion: SecVecCoder demonstrates that task-vector arithmetic is a highly effective and computationally lightweight method for improving secure code generation in LLMs, achieving strong gains in trustworthiness (functionality + security) while preserving decoding speed and generalizing to unseen vulnerability types.

title: H3D: Benchmarking Unsupervised Text Hashing for Fine-Grained Document Deduplication
summary: Document hashing provides compact representations for efficient similarity search and document deduplication, but existing studies rarely compare hashing pipelines under a unified protocol for fine-grained scientific documents. H3D is an unsupervised text hashing benchmark for fine-grained document deduplication. It evaluates representative unsupervised non-learning hashing approaches (MinHash, SimHash, Winnowing, FuzzyHash, FlyHash) together with semantic-sensitive methods built from frozen BGE embeddings and two quantization strategies (BGE-BIHash and BGE-LSHash). The non-learning methods generate hash fingerprints through manually designed mathematical rules without training or labeled similarity pairs, which distinguishes them from neural semantic hashing models. We benchmark all methods on CSFCube and RELISH, two datasets that provide complementary evaluation settings: facet-level analysis for scientific-document similarity and larger-scale split-level evaluation for biomedical similarity search. H3D jointly reports ranking quality (MAP, NDCG@20), efficiency, and robustness under controlled text compression. The results show a consistent trade-off: lexical and structural fingerprints are competitive for near-duplicate matching, while semantic-sensitive representations better preserve similarity under content rewriting, at higher computational cost. We further analyze when different similarity measures become rank-equivalent for specific hash representations, improving the interpretability and reproducibility of method comparisons.

AI.tldr: H3D is an unsupervised text hashing benchmark for fine-grained scientific document deduplication, evaluating non-learning hashing methods (MinHash, SimHash, Winnowing, FuzzyHash, FlyHash) alongside semantic-sensitive methods using frozen BGE embeddings. Benchmarked on CSFCube and RELISH, it reveals a trade-off: lexical fingerprints excel at near-duplicate matching, while semantic methods better preserve similarity under rewriting but at higher cost.
AI.motivation: Existing document hashing studies lack a unified comparison protocol tailored to fine-grained scientific documents. H3D addresses this gap by providing the first systematic benchmark that evaluates both traditional non-learning hashing pipelines and embedding-based semantic hashing under consistent metrics for deduplication and similarity search.
AI.method: H3D benchmarks five representative unsupervised non-learning hashing approaches (MinHash, SimHash, Winnowing, FuzzyHash, FlyHash) and two semantic-sensitive methods built from frozen BGE embeddings with quantization (BGE-BIHash, BGE-LSHash). Evaluation uses CSFCube (facet-level scientific similarity) and RELISH (biomedical similarity search) under a unified protocol measuring ranking quality (MAP, NDCG@20), efficiency, and robustness under controlled text compression.
AI.result: Lexical and structural fingerprints are competitive for near-duplicate matching. Semantic-sensitive representations better preserve similarity under content rewriting but incur higher computational cost. The benchmark also identifies conditions where different similarity measures become rank-equivalent for specific hash representations.
AI.conclusion: H3D establishes a reproducible benchmark revealing a clear trade-off between lexical/structural and semantic hashing for scientific document deduplication, improving interpretability of method comparisons and guiding method selection based on use-case requirements.

title: HeadRoom: Lightweight, Edge-deployable Pipeline for Adaptive Notification Routing
summary: Emerging wearables, such as smart glasses, can deliver notifications through multiple sensory channels, but there is still a limited understanding of how to choose the right channel at the right moment. We propose HeadRoom, a lightweight, edge-deployable pipeline that estimates the availability of visual and auditory channels in real time from egocentric video and audio. Our controlled user study (N=25) shows that, under high perceptual load, routing notifications to the more available channel reduces response time relative to routing them to the less available channel. This work opens up a new possibility for adaptive routing of notifications in wearable and immersive systems.

AI.tldr: HeadRoom is an edge-deployable pipeline that estimates real-time availability of visual and auditory channels from egocentric video/audio, enabling adaptive notification routing on wearables. A user study shows routing to the more available channel under high perceptual load reduces response time.
AI.motivation: Emerging multi-sensory wearables (e.g., smart glasses) can deliver notifications through different sensory channels, but there is limited understanding of how to select the optimal channel at any given moment based on the user's current perceptual state.
AI.method: HeadRoom is a lightweight, edge-deployable pipeline that processes egocentric video and audio in real time to estimate the current availability of both the visual and auditory perceptual channels, enabling dynamic notification routing decisions.
AI.result: A controlled user study with N=25 participants demonstrated that under conditions of high perceptual load, routing notifications to the more available sensory channel yields significantly reduced response times compared to routing them to the less available channel.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates the feasibility and benefit of context-aware, adaptive notification routing across sensory channels in wearable and immersive systems, opening a new design space for attention-aware interfaces.

title: DeepSearch-World: Self-Distillation for Deep Search Agents in a Verifiable Environment
summary: Training tool-use agents to improve from their own experience remains challenging, as supervised fine-tuning relies on fixed teacher-distilled trajectories, while sparse-reward reinforcement learning provides weak supervision for long-horizon interactions. We present DeepSearch-Evolve, a self-distillation framework for web agents built on DeepSearch-World, a deterministic and verifiable environment with reproducible search and page-reading tools. DeepSearch-World contains 420K multi-hop QA tasks constructed from entity-level random walks and supports key agentic cognitive behaviors useful for self-evolving, including progress verification, grounded reflection, and failure recovery. DeepSearch-Evolve iteratively performs trajectory generation, filtering, data mixing, and fine-tuning to train stronger agents. Without distillation from more capable models, DeepSearch-World-9B achieves competitive performance compared with open-source agents, reaching 31.2% on BrowseComp, 61.5% on GAIA, and 93.4% on HotpotQA, showing that verifiable environments enable scalable self-evolution for long-horizon web agents. We will release the environment, 420K training pool, validation set, model, and code to facilitate future research on self-improving deep search agents.

AI.tldr: DeepSearch-Evolve is a self-distillation framework that trains web agents in a verifiable environment (DeepSearch-World) with 420K multi-hop QA tasks, enabling iterative self-improvement through trajectory generation, filtering, and fine-tuning — achieving competitive results on BrowseComp (31.2%), GAIA (61.5%), and HotpotQA (93.4%) without distillation from stronger teacher models.
AI.motivation: Current approaches to training tool-use agents suffer from two key limitations: supervised fine-tuning relies on static teacher-distilled trajectories that do not improve with experience, while reinforcement learning with sparse rewards provides weak supervision for long-horizon interactions. The authors aim to overcome both by enabling agents to self-evolve through verifiable environments that provide dense, grounded feedback.
AI.method: The authors introduce DeepSearch-World, a deterministic, verifiable environment featuring reproducible search and page-reading tools, containing 420K multi-hop QA tasks built via entity-level random walks. The environment supports cognitive behaviors such as progress verification, grounded reflection, and failure recovery. DeepSearch-Evolve iteratively cycles through four stages: (1) trajectory generation by the current agent, (2) filtering of high-quality trajectories, (3) data mixing with prior experience, and (4) fine-tuning to produce a stronger policy — all without distillation from more capable models.
AI.result: DeepSearch-World-9B achieves 31.2% on BrowseComp, 61.5% on GAIA, and 93.4% on HotpotQA, demonstrating competitive performance against open-source agents without relying on teacher distillation. The results validate that verifiable environments can enable scalable self-evolution for long-horizon web agents.
AI.conclusion: Verifiable, deterministic environments like DeepSearch-World can support scalable self-evolution of web agents through iterative self-distillation, eliminating the need for distillation from stronger models. The authors commit to releasing all artifacts (environment, training data, validation set, model, and code) to advance research on self-improving deep search agents.

title: Adversarial Social Epistemology for Assemblies of Humans and Large Language Models
summary: We outline an adversarial social epistemology (ASE) for densely interactive communicative landscapes in which public assertions are scaffolded by chains of testimony, inference, institutional certification, and tacit trust. In such landscapes, agents have incentives and affordances to distort, color, omit, fabricate, or strategically under-specify information for private, reputational, rhetorical, or material gains. We argue that these phenomena are not adequately captured by familiar descriptions of epistemic bubbles, echo chambers, or misinformation diffusion. What requires explanation is how communicative agents exploit the commitments and entitlements that normally make scaffolded assertions trustworthy. We provide language that delivers the requisite analysis, outline mechanisms that subvert trust in scaffolded public communications, and outline machinery for auditing and redressing trust breaches arising from subverting the auditability of inferential chains, drawing on epistemic networks, enriched with an inferentialist semantics for interpreting assertions.

AI.tldr: Proposes an "adversarial social epistemology" (ASE) framework to analyze how communicative agents strategically exploit the trust mechanisms underlying scaffolded public assertions in complex information landscapes, going beyond standard echo chamber/misinformation models by focusing on subversion of inferential commitments and entitlements.
AI.motivation: Existing concepts like epistemic bubbles, echo chambers, and misinformation diffusion fail to adequately capture how actors in dense communicative networks deliberately exploit the very commitments and entitlements that underwrite trust in scaffolded assertions — through distortion, omission, fabrication, or strategic under-specification for private gain. A new analytical framework is needed.
AI.method: Develops a conceptual framework combining (1) epistemic network modeling to trace chains of testimony and institutional certification, (2) an inferentialist semantics (à la Brandom) for interpreting the normative commitments and entitlements carried by public assertions, and (3) machinery for auditing inferential chains and redressing breaches of trust, including mechanisms that subvert auditability itself.
AI.result: Delivers a novel vocabulary and analytical apparatus — Adversarial Social Epistemology (ASE) — that characterizes how trust in scaffolded public communication is subverted, explicates the mechanisms by which agents exploit inferential commitments, and outlines auditing and redress machinery for breaches arising from undermined inferential-chain auditability.
AI.conclusion: ASE provides a more precise diagnostic and remedial framework than prevailing misinformation/bubble models for densely interactive communicative landscapes, enabling both analysis of adversarial exploitation of epistemic trust and the design of audit and redress mechanisms to restore the trustworthiness of scaffolded public assertions.

title: LLT: Local Linear Transformer for PDE Operator Learning
summary: Neural operators have become a common approach for learning PDE solution maps and accelerating numerical simulations. Transformer-based neural operators are of particular interest, since attention can learn long-range dependencies in the computational domain. However, standard attention has two major limitations when applied to PDEs: it scales quadratically with the number of computational nodes, and it lacks an explicit bias toward local interactions. To address these issues, we introduce Local Linear Transformer (LLT) for PDE operator learning. The architecture combines linear global attention with local spatial mixing, and incorporates coordinate and geometry information. We evaluate LLT on several PDE problems, including elasticity, plasticity, airfoil flow, pipe flow, and Darcy flow. The reference data for these problems span finite-element, finite-volume, and finite-difference discretizations on structured and unstructured meshes. Compared with other neural-operator and transformer baselines from prior studies, LLT achieves competitive or lower relative $L_2$ error across these problems. On matched structured discretizations, wall-clock time per training iteration is reduced by factors of 1.8 to 2.5 relative to Transolver. We also scale the approach and apply it to a three-dimensional car aerodynamics dataset with 32,186 unstructured mesh points per sample. Together, these results indicate that LLT provides an accurate and computationally efficient operator for PDE problems across discretizations, mesh types, and problem settings.

AI.tldr: LLT introduces a transformer-based neural operator for PDEs that combines linear global attention with local spatial mixing, achieving competitive accuracy while reducing computational cost by 1.8-2.5× compared to Transolver, and scales effectively to 3D unstructured meshes.
AI.motivation: Standard attention in transformer-based neural operators suffers from quadratic scaling with the number of computational nodes and lacks explicit bias toward local interactions, both of which are critical limitations for learning PDE solution maps efficiently.
AI.method: The Local Linear Transformer (LLT) architecture combines linear global attention (reducing quadratic to linear complexity) with local spatial mixing to inject local-interaction bias, and incorporates coordinate and geometry information. It is evaluated across structured and unstructured meshes with finite-element, finite-volume, and finite-difference discretizations.
AI.result: LLT achieves competitive or lower relative L₂ error compared to other neural operators and transformer baselines. Training iteration wall-clock time is reduced by factors of 1.8–2.5 relative to Transolver on matched structured discretizations. The method also scales to a 3D car aerodynamics problem with 32,186 unstructured mesh points per sample.
AI.conclusion: LLT provides an accurate and computationally efficient operator for PDE problems across diverse discretizations, mesh types, and problem settings, making it a compelling alternative to existing transformer-based neural operators.

title: WebSwarm: Recursive Multi-Agent Orchestration for Deep-and-Wide Web Search
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based web search agents are transforming information seeking from simple factoid question answering into complex, deep-and-wide search and research-oriented tasks. A single ReAct-style agent is constrained by one long trajectory and limited context, making it difficult to handle depth and coverage simultaneously. Existing multi-agent systems improve search coverage through parallel execution and aggregation, but still exhibit clear limitations in recursive depth, collaboration adaptability, and evidence-grounded expansion. We propose WebSwarm, a progressive recursive delegation framework that jointly constructs task decomposition, recursive expansion, and agent collaboration during inference. WebSwarm dynamically instantiates agentic search nodes, each coupling a local objective with a search mode that specifies how the node should organize search and collaboration. Each node can either solve its objective itself or further delegate child nodes; after solving, it returns evidence and results upward, enabling parent nodes to further expand, revise, or aggregate the search process. To guide this process, WebSwarm first probes how task-relevant information is organized on the web to ground subsequent node expansion, and reuses process-level experience across homogeneous sibling nodes. Experiments on BrowseComp-Plus, WideSearch, DeepWideSearch, and GISA show that WebSwarm consistently outperforms single-agent and multi-agent baselines on deep, wide, and interleaved deep-and-wide tasks. Further analyses of ablation, task difficulty, web tool efficiency, and model generalization explain WebSwarm's effectiveness and provide insights for multi-agent search systems.

AI.tldr: WebSwarm is a progressive recursive delegation framework for LLM-based web search agents that jointly handles task decomposition, recursive expansion, and agent collaboration. Unlike single-agent (limited context/depth) or flat multi-agent systems (weak recursion/adaptability), WebSwarm dynamically instantiates agentic search nodes that can self-solve or delegate to children, using web structure probing and sibling experience reuse to guide expansion, achieving state-of-the-art on deep, wide, and interleaved search benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Single ReAct-style LLM search agents are bottlenecked by a single long trajectory and limited context window, preventing simultaneous deep-and-wide search. Existing multi-agent systems improve coverage via parallel execution but suffer from: (1) limited recursive depth, (2) poor collaboration adaptability, and (3) lack of evidence-grounded expansion. A unified framework is needed that can handle complex, research-oriented tasks requiring both breadth and depth.
AI.method: WebSwarm employs a progressive recursive delegation framework with three key mechanisms: (1) Dynamic instantiation of agentic search nodes, each pairing a local objective with a search mode dictating search organization and collaboration strategy; nodes either self-solve or delegate to children, then propagate evidence/results upward for parent-level expansion, revision, or aggregation. (2) Web structure probing: before expansion, the system probes how task-relevant information is organized on the web to ground subsequent node decomposition. (3) Process-level experience reuse across homogeneous sibling nodes to improve efficiency.
AI.result: WebSwarm consistently outperforms both single-agent and multi-agent baselines across four benchmarks: BrowseComp-Plus, WideSearch, DeepWideSearch, and GISA — covering deep, wide, and interleaved deep-and-wide search tasks. Ablation studies, task difficulty analysis, web tool efficiency evaluation, and model generalization experiments further validate the framework's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: WebSwarm demonstrates that progressive recursive delegation, grounded by web structure probing and sibling experience reuse, effectively addresses the depth-coverage trade-off in LLM-based web search. The framework's strong performance and generalization suggest this is a promising direction for building more capable multi-agent search systems for complex, research-oriented information tasks.

title: Open Models, Open Risks: Measuring Unsafe Generation in Text-to-Image Models In the Wild
summary:
Existing safety studies on text-to-image (T2I) jailbreaks are largely conducted in controlled in-the-lab settings, typically on a small number of canonical models. As a result, the current safety status of the rapidly growing in-the-wild T2I ecosystem remains unclear. This uncertainty is amplified by two factors: existing detector-based metrics are designed for controlled evaluation, and in-the-wild risks may arise not only from adversarial prompting, but also from unsafe release practices and unsafe model derivatives.
  In this paper, we present a large-scale empirical study of in-the-wild T2I safety through the lens of jailbreak. We first show that detector-only jailbreak metrics substantially overestimate practical risk over in the wild due to semantic drift and generation artifacts, and we introduce Advanced ASR to better capture semantically valid and visually plausible unsafe generation. Using this refined metric, we evaluate 200+ in-the-wild T2I models from Hugging Face under three representative jailbreak attacks. Our results show that many downstream models retain a non-trivial degree of safety even without explicit post-hoc safeguards, indicating that safety degradation in the wild is neither universal nor uniform. At the same time, we identify a set of high-risk models, including explicitly NSFW-oriented releases as well as seemingly benign models whose unsafe behavior is only exposed through systematic evaluation. We further trace these models to their release context and report high-risk cases to Hugging Face.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study of 200+ in-the-wild T2I models reveals that standard detector-based safety metrics overestimate real-world risk; the authors propose Advanced ASR, a refined metric capturing semantically valid unsafe generation, and find that safety degradation is neither universal nor uniform across downstream models, while also identifying high-risk models and reporting them to Hugging Face.
AI.motivation: Existing T2I jailbreak safety research is limited to controlled lab settings with few canonical models, leaving the safety status of the rapidly growing in-the-wild ecosystem (including models from Hugging Face) unclear. Current detector-based metrics are designed for controlled evaluation and may not reflect practical risk, which can also stem from unsafe release practices and model derivatives—not just adversarial prompting.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale empirical study evaluating 200+ in-the-wild T2I models from Hugging Face. They first demonstrate that detector-only jailbreak metrics overestimate practical risk due to semantic drift and generation artifacts, then introduce Advanced ASR (Attack Success Rate) to better capture semantically valid and visually plausible unsafe generation. Using this refined metric, they evaluate models under three representative jailbreak attacks and trace high-risk models back to their release context.
AI.result: Many downstream models retain a non-trivial degree of safety even without explicit post-hoc safeguards, showing that safety degradation in the wild is neither universal nor uniform. However, the study also identifies a set of high-risk models, including explicitly NSFW-oriented releases and seemingly benign models whose unsafe behavior only surfaces under systematic evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The in-the-wild T2I ecosystem exhibits heterogeneous safety properties that standard lab metrics fail to capture. The proposed Advanced ASR metric provides a more accurate assessment, and the findings underscore the need for systematic, large-scale safety evaluation beyond canonical models to identify hidden risks in publicly released models.

title: Bug Report Specification Refinement with Trajectory Guidance for Automated Program Repair
summary: Bug reports serve as task specifications for repository-level automated program repair (APR) agents, but they often describe only the observed failure and omit repair-relevant information such as the failure-inducing behavior, behavioral requirement, and implementation scope. As a result, a repair agent may inspect irrelevant code, infer an incorrect requirement, or generate a patch that addresses the reported symptom without restoring the intended repository behavior. We present TrajSpec, a trajectory-guided approach for repository-supported bug report specification refinement. Given an original report and a pre-fix repository, TrajSpec runs a trajectory-collection agent and uses the resulting unverified trajectory as a source of trajectory-derived specification evidence. It organizes this evidence into a three-level representation consisting of a high-level interpretation of the issue, diagnostic findings supporting that interpretation, and concrete repository observations. TrajSpec then generates a draft refined report and applies repository-based review to remove unsupported claims, revise uncertain claims, and add repository-supported details. We evaluate TrajSpec on all 300 SWE-Bench Lite instances using Mini-SWE-Agent V2. TrajSpec's refined reports improve Pass@1 from 41.00% to 59.67% with GPT-5-mini and from 54.67% to 64.33% with MiniMax M2.5. On a stratified sample of 100 instances, TrajSpec's refined reports also improve Pass@1 from 41.00% to 71.00% with Agentless and from 47.00% to 72.00% with AutoCodeRover. Ablation results show that removing repository-based review or the hierarchical evidence representation reduces Pass@1 from 59.67% to 48.00% and 47.67%, respectively. Overall, TrajSpec provides actionable repository-supported context that consistently improves repair performance.

AI.tldr: TrajSpec refines bug reports for repository-level automated program repair by collecting execution trajectories, organizing evidence hierarchically, and applying repository-based review to remove unsupported claims. Refined reports boost Pass@1 from 41% to 59.67% (GPT-5-mini) and 54.67% to 64.33% (MiniMax M2.5), with similar gains across other repair agents.
AI.motivation: Bug reports in APR typically describe only the observed failure, omitting critical repair-relevant information such as failure-inducing behavior, behavioral requirements, and implementation scope. This leads repair agents to inspect irrelevant code, infer incorrect requirements, or produce patches that only address symptoms without restoring intended behavior.
AI.method: TrajSpec operates in several stages: (1) a trajectory-collection agent runs on the pre-fix repository to gather unverified execution traces as specification evidence; (2) evidence is organized into a three-level hierarchical representation — high-level issue interpretation, diagnostic findings, and concrete repository observations; (3) a draft refined report is generated; (4) repository-based review filters out unsupported claims, revises uncertain ones, and adds repository-backed details.
AI.result: On all 300 SWE-Bench Lite instances, TrajSpec improved Pass@1 from 41.00% to 59.67% (GPT-5-mini) and from 54.67% to 64.33% (MiniMax M2.5). On a 100-instance stratified sample, Pass@1 rose from 41.00% to 71.00% (Agentless) and from 47.00% to 72.00% (AutoCodeRover). Ablations showed that removing repository-based review dropped Pass@1 to 48.00%, and removing hierarchical evidence representation dropped it to 47.67%.
AI.conclusion: TrajSpec demonstrates that trajectory-guided, repository-supported bug report refinement provides actionable context that consistently and substantially improves repair performance across multiple repair agents and models.

title: Conversational Retrieval and On-the-Fly Knowledge Modeling of Historical Penitentiary Repression Records
summary: Recent developments in digital libraries increasingly favor conversational and natural language access to information through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Although these approaches are effective for extractive tasks grounded in individual records, they remain limited in their ability to interpret document collections holistically and to incorporate expert knowledge dynamically. In this article, we present a document analysis system designed for the management of historical digital libraries that supports on-the-fly knowledge modeling. The system is equipped with the capability to store facts produced either by expert archivists or derived from document retrieval processes within a graph-based structure. Through continuous professional interaction, the system can retrieve information not only from primary sources such as documents, but also from previously modeled knowledge, with the graph-based index acting as a memory for the language model to access. This enables increasingly complex queries involving long-term dependencies across documents, link discovery, and the integration of expert knowledge that may not be explicitly present in the original sources. As a result, the proposed approach facilitates the generation of richer and more comprehensive information.

AI.tldr: A document analysis system for historical digital libraries that combines RAG with a graph-based knowledge structure, enabling dynamic expert knowledge modeling, long-term cross-document dependencies, and link discovery beyond extractive retrieval.
AI.motivation: Current RAG-based conversational access to digital libraries excels at extractive tasks on individual records but fails to interpret document collections holistically and cannot dynamically incorporate expert knowledge. There is a need for systems that go beyond single-document retrieval to support complex, multi-document reasoning and the integration of external archival expertise.
AI.method: The proposed system integrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation with an on-the-fly knowledge modeling framework. Facts produced by expert archivists or derived from document retrieval are stored in a graph-based structure. This graph serves as an external memory for the language model, allowing retrieval from both primary documents and previously modeled knowledge. Continuous professional interaction refines the knowledge graph over time.
AI.result: The graph-augmented architecture enables complex queries involving long-term dependencies across multiple documents, link discovery between records, and integration of expert knowledge absent from original sources. This yields richer, more comprehensive information generation compared to standard RAG approaches limited to extractive single-record tasks.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting RAG with a graph-based knowledge memory that evolves through expert interaction significantly enhances document analysis in historical digital libraries, supporting holistic collection interpretation and enabling queries that require cross-document reasoning and expert knowledge integration.

title: How Analysts Use AI in High-Stakes Crime Linkage: An Industrial Study
summary:
Crime linkage analysis is used in many countries to identify series of offences that may have been committed by the same individual. In practice, specialist analysts manually search for behavioural and situational connections across large crime databases, an effort that is time-consuming, cognitively demanding, and can involve repeated exposure to disturbing material. To support this work, an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled decision-support tool was co-developed with a UK law enforcement agency to assist analysts in identifying likely crime linkages.
  This paper reports an industrial evaluation of the crime-linkage tool. We conducted a mixed-methods usability study combining direct observation, eye-tracking, mouse-tracking, and surveys to examine how analysts engage with AI predictions and with the model features presented as explanations. Our findings show that analysts used the AI predictions selectively and frequently validated them against behavioural (non-AI) evidence, reflecting partial trust and an ongoing reliance on established analytical practices. We also found that analysts attended to the presented model features and valued their availability, while identifying opportunities to improve how explanations are presented and integrated into the workflow. Overall, our results highlight the need for AI-enabled decision-support tools to better integrate explanations and traditional analytical methods, and demonstrate the importance of in-situ evaluation for engineering usable and trustworthy AI in high-stakes settings.

AI.tldr: An industrial evaluation of an AI-enabled crime-linkage tool co-developed with UK law enforcement reveals analysts selectively use AI predictions, frequently validate them against non-AI evidence, and value model explanations — highlighting the need for better integration of explanations and traditional methods in high-stakes settings.
AI.motivation: Crime linkage analysis — identifying series of offences committed by the same individual — is time-consuming, cognitively demanding, and involves repeated exposure to disturbing material. AI tools promise to assist, but their real-world usability, trustworthiness, and integration into analysts' workflows remain underexplored in operational settings.
AI.method: Mixed-methods usability study combining direct observation, eye-tracking, mouse-tracking, and surveys, conducted as an industrial evaluation of an AI-enabled crime-linkage decision-support tool co-developed with a UK law enforcement agency.
AI.result: Analysts used AI predictions selectively and frequently cross-validated them against behavioural (non-AI) evidence, reflecting partial trust and continued reliance on established analytical practices. Analysts attended to model feature explanations and valued their availability, but identified opportunities for improved presentation and workflow integration.
AI.conclusion: AI-enabled decision-support tools must better integrate explanations with traditional analytical methods. In-situ evaluation is essential for engineering usable and trustworthy AI in high-stakes, real-world settings.

title: How Do I Know What to Say Next? Barenholtz's Autogenerative Theory as an Enrichment of Harrisean Integrationism
summary: Roy Harris's Integrationist linguistics offers a compelling critique of the referentialist tradition embedded deep at the heart of computational approaches to language, arguing that language is not a code that maps onto a pre-given world but a situated, bipartite activity oriented toward prospective joint action. Yet Integrationism leaves certain explanatory gaps: it does not fully account for the structural mechanism by which signs sustain prospective openness, it undertheorises the continuity between linguistic and non-linguistic semiotic activity, and it offers no detailed account of the structural properties of the accumulated archive of past integrations. This paper argues that Elan Barenholtz's autogenerative theory of language, developed in response to the behaviour of Large Language Models (LLMs), can fill precisely these gaps, enriching Integrationism without undermining any of its core commitments. Specifically, the autogenerative account provides: a structural mechanism for the prospective openness that Harris identifies as central to bipartite communication; a computational correlate for Harris's thesis of semiotic continuity between language and other sign-making activity; and a theory of the archive: what the accumulated residue of past integrations looks like and how new participants draw upon it. The synthesis preserves Harris's ontological primacy of the situated integrative act while adding explanatory content that Integrationism itself does not supply. For practitioners and researchers in natural language processing and large language model design, the argument offers a principled account of what the statistical structure that LLMs so effectively exploit actually is, and of what it cannot, by its nature, provide.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a synthesis between Roy Harris's Integrationist linguistics and Elan Barenholtz's autogenerative theory of language, arguing that the latter fills key explanatory gaps in the former — specifically regarding the structural mechanism of prospective openness, semiotic continuity, and the nature of the semiotic archive — while preserving Integrationism's core ontological commitments. The synthesis also offers NLP/LLM researchers a principled account of what statistical language models exploit and what they inherently lack.
AI.motivation: Integrationist linguistics, though compelling in its critique of referentialism in computational language models, suffers from three explanatory gaps: (1) no structural account of how signs sustain prospective openness, (2) underdeveloped theory of continuity between linguistic and non-linguistic semiotic activity, and (3) no detailed theory of the accumulated archive of past integrations.
