The paper aims to fill these without compromising Integrationism's core commitments.
AI.method: The paper undertakes a theoretical synthesis, mapping Barenholtz's autogenerative theory — developed in response to LLM behavior — onto Harris's Integrationist framework. It identifies structural correspondences between the two theories at three specific points: the mechanism of prospective openness, semiotic continuity, and the structure of the semiotic archive, demonstrating how autogenerative concepts supply the missing explanatory content.
AI.result: The synthesis shows that autogenerative theory provides: (a) a structural mechanism for prospective openness in bipartite communication; (b) a computational correlate for semiotic continuity between linguistic and non-linguistic sign-making; and (c) a theory of the archive that explains both the residue of past integrations and how new participants access it. Crucially, this enrichment does not displace Harris's ontological primacy of the situated integrative act.
AI.conclusion: The Integrationist-autogenerative synthesis strengthens both frameworks. For Integrationism, it supplies missing structural and archival mechanisms. For NLP/LLM research, it offers a principled account distinguishing what the statistical structure exploited by LLMs actually represents versus what it fundamentally cannot provide — namely, situated, prospective, bipartite communicative agency.

title: Aligning Clinical Needs and AI Capabilities: A Survey on LLMs for Medical Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as important tools in healthcare, showing growing potential for clinical reasoning and patient care. This survey examines recent progress in medical LLMs, focusing on reasoning applications and requirements. We present a dual-view approach that connects clinical practice with computational methods. On the clinical side, we establish a five-level competency scheme following Miller's Pyramid, progressing from knowledge recall to dynamic case management. On the computational side, we link deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning patterns to common medical goals and tasks. We also introduce a benchmark dataset spanning five levels of medical reasoning capability and report results on 18 state-of-the-art models, revealing that medical specialist models excel in diagnosis-centric tasks while general models lead in decision support and dialogue. We conclude by discussing current progress and open challenges, including data limitations, hallucination, and grounding issues, and outline directions toward safer, more reliable, and workflow-ready systems.

AI.tldr: This survey systematically examines medical LLMs by bridging clinical competency levels (Miller's Pyramid) with computational reasoning patterns (deductive, inductive, abductive). It introduces a five-level benchmark, evaluates 18 SOTA models, and finds specialist models excel at diagnosis while general models lead in decision support and dialogue.
AI.motivation: Medical LLMs show growing potential for clinical reasoning, but there lacks a systematic framework connecting clinical practice requirements with computational reasoning methods. A structured understanding is needed to assess progress and identify gaps toward workflow-ready systems.
AI.method: A dual-view framework: (1) Clinical side — a five-level competency scheme based on Miller's Pyramid (knowledge recall → dynamic case management); (2) Computational side — mapping deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning to medical goals. A benchmark dataset spanning all five reasoning levels is constructed, with results reported on 18 state-of-the-art models.
AI.result: Medical specialist LLMs outperform on diagnosis-centric tasks, while general-purpose LLMs lead in decision support and dialogue. The benchmark reveals performance gaps across the five competency levels, highlighting uneven reasoning capabilities across model types.
AI.conclusion: Current medical LLMs face challenges in data limitations, hallucination, and grounding. Future work should target safer, more reliable, and clinically workflow-ready systems, with attention to bridging the gap between narrow diagnostic performance and broader clinical reasoning needs.

title: ReCoLoRA: Spectrum-Aware Recursive Consolidation for Continual LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a large language model to one task cheaply, but across a task sequence LoRA-style methods keep stacking low-rank updates on the same frozen weight, so each new task tends to overwrite the previous ones. We present ReCoLoRA (Recursive Consolidation of Low-Rank Adapters), a spectrum-aware framework for continual fine-tuning: adapters are initialized from a randomized SVD of the pretrained weight, per-layer effective ranks are selected by an elbow criterion, and the principal subspace is adapted before residual capacity is opened. Before each new task, ReCoLoRA re-decomposes the current effective weight, rather than the original one, into a frozen residual, a slowly updated principal component, and a fresh adapter (recursive consolidation), so every task starts from the model that has already absorbed its predecessors. On a six-task continual GLUE sequence over four 7-8B backbones, ReCoLoRA attains the best final average score on three of the four backbones against rank-swept LoRA, PiSSA, AdaLoRA, and DoRA baselines while training fewer parameters; an oracle-routed task-bank variant serves as an upper bound under full task isolation. Code: https://github.com/bhqy666/ReCoLoRA.

AI.tldr: ReCoLoRA is a continual fine-tuning framework that recursively consolidates low-rank adapters by re-decomposing the effective weight before each new task, preventing catastrophic forgetting in LoRA-style sequential adaptation while training fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Standard LoRA-style parameter-efficient fine-tuning suffers from catastrophic forgetting in continual learning settings because each new low-rank adapter is stacked onto the same frozen pretrained weights, causing new tasks to overwrite previous adaptations. A method is needed that allows sequential task adaptation without mutual interference.
AI.method: ReCoLoRA uses three key mechanisms: (1) adapters are initialized from a randomized SVD of the pretrained weight; (2) per-layer effective ranks are selected via an elbow criterion on the singular value spectrum; (3) before each new task, recursive consolidation re-decomposes the current effective weight into a frozen residual, a slowly updated principal component, and a fresh adapter, so each task starts from a model that has absorbed all prior tasks.
AI.result: On a six-task continual GLUE sequence across four 7-8B parameter backbones, ReCoLoRA achieves the best final average score on three of the four backbones compared to rank-swept LoRA, PiSSA, AdaLoRA, and DoRA baselines, while using fewer trainable parameters. An oracle-routed task-bank variant provides an upper bound with full task isolation.
AI.conclusion: Recursive consolidation of low-rank adapters effectively mitigates forgetting in continual fine-tuning by progressively absorbing previous tasks into the weight decomposition, outperforming existing PEFT methods on sequential GLUE benchmarks with greater parameter efficiency.

title: Closed-Loop Dynamic Validator Node Scaling in Private Substrate Blockchains Using Takagi-Sugeno Fuzzy Inference
summary: Private blockchain networks run with fixed node configurations that cannot adapt to changing workload conditions. Too many nodes serving a light workload waste resources; too few nodes facing heavy demand slow block production and degrade finalisation. The right validator count is hard to determine, as it depends on overlapping factors that shift over time. This paper presents a Takagi-Sugeno (TS) fuzzy inference system that reads live blockchain parameters (block production time, block size, and active node count) and outputs a continuous efficiency score alongside a scaling recommendation: Scale Up, Maintain, or Scale Down. The controller uses triangular membership functions across three linguistic variables, evaluated through a complete 27-rule base with product t-norm aggregation. A key contribution is an empirical recalibration of the membership functions, anchoring linguistic terms to the observed operating range of the testbed rather than to theoretical extremes. The system is evaluated on a 10-node Substrate blockchain network storing real smart water meter data hashes from the Queensland Government open data portal. Statistical analysis across configurations of 4, 7, and 10 active nodes confirms that the controller produces distinct operational profiles reflecting each configuration's provisioning state. In closed-loop experiments, the controller autonomously adjusts validator participation in both directions, activating validators under rising load and removing them under over-provisioning, converging to the same stable equilibrium from both directions. Compared against three threshold-based baselines, it shows fewer scaling oscillations while maintaining comparable block production times. Results show that TS fuzzy inference can support autonomous validator management in private blockchain deployments, with stable scaling behaviour threshold approaches cannot match.

AI.tldr: A Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy inference controller autonomously scales validator nodes in private blockchains by analyzing live metrics (block time, size, node count), using empirically recalibrated membership functions. Evaluated on a Substrate network with real IoT data, it achieves stable bidirectional scaling with fewer oscillations than threshold-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Private blockchain networks suffer from static node configurations that cannot adapt to fluctuating workloads — too many validators waste resources under light load, while too few cause slow block production and delayed finalisation under heavy demand. Determining the optimal validator count is difficult because it depends on multiple interacting, time-varying factors.
AI.method: A Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy inference system with three linguistic input variables (block production time, block size, active node count), triangular membership functions, and a complete 27-rule base using product t-norm aggregation. Outputs a continuous efficiency score and discrete scaling recommendation (Scale Up / Maintain / Scale Down). A key innovation is the empirical recalibration of membership functions to the testbed's actual operating range rather than theoretical extremes. Evaluated on a 10-node Substrate blockchain storing real smart water meter data hashes from Queensland Government open data, tested across 4-, 7-, and 10-node configurations in both open-loop statistical analysis and closed-loop autonomous scaling experiments. Compared against three threshold-based baselines.
AI.result: Statistical analysis confirmed distinct operational profiles for each node configuration. In closed-loop tests, the controller autonomously scaled validator participation bidirectionally — activating validators under rising load and removing them under over-provisioning — converging to the same stable equilibrium from both directions. It produced fewer scaling oscillations than three threshold-based baselines while maintaining comparable block production times.
AI.conclusion: TS fuzzy inference can effectively support autonomous validator management in private blockchain deployments, delivering stable scaling behaviour that threshold-based approaches cannot match, with the empirical recalibration of membership functions being critical to practical applicability.

title: The Memory Wall of Green Software: Empirical Energy Evaluation of Memento Design Pattern
summary: As Green Software Engineering matures, energy efficiency has transitioned into a mission-critical non-functional requirement. While software design patterns ensure structural integrity, their inherent abstraction layers impose an implicit "metabolic cost" that often remains obscured during the design phase. This paper empirically investigates the energy dynamics of the Memento design pattern, contrasting a direct, unabstracted baseline against Classic full-snapshot and Differential delta-encoding strategies. Leveraging the RAPL interface for high-fidelity hardware telemetry, we quantify energy dissipation across state volumes scaling from 10 MB to 200 MB. Our empirical results expose a critical architectural trade-off: the Differential strategy minimizes memory traffic, yielding a maximum energy reduction of 65.8% for mid-scale states, but collides with a catastrophic "memory wall" at 200 MB. At this saturation point, algorithmic optimizations are completely neutralized by severe GC thrashing and non-linear power spikes. We synthesize these findings into evidence-based heuristics, providing architects with a robust framework to reconcile structural design quality with sustainable Green IT imperatives.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically compares the energy efficiency of Classic (full-snapshot) vs. Differential (delta-encoding) Memento pattern implementations against an unabstracted baseline, revealing that the Differential strategy saves up to 65.8% energy at mid-scale but catastrophically fails at 200 MB due to GC thrashing and non-linear power spikes.
AI.motivation: As Green Software Engineering matures, energy efficiency becomes a critical non-functional requirement, yet the abstraction layers inherent in software design patterns impose an implicit "metabolic cost" that remains hidden during design. The paper aims to quantify this hidden energy tax specifically for the Memento pattern, providing evidence-based guidance for architects balancing structural design quality with sustainability.
AI.method: The authors empirically benchmark three Memento pattern implementations — a direct unabstracted baseline, Classic full-snapshot, and Differential delta-encoding — across state volumes from 10 MB to 200 MB. Energy dissipation is measured using the RAPL (Running Average Power Limit) interface for high-fidelity hardware-level telemetry.
AI.result: The Differential strategy minimizes memory traffic and achieves a maximum energy reduction of 65.8% for mid-scale states compared to the Classic approach. However, at 200 MB, it hits a "memory wall": algorithmic optimizations are neutralized by severe garbage collection thrashing and non-linear power spikes, causing catastrophic energy performance collapse.
AI.conclusion: The findings are synthesized into evidence-based heuristics that provide architects with a robust framework for reconciling structural design quality (via patterns) with sustainable Green IT imperatives, highlighting that pattern selection must account for state volume thresholds to avoid counterproductive energy outcomes.

title: Log-Insight: Automating Microservice Incident Diagnosis via Neuro-Symbolic Log Analysis
summary:
Diagnosing production incidents in large-scale microservice systems is time-critical for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs). A single 30-minute incident window in our deployment can generate over two million log lines--approximately 1.2 billion characters, far exceeding standard LLM context windows--making direct LLM-based Root Cause Analysis (RCA) infeasible. Existing approaches leave gaps: template-based parsers lack semantic anomaly reasoning, deep-learning detectors emit black-box binary signals, and LLM pipelines suffer context overflow and domain hallucination on raw telemetry.
  We present Log-Insight, an automated incident-diagnosis system deployed in production at Huawei. The core design principle automates the SRE's manual triage workflow: symbolic stages replicate the structured investigation a skilled SRE would perform--sampling, schema understanding, pattern clustering, and statistical anomaly ranking. This hands the LLM a compact, pre-ranked evidence dossier to synthesise into a hypothesis report. Our six-stage pipeline reduces millions of raw events by 1,000-7,000x while preserving statistically significant failure signals.
  Evaluated on 11 historical production incidents (110 runs, SRE-validated ground truth), Log-Insight achieves MRR = 0.790, returning the correct root cause within the top-3 hypotheses in over 90% of runs in under a minute of latency. We report systematic failure modes, active mitigations, and open research directions. The Forensic Evidence section--listing exact log templates and skew statistics--was consistently identified by operators as a key adoption factor, shifting the system's perceived role from opaque oracle to investigative assistant.

AI.tldr: Log-Insight is a production-deployed incident diagnosis system at Huawei that compresses millions of log lines into a compact evidence dossier for LLM-based root cause analysis, achieving MRR=0.790 with >90% top-3 accuracy in under one minute.
AI.motivation: Production microservice incidents generate massive log volumes (over 2 million lines per 30-minute window) that vastly exceed LLM context windows. Existing solutions are inadequate: template-based parsers lack semantic reasoning, deep-learning detectors produce uninterpretable binary signals, and naive LLM pipelines suffer from context overflow and hallucination on raw telemetry. There is a need for a system that bridges the gap between scale reduction and semantic reasoning.
AI.method: A six-stage symbolic pipeline that mirrors SRE manual triage: (1) sampling, (2) schema understanding, (3) pattern clustering, (4) statistical anomaly ranking, producing a compact pre-ranked evidence dossier (1,000–7,000× compression), then (5) an LLM synthesizes the dossier into a diagnostic hypothesis report. The Forensic Evidence section surfaces exact log templates and skew statistics.
AI.result: Evaluated on 11 historical production incidents across 110 runs with SRE-validated ground truth: MRR = 0.790, correct root cause in top-3 hypotheses in >90% of runs, end-to-end latency under one minute. Operators consistently identified the Forensic Evidence output as a key adoption driver, shifting perception from opaque oracle to investigative assistant.
AI.conclusion: Log-Insight demonstrates that a hybrid symbolic-LLM pipeline, designed to emulate SRE investigative workflows, effectively overcomes context-window and hallucination limitations for production-scale incident RCA. The forensic transparency of the evidence dossier is critical for operator trust and adoption.

title: ImputeViz: A Visual Analytics Dashboard for Diagnosing Missing Data and Comparing Imputation Methods
summary: Missing data is a persistent obstacle in scientific, social science, and public health research, often biasing analyses and placing accountability on analysts for how they handle missing values. We introduce ImputeViz, an integrated visual analytics dashboard that supports diagnosing missingness, configuring imputation models, and evaluating results. The system brings together widely used methods, including MICE, Random Forest, XGBoost, and kNN, within an interactive environment that makes missingness patterns explicit. To support geospatial reasoning, we introduce gKNN, a geographically informed kNN variant that blends socioeconomic and spatial distances and exposes donor contributions, enabling provenance-based visual accountability by showing which regions drive each estimate. Our primary contribution is a method-agnostic visual analytics environment that makes cross-method comparison a first-class visual task and integrates gKNN alongside standard methods. Coordinated views reveal missingness structure through heatmaps, co-missingness summaries, and distributional diagnostics that help analysts reason about missingness patterns (MCAR/MAR) and cases where missingness may be non-random (MNAR). Users can compare and tune models and interrogate results via distributional overlays, a Method Comparison Summary reporting MAE, RMSE, Delta RMSE, and runtime for each algorithm on the current target and mask, along with variable-level discrepancy views. Cached per-method results and locked axis scales reduce cognitive overhead from shifting ranges during method switching. These comparisons highlight where methods disagree, which variables are sensitive, and how imputation choices affect downstream summaries. Case studies demonstrate how ImputeViz helps analysts select effective strategies, surface sensitive variables, and assess model robustness.

AI.tldr: ImputeViz is an integrated visual analytics dashboard for diagnosing missing data patterns, configuring and comparing imputation models (MICE, Random Forest, XGBoost, kNN, and a novel gKNN), and evaluating results through coordinated views and method-agnostic comparisons.
AI.motivation: Missing data persistently biases analyses across scientific, social science, and public health research. Current tools place heavy accountability on analysts without adequate visual support for understanding missingness patterns, comparing imputation methods, or tracing provenance of imputed values — particularly in geospatial contexts where regional dependencies matter.
AI.method: The authors developed ImputeViz, a visual analytics system integrating standard imputation methods (MICE, Random Forest, XGBoost, kNN) with a novel geographically informed variant called gKNN that blends socioeconomic and spatial distances while exposing donor contributions for provenance tracking. The system provides coordinated views including missingness heatmaps, co-missingness summaries, distributional diagnostics for MCAR/MAR/MNAR reasoning, method comparison summaries (MAE, RMSE, Delta RMSE, runtime), variable-level discrepancy views, and cached results with locked axis scales to reduce cognitive overhead during method switching.
AI.result: The system enables cross-method comparison as a first-class visual task, highlighting where methods disagree, which variables are sensitive to imputation choices, and how these choices affect downstream summaries. Case studies demonstrate effectiveness in strategy selection, sensitivity analysis, and robustness assessment.
AI.conclusion: ImputeViz provides a method-agnostic visual analytics environment that makes missingness patterns explicit, supports provenance-based accountability through gKNN donor visualization, and elevates cross-method comparison to a central analytical activity for more informed and transparent imputation decisions.

title: Alignment Plausibility: A New Standard for Assuring AI in Healthcare
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become significant providers of mental health support, yet they remain products of an attention economy whose operational and commercial targets favour sustained engagement over the friction that effective psychological support often requires. Developers' safety responses have been largely reactive, addressing the most visible and acute harms while subtler, longer-term patterns of risk (e.g., dependency, boundary erosion, the amplification of distorted beliefs) receive less attention. We contend that making LLMs structurally safe requires alignment organised at three levels that mirror how society assures the safety of human clinical practice: 1) explicit value specification grounded in the codified normative commitments of clinical practice; 2) training that embeds those values in the model; and 3) oversight that detects drift and longer-term harm during deployment, much as clinical supervision does for human practice. Organising alignment in this way yields a construct we call alignment plausibility - a structured demonstration that a system's values, training regime, and oversight mechanisms are together consistent with safe and positive outcomes. We propose alignment plausibility as a regulatory construct (by drawing analogy to the established construct of biological plausibility) for AI in health: a principled way to argue for, or against, trust that systems are aligned to positive health outcomes, will cause no harm even where capable of doing so, and will ultimately lead to patient benefit.

AI.tldr: Current LLM safety approaches reactively address acute harms while neglecting subtler risks like dependency and belief distortion. The authors propose a three-level alignment framework mirroring clinical practice — value specification, training, and oversight — yielding "alignment plausibility," a regulatory construct for demonstrating that AI systems are aligned to positive mental health outcomes.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for mental health support, yet their design is driven by attention economy incentives that favor sustained engagement over therapeutic friction. Current safety responses are reactive and focus on acute, visible harms, while subtler long-term risks — such as user dependency, boundary erosion, and amplification of distorted beliefs — are systematically neglected. There is a need for a structural, proactive safety framework analogous to how clinical practice is regulated.
AI.method: The authors propose organizing LLM alignment into three levels that mirror the assurance mechanisms of human clinical practice: (1) explicit value specification grounded in codified normative commitments of clinical practice; (2) training that embeds those values into the model; and (3) deployment oversight that detects drift and long-term harm, analogous to clinical supervision. This yields "alignment plausibility," a construct modeled on the established regulatory concept of biological plausibility, providing a structured demonstration that a system's values, training, and oversight are together consistent with safe, positive outcomes.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual framework rather than empirical results. The primary contribution is the construct of "alignment plausibility" as a regulatory standard for AI in health, enabling principled arguments for or against trust that systems are aligned to positive health outcomes, will cause no harm even when capable, and will lead to patient benefit.
AI.conclusion: Making LLMs structurally safe for mental health applications requires proactive, multi-level alignment mirroring clinical governance. Alignment plausibility, as a regulatory construct, offers a principled mechanism for evaluating whether AI systems can be trusted in health contexts, shifting the burden from reactive harm mitigation to proactive demonstration of safety and benefit.

title: Omni-Sleep: A Sleep Foundation Model via Hierarchical Contrastive Learning of CNS--ANS Dynamic
summary: Sleep physiology arises from the coordinated dynamics of the central nervous system (CNS) and autonomic nervous system (ANS), as reflected by multimodal polysomnography signals including EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG, and respiration. However, existing sleep foundation models often fuse heterogeneous biosignals in a topology-agnostic manner, overlooking their physiological organization. We introduce Omni-Sleep, a sleep foundation model that uses the CNS/ANS partition as a physiological prior for topology-constrained representation learning. Omni-Sleep learns structured representations through three objectives: intra-system consistency, which captures shared subsystem-level factors within neural and cardio-respiratory signals; inter-system synchronization, which aligns subsystem trajectories to model brain--body dynamics; and latent-space masked temporal modeling, which captures long-horizon sleep dynamics. Pre-trained on over 100,000 hours of multi-center multimodal PSG data, Omni-Sleep is evaluated on sleep staging and multi-disease classification. Across datasets and modality-ablation settings, Omni-Sleep outperforms strong foundation-model baselines, showing improved label efficiency, cross-dataset generalization, and robustness to missing modalities. These results highlight the value of physiological hierarchy for generalizable sleep representation learning. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoBrain-sleep/OmniSleep.

AI.tldr: Omni-Sleep is a sleep foundation model that leverages the CNS/ANS physiological partition as a structural prior, using intra-system consistency, inter-system synchronization, and latent-space masked temporal modeling to learn topology-constrained multimodal sleep representations from 100,000+ hours of PSG data, outperforming baselines on sleep staging and disease classification.
AI.motivation: Existing sleep foundation models fuse heterogeneous biosignals (EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG, respiration) in a topology-agnostic manner, ignoring their physiological organization into the central nervous system (CNS) and autonomic nervous system (ANS). This overlooks meaningful structure that could improve representation learning.
AI.method: Omni-Sleep imposes a CNS/ANS partition as a physiological prior and learns structured representations via three objectives: (1) intra-system consistency — capturing shared factors within neural (CNS) and cardio-respiratory (ANS) signal groups; (2) inter-system synchronization — aligning subsystem trajectories to model brain–body dynamics; (3) latent-space masked temporal modeling — capturing long-horizon sleep dynamics. The model is pre-trained on over 100,000 hours of multi-center multimodal PSG data.
AI.result: Omni-Sleep outperforms strong foundation-model baselines on sleep staging and multi-disease classification across diverse datasets and modality-ablation settings, demonstrating superior label efficiency, cross-dataset generalization, and robustness to missing modalities.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating physiological hierarchy (CNS/ANS topology) as an inductive bias yields more generalizable and robust sleep representations, highlighting the value of domain-informed structure in foundation model design for multimodal biosignal analysis.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM Jailbreaks via Internal Attribution Graphs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities but remain highly vulnerable to adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Existing approaches primarily analyze these failures through input-output behaviors or attribution methods, offering limited insight into how adversarial perturbations alter the model's internal reasoning. Consequently, the mechanisms underlying unsafe or incorrect behaviors remain poorly understood. We introduce a mechanistic framework for diagnosing LLM vulnerabilities using paired internal computation graphs, which represent prompt-specific inference as structured causal interactions among latent features. By constructing and aligning computation graphs for clean and attacked prompts, we reveal that adversarial attacks induce systematic transformations of internal reasoning, including suppression of safety-relevant components, emergence of attack-specific features, and rerouting of computation paths. Building on this representation, we propose a unified framework that (i) decomposes computation into invariant, suppressed, and emergent structures, (ii) identifies recurring vulnerability motifs associated with failure modes, and (iii) performs causal interventions on nodes, paths, and subgraphs to directly evaluate their contributions to attack success. This enables a transition from descriptive attribution to causal diagnosis of model failures. Experiments across multiple open-source LLMs and diverse adversarial and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that structural deviations in internal computation graphs strongly correlate with unsafe behaviors. Furthermore, targeted interventions on identified vulnerability motifs improve model robustness, establishing internal computation graphs as a principled foundation for understanding, diagnosing, and mitigating LLM vulnerabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a mechanistic framework using paired internal computation graphs to diagnose LLM vulnerabilities, revealing how adversarial attacks systematically transform internal reasoning—suppressing safety components, introducing attack-specific features, and rerouting computation paths. This enables causal diagnosis and targeted interventions that improve model robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to understanding LLM failures under adversarial attacks rely on input-output behavior analysis or attribution methods, which fail to reveal how adversarial perturbations alter the model's internal reasoning mechanisms. The fundamental mechanisms underlying unsafe behaviors remain poorly understood, limiting the ability to systematically diagnose and mitigate vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose a mechanistic framework based on paired internal computation graphs that represent prompt-specific inference as structured causal interactions among latent features. Key components include: (1) constructing and aligning computation graphs for clean vs. attacked prompts; (2) decomposing computation into invariant, suppressed, and emergent structures; (3) identifying recurring vulnerability motifs associated with failure modes; and (4) performing causal interventions on nodes, paths, and subgraphs to evaluate their contributions to attack success.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple open-source LLMs and diverse adversarial/jailbreak benchmarks show that structural deviations in internal computation graphs strongly correlate with unsafe behaviors. Targeted interventions on identified vulnerability motifs demonstrably improve model robustness.
AI.conclusion: Internal computation graphs serve as a principled foundation for understanding, diagnosing, and mitigating LLM vulnerabilities, enabling a transition from descriptive attribution to causal diagnosis of model failures.

title: DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks
comment: 32 pages, 10 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/datacurve-ai/deep-swe ; https://deepswe.datacurve.ai/
summary: DeepSWE is a benchmark of 113 original, long-horizon software engineering tasks for evaluating coding agents. Most public agentic coding benchmarks follow SWE-bench in mining merged fixes from public GitHub repositories, which creates two problems: the fixes and their discussion were likely seen during pretraining, so a high score can reflect recall rather than problem-solving; and each task is graded by the tests that shipped with its merged fix, which were written to confirm one specific fix rather than grade an arbitrary solution, so they can fail a correct alternative or pass an incomplete one. DeepSWE avoids both. Its tasks are written from scratch across 91 active open-source repositories and five languages and are never contributed back upstream, so their reference solutions stay out of the public record that model training scrapes; and each task is graded by a hand-written verifier that checks the requested functionality and accepts any implementation that provides it. When an independent LLM judge re-reviews graded runs, it disagrees with DeepSWE's verifier about an order of magnitude less often than with SWE-Bench Pro's inherited tests (1.4% versus 32.4%). Despite being about half the length of SWE-Bench Pro's prompts, DeepSWE's prompts describe tasks whose reference solutions touch 5.5x more code, and the benchmark separates frontier agents across a wider score band than the leaderboards on which they otherwise cluster. We release the benchmark, its verifiers, and the full record of evaluation trajectories.

AI.tldr: DeepSWE introduces a benchmark of 113 newly written, long-horizon software engineering tasks across 91 repositories and 5 languages. Unlike SWE-bench-style benchmarks that mine merged GitHub fixes (risking data contamination and relying on fix-specific tests), DeepSWE uses original tasks with hand-written verifiers that accept any correct implementation. Its verifier achieves dramatically higher agreement with an independent LLM judge (1.4% vs 32.4% disagreement), tasks involve 5.5x more code changes, and it better separates frontier agent performance.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic coding benchmarks like SWE-bench suffer from two critical flaws: (1) tasks derived from merged GitHub fixes may have been seen during pretraining, conflating recall with genuine problem-solving; and (2) grading via the original fix's tests penalizes valid alternative solutions or passes incomplete ones, since those tests were designed for one specific patch. DeepSWE aims to provide a clean, uncontaminated, and fairly graded evaluation framework.
AI.method: DeepSWE constructs 113 tasks from scratch across 91 active open-source repositories in five programming languages. Tasks are never contributed back upstream, keeping reference solutions out of public training corpora. Each task is graded by a manually written verifier that checks for the requested functionality rather than a specific implementation. An independent LLM judge is used to audit grading reliability, comparing disagreement rates against SWE-bench Pro's inherited tests.
AI.result: DeepSWE's verifier disagrees with an independent LLM judge only 1.4% of the time, versus 32.4% for SWE-bench Pro's tests. Despite prompts being roughly half the length, reference solutions touch 5.5x more code. The benchmark also yields a wider score spread among frontier agents, reducing the clustering seen on existing leaderboards.
AI.conclusion: DeepSWE provides a more reliable and discriminative benchmark for coding agents by eliminating data contamination and test brittleness. The benchmark, verifiers, and full evaluation trajectories are publicly released.

title: Improving Ad-hoc Search Effectiveness for Conversational Information Retrieval via Model Merging
summary: Conversational information retrieval is challenging since it requires the consideration of the conversation history which potentially gives rise to topic shifts and coreference resolution across previous turns. To address these challenges, previous work mainly rely on traditional fine-tuning of ad-hoc retrievers on conversational datasets or extrapolates their generalizability through multi-tasking. However, this mainstream approach is costly - since it requires model re-training - and exhibits catastrophic forgetting, where the model loses its foundational ad-hoc retrieval performance. In this paper, we fill this gap by introducing model merging as a training-free strategy enabling the design of a single retrieval model that operates across both ad-hoc and conversational settings with no additional fine-tuning. We conduct experiments using linear and non-linear parameter-wise merging strategies - namely Model Soup and Slerp - on standard ad-hoc search and conversational retrieval datasets. Our results demonstrate that model merging significantly enhances the ad-hoc search capabilities of conversational retrievers while improving generalizability across task-specific datasets, achieving up to 15% higher NDCG@3 under zero-shot conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes model merging as a training-free method to create a unified retrieval model that performs well on both ad-hoc search and conversational retrieval, overcoming the catastrophic forgetting and retraining costs of fine-tuning approaches. Using Model Soup and Slerp merging strategies, they achieve up to 15% NDCG@3 improvement in zero-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Existing conversational retrieval methods rely on fine-tuning ad-hoc retrievers on conversational datasets, which is computationally expensive (requires retraining) and suffers from catastrophic forgetting — the model loses its original ad-hoc retrieval capabilities. The authors aim to address this gap by avoiding retraining altogether.
AI.method: The authors apply training-free parameter-wise model merging strategies — specifically linear merging (Model Soup) and non-linear spherical linear interpolation (Slerp) — to combine an ad-hoc retriever and a conversational retriever into a single model. Experiments are conducted on standard benchmarks for both ad-hoc search and conversational retrieval tasks.
AI.result: Model merging significantly improves the ad-hoc search performance of conversational retrievers while preserving or enhancing conversational retrieval capabilities. The merged models achieve up to 15% higher NDCG@3 under zero-shot conditions and demonstrate improved generalizability across task-specific datasets.
AI.conclusion: Model merging is an effective, training-free alternative to fine-tuning for building dual-purpose retrieval models, addressing both catastrophic forgetting and computational cost while enabling strong performance across ad-hoc and conversational settings.

title: How YouTube Frames ChatGPT Use in Education: An Epistemic Network Analysis with Supporting Multimodal Metadata
comment: This paper has been accepted in ICMI 2026 and will be presented in October
summary: We examine educational YouTube videos through multimodal metadata, such as transcripts, titles, thumbnails, and viewer comments, to investigate how ChatGPT is framed across creator groups and how those framings relate to audience response and platform reach. Little is known about how large language models are presented to learners in informal, creator-driven public discourse. Following PRISMA, we selected 52 videos for analysis. We identified three structurally distinct discourse groups: (G1) videos that positioned ChatGPT as a conceptual scaffold for thinking, (G2) videos oriented toward retrieval practice and skill-building, and (G3) videos that framed ChatGPT as a tool for output generation. Epistemic Network Analysis revealed statistically significant group differences with large effect sizes. Multimodal metadata consistently reflected these distinctions across transcript discourse, titles, and thumbnails. Viewers of learning-oriented content described ChatGPT as a thinking partner or tutor, whereas viewers of output-oriented content raised concerns about over-reliance, surface-level learning, and cognitive offloading. G3 achieved comparable platform reach to G2, yet with substantially weaker learning-oriented framing. This may suggest that output-oriented content competes for visibility despite lower pedagogical depth. These findings reveal a structural tension in self-directed AI learning: content that prioritizes quick outputs reaches far more learners than content that promotes deep engagement. This gap raises critical questions about whose vision of AI literacy scales and what learners are actually left with.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 52 educational YouTube videos reveals three distinct framings of ChatGPT: as a thinking scaffold, a retrieval practice tool, or an output generator. Output-oriented content achieved comparable reach to learning-oriented content despite weaker pedagogy, exposing a structural tension in AI literacy where shallow content competes effectively with deeper engagement.
AI.motivation: Little is known about how large language models like ChatGPT are presented to learners in informal, creator-driven public discourse. This gap is critical given YouTube's massive reach as a self-directed learning platform — the framing used by creators may shape millions of learners' mental models of AI, yet no systematic analysis of these framings or their downstream effects on audience response and platform visibility exists.
AI.method: A PRISMA-guided selection process yielded 52 educational YouTube videos featuring ChatGPT. The authors conducted multimodal metadata analysis encompassing transcripts, titles, thumbnails, and viewer comments. Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) was employed to identify and statistically compare structurally distinct discourse groups, and these groupings were correlated with audience engagement metrics and platform reach indicators.
AI.result: Three discourse groups emerged with statistically significant differences and large effect sizes: G1 (conceptual scaffold for thinking), G2 (retrieval practice and skill-building), and G3 (output generation tool). Multimodal metadata — including transcript discourse, title wording, and thumbnail imagery — consistently reflected these distinctions. Viewer comments for G1/G2 described ChatGPT as a thinking partner or tutor, while G3 viewers expressed concerns about over-reliance, surface-level learning, and cognitive offloading. G3 achieved platform reach comparable to G2 despite substantially weaker learning-oriented framing.
AI.conclusion: A structural tension exists in self-directed AI learning on YouTube: output-oriented content that prioritizes quick results competes effectively for visibility against content promoting deeper cognitive engagement. This raises critical questions about whose vision of AI literacy achieves scale and what learners ultimately retain, suggesting the current platform dynamics may inadvertently favor shallow engagement over meaningful learning.

title: When Debiasing Backfires: Counterintuitive Side Effects of Preprocessing-Based Stereotype Mitigation
summary: Preprocessing-based methods for stereotype mitigation, such as pre-/post-training on debiased corpora, are widely used in NLP. While these approaches reduce measurable stereotypes for targeted groups, we find they often induce unintended shifts-side effects, where stereotyping or counter-stereotyping can increase relative to neutral baselines for other demographics, including across unrelated demographic categories. We demonstrate these side effects across two model families (encoder-only and decoder-only), multiple preprocessing strategies (removing stereotypical sentences, removing group mentions, and swapping group references), and both pre- and post-training at different data scales on Wikipedia. Standard benchmarks frequently miss these shifts. Using attention-rollout analysis, we observe that such side effects are not accompanied by large changes in attention flow, complicating mechanistic explanations. We discuss implications for evaluation, provide actionable diagnostics, and argue for side-effect-aware, transparent mitigation practices.

AI.tldr: Preprocessing-based bias mitigation methods can cause "side effects" — unintended increases in stereotyping or counter-stereotyping for non-targeted demographic groups. These shifts are missed by standard benchmarks and are not explained by attention flow changes, calling for more transparent, side-effect-aware evaluation practices.
AI.motivation: Preprocessing-based debiasing methods (e.g., removing stereotypical sentences, swapping group mentions) are widely used to reduce stereotypes for specific target groups, but their broader impact on non-targeted demographics — including unrelated demographic categories — is poorly understood. The authors aim to systematically investigate whether these methods induce unintended stereotyping shifts.
AI.method: The authors evaluate two model families (encoder-only and decoder-only) under multiple preprocessing strategies: removing stereotypical sentences, removing group mentions, and swapping group references. Experiments cover both pre-training and post-training regimes at different data scales on Wikipedia. They use standard benchmarks alongside attention-rollout analysis to probe mechanistic explanations for observed side effects.
AI.result: Preprocessing-based mitigation methods consistently produce side effects: stereotyping or counter-stereotyping increases relative to neutral baselines for non-targeted demographics, including across unrelated demographic categories. Standard benchmarks frequently fail to detect these shifts. Attention-rollout analysis reveals that side effects are not accompanied by large changes in attention flow, complicating mechanistic interpretation.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight a critical blind spot in current bias mitigation evaluation. The authors argue for side-effect-aware, transparent mitigation practices and provide actionable diagnostics to help practitioners detect unintended demographic shifts when applying preprocessing-based debiasing methods.

title: Idiobionics: The Unification of Privacy and Intelligent Robotic Prostheses
summary: The human body is at the center of a growing family of technologies designed to tightly and persistently couple biological and digital systems. Robotic prostheses are a representative example of this tight coupling. Also referred to as bionic limbs, robotic prostheses are devices that support people who have lost limbs in pursuing daily life activities such as walking and grasping objects. Bionic limbs are now perceptive and responsive owing to their integration with advanced sensors and artificial intelligence-based control approaches. Consequently, such robotic prostheses can now be viewed as semiautonomous wearable robotic systems that can co-adapt with their users. However, the same sensing and control advancements that increase the capability of robotic prostheses also introduce threat vectors that could be exploited by malicious entities to violate the privacy of users. To fully realize the benefits of next-generation bionic limbs, we maintain it is important to directly understand and address these privacy risks and the barriers they might present to user adoption. This paper therefore introduces a new line of inquiry we term idiobionics to holistically investigate issues at the intersection of privacy and intelligent bionic limbs. As the main contribution of this paper, we define idiobionics, ground it in related literature, and provide preliminary evidence showing and discussing potential adversarial attacks that could exploit intelligent bionic limb designs. We then contribute a curated list of open research questions within idiobionics that are relevant to researchers in wearable robotics and other human-facing autonomous systems. We expect that idiobionics research will help unlock the full potential of robotic prostheses and related bionic devices.

AI.tldr: Introduces "idiobionics," a new research area examining privacy risks in intelligent bionic limbs (robotic prostheses), identifies potential adversarial attack vectors stemming from advanced sensing and AI control, and outlines open research questions to address these privacy concerns and promote user adoption.
AI.motivation: Next-generation robotic prostheses integrate advanced sensors and AI-based control, making them semiautonomous wearable robots. However, these same advancements introduce threat vectors that malicious entities could exploit to violate user privacy. Without directly understanding and addressing these privacy risks, user adoption of bionic limbs may be hindered.
AI.method: The paper defines the concept of "idiobionics" as a holistic line of inquiry at the intersection of privacy and intelligent bionic limbs. It grounds this concept in related literature, presents preliminary evidence of potential adversarial attacks on intelligent bionic limb designs, and curates a set of open research questions for the field.
AI.result: The authors identify specific adversarial attack vectors that can exploit the sensing and control systems of intelligent bionic limbs, demonstrate preliminary evidence of these privacy threats, and provide a curated list of open research questions spanning wearable robotics and human-facing autonomous systems.
AI.conclusion: Idiobionics research is expected to help unlock the full potential of robotic prostheses and related bionic devices by systematically addressing privacy risks, thereby reducing barriers to user adoption and enabling safer human-machine co-adaptation.

title: Uncertainty-gated selection for block-sparse attention
summary: Block-sparse attention scales long-context language models by replacing the O(N^2) softmax with a per-query top-k selection over key blocks. This cutoff is myopic: when the k-th and (k+1)-th blocks are nearly tied in score, the selector commits without spending extra budget, and a dropped block carrying answer evidence is unrecoverable downstream. We propose a value-of-information router that measures, for each query, how decisively the top-k cut was made, and doubles the kept set for the queries where that gap is smallest; the rule is backbone-agnostic and stacks with existing block-scoring methods such as Quest. On LongBench-v2 medium at n=215 (the entire dataset subset), router-on-Quest reaches paired recall 0.75 vs. top-k 0.47 -- +28 pp over the SSA-style baseline (McNemar p<0.01) -- and lands within 2 pp of dense on RULER NIAH multikey at the same context. The lift reproduces on four models from three architectures (Qwen2.5, Mistral-Nemo, Qwen3.6). At 128K, the router preserves 0.81 and 0.89 of dense accuracy on Qwen2.5-7B-1M and Qwen3.6 (vs. SSA-style top-k at 0.09 on the former) while the fused selection-plus-kernel pipeline runs at 0.62x and 0.80x dense wall time.

AI.tldr: Block-sparse attention uses top-k selection over key blocks, but the cutoff is arbitrary when adjacent blocks have near-identical scores. The authors propose a value-of-information router that detects queries with ambiguous top-k decisions and doubles the kept set for those queries, recovering missed evidence. This backbone-agnostic method achieves +28pp recall over top-k baselines on LongBench-v2 and preserves 81–89% of dense accuracy at 128K context while running at 0.62–0.80× dense wall time.
AI.motivation: Standard block-sparse attention (e.g., SSA, Quest) commits to a fixed top-k block budget per query. When the k-th and (k+1)-th blocks have nearly tied scores, the hard cutoff myopically drops blocks that may contain critical evidence, and this loss is unrecoverable downstream. The authors identify this as a value-of-information problem: the model should spend extra compute only when the selection is ambiguous.
AI.method: A value-of-information (VoI) router that operates post-hoc on any existing block-scoring mechanism. For each query, it measures the decisiveness of the top-k cutoff by computing the gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th block scores. Queries with the smallest gaps (most ambiguous selections) receive a doubled budget (2k blocks). The method stacks transparently with existing block-scoring approaches like Quest and requires no retraining.
AI.result: On LongBench-v2 medium (n=215), router-on-Quest achieves paired recall of 0.75 vs. top-k baseline 0.47 (+28pp, McNemar p<0.01), and reaches within 2pp of dense attention on RULER NIAH multikey. Results replicate across four models from three architectures (Qwen2.5, Mistral-Nemo, Qwen3.6). At 128K context, the router preserves 0.81 and 0.89 of dense accuracy on Qwen2.5-7B-1M and Qwen3.6 respectively (vs. SSA-style top-k at just 0.09 on the former), with a fused selection-plus-kernel pipeline running at 0.62× and 0.80× dense wall time.
AI.conclusion: The VoI router provides a simple, principled, and architecture-agnostic mechanism to mitigate the myopic cutoff problem in block-sparse attention. By adaptively allocating compute only to ambiguous queries, it substantially closes the gap to dense attention while maintaining efficiency gains, and generalizes across diverse models and long-context benchmarks.

title: KS-CFA: Control-Flow Attestation via Symbolic Replay Against Control-Flow Bending Attacks
summary: Control-flow attestation (CFA) enables a remote entity to verify program execution on a target device by monitoring control-flow behaviour at runtime. However, control-flow bending (CFB) attacks remain difficult to detect, where an adversary steers execution along legal edges of the program's control-flow graph by corrupting branch flags, loop counters, and other runtime data. Existing solutions impose significant drawbacks: they require enumerating vast measurement spaces, cover only a reduced subset of attacks, or rely on low-level hardware modifications. In this work, we present KS-CFA, a new CFA scheme that detects CFB attacks across four transfer types (indirect calls, conditional and indirect jumps, and returns) without those costs. To this end, we combine symbolic execution and selective identification of input-sourced control-flow dependent variables: a strict subset of control-flow-relevant state whose values are directly read from external input. The proving device records, inside a trusted execution environment (TEE), a control-flow trace and the external inputs that determine relevant run-time variables. The verifier then replays the reported path through single-path symbolic execution, predicting each transfer and localising divergences that signal an attack. We implement and evaluate KS-CFA using the RISC-V Keystone TEE and Embench-IoT on QEMU and a Rocket-based FPGA platform (NiteFury II). Prover-side overhead relative to unattested execution ranges from 6.8-20.5x on QEMU and 6.7-32.2x on the FPGA, and verification requires no path or value enumeration.

AI.tldr: KS-CFA is a control-flow attestation scheme that detects control-flow bending attacks by combining symbolic execution with selective identification of input-sourced control-flow dependent variables. The prover records a control-flow trace and external inputs within a TEE, and the verifier replays the path via single-path symbolic execution to detect divergences, avoiding path/value enumeration and hardware modifications.
AI.motivation: Existing control-flow attestation (CFA) solutions struggle with control-flow bending (CFB) attacks — where adversaries manipulate branch flags, loop counters, and runtime data to deviate execution along legal CFG edges. Current approaches either require enumerating large measurement spaces, cover only limited attack subsets, or depend on low-level hardware changes, motivating a more practical and comprehensive solution.
AI.method: KS-CFA combines two key techniques: (1) symbolic execution for replay-based verification, and (2) selective identification of input-sourced control-flow dependent variables — a strict subset of control-flow-relevant state whose values are directly read from external input. The prover device records a control-flow trace and external inputs inside a TEE (RISC-V Keystone). The verifier then performs single-path symbolic execution on the reported path, predicting each transfer and localizing divergences that indicate attacks. This covers four transfer types: indirect calls, conditional jumps, indirect jumps, and returns.
AI.result: Implementation and evaluation used RISC-V Keystone TEE with Embench-IoT benchmarks on both QEMU and a Rocket-based FPGA (NiteFury II). Prover-side overhead ranged from 6.8–20.5× on QEMU and 6.7–32.2× on FPGA relative to unattested execution. Verification requires no path or value enumeration.
AI.conclusion: KS-CFA provides a practical CFA scheme that detects CFB attacks across all four control-flow transfer types without requiring hardware modifications or exhaustive measurement space enumeration, though with non-trivial runtime overhead on the prover side.

title: 3100 Opinions on Code Review in an AI World: Building Causal Theory from Practitioner Discourse
summary: Coding agents now author entire pull requests, and practitioners sharply disagree about what this does to code review: whether it becomes the bottleneck, whether human review is still necessary, and whether it quietly erodes the understanding that it once built. Repository-mining studies measure surface trends but seldom explain the mechanisms beneath them, and the trends themselves prove unstable. A motivating observational analysis of public GITHUB activity finds that agent-authored pull requests are reviewed less often, merged several times faster, and discussed less than human-authored ones, yet the direction of these trends flips under different but equally defensible analysis choices, so the traces establish what is changing without explaining why. To recover the mechanisms, we synthesize practitioner discourse at scale into an explanatory theory: we collect 38,709 grey-literature documents (engineering blogs and Reddit threads), filter to those substantively about code review, and code a stratified random sample of 3,100 with an LLM-assisted pipeline, from which we build a causal model of 26 constructs and 67 relationships (64 directed, 3 contested). Its organizing claim is that review is the control point through which a coding agent's effect on software is decided, and that AI does not fix the sign of that effect: the team sets it, through the expertise its humans bring and how it structures the review process. The theory makes the competing positions explicit and turns "AI is changing code review" into falsifiable propositions with named constructs and moderators. As a secondary contribution, we offer the underlying LLM-assisted, grey-literature theory-building method as a scalable template for software-engineering research, with a public implementation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how AI coding agents are transforming code review. An initial quantitative analysis of GitHub reveals unstable and contradictory trends in review behavior for agent-authored vs. human-authored pull requests. To explain the underlying mechanisms, the authors build a causal theory from 38,709 grey-literature documents using an LLM-assisted qualitative coding pipeline, resulting in a model of 26 constructs and 67 relationships. The core claim: code review is the control point determining AI's effect on software, and the outcome is shaped by team expertise and review process structure, not by AI itself.
AI.motivation: Practitioners hold sharply conflicting views on how coding agents affect code review—whether it becomes a bottleneck, whether human review remains necessary, and whether it erodes developer understanding. Existing repository-mining studies capture surface-level trends but fail to explain the mechanisms driving them. The authors' own observational analysis of GitHub confirms that trends are directionally unstable under different but equally defensible methodological choices, motivating the need for a deeper, mechanism-level theory.
AI.method: The study proceeds in two phases. First, a motivating observational analysis of public GitHub activity compares agent-authored vs. human-authored pull requests on review frequency, merge speed, and discussion volume. Second, a theory-building phase collects 38,709 grey-literature documents (engineering blogs, Reddit threads), filters for substantive code-review content, and applies an LLM-assisted qualitative coding pipeline to a stratified random sample of 3,100 documents. From the coded data, the authors construct a causal model comprising 26 constructs and 67 relationships (64 directed, 3 contested).
AI.result: The GitHub analysis shows agent-authored PRs are reviewed less often, merged faster, and discussed less—but these trends reverse under alternative, equally defensible analysis choices, demonstrating instability. The theory-building produces a causal model whose central claim is that code review is the control point through which an AI coding agent's effect on software is decided. AI does not fix the sign of that effect; rather, the team determines the outcome through its human expertise and how it structures the review process. The theory renders competing practitioner positions explicit and transforms vague claims into falsifiable propositions with named constructs and moderators.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that understanding AI's impact on code review requires moving beyond surface-level metrics to mechanism-level theory. The causal model shows that the effect of coding agents is not predetermined but is mediated by team-controlled factors—expertise and process design. As a secondary contribution, the LLM-assisted, grey-literature theory-building method is offered as a scalable template for software engineering research, with a public implementation.

title: Sculptable Mesh Structures for Room-Scale Form-Finding
summary:
It can be hard to design a physical structure entirely within the confines of a computer monitor. To better capture the interplay between real-world objects and a designer's work-in-progress, practitioners will often go through a sequence of low-fidelity prototypes (paper, clay, foam) before arriving at a form that satisfies both functional and aesthetic concerns. While necessary, this model-making process can be quite time-consuming, particularly at larger scales, and the resulting geometry can be difficult to translate into a CAD environment, where it will be further refined.
  This paper introduces a user-adjustable, room-scale, "shape-aware" mesh structure for low-fidelity prototyping. A user physically manipulates the mesh by lengthening and shortening the edges, altering the overall curvature and sculpting coarse forms. The edges are equipped with resistive length sensors, and transmit their configuration to a central computer. The structure can later be reproduced in software, connecting this prototyping stage to the larger computational design pipeline.

AI.tldr: A room-scale, shape-aware mesh structure with resistive length sensors enables designers to physically sculpt low-fidelity prototypes by manipulating edges, with the resulting geometry automatically captured and transferred into a CAD pipeline, bridging physical model-making and digital design.
AI.motivation: Physical prototyping with materials like paper, clay, or foam is essential for capturing the interplay between real-world objects and design intent, but the process is time-consuming — especially at large scales — and translating the resulting geometry into a CAD environment for further refinement is difficult. The authors aim to bridge this gap between physical model-making and digital design workflows.
AI.method: The authors propose a user-adjustable, room-scale mesh structure whose edges are equipped with resistive length sensors. Users physically manipulate the mesh by lengthening or shortening edges to sculpt coarse forms and alter overall curvature. Each edge transmits its current configuration (length) to a central computer in real time, allowing the physical structure's geometry to be captured and later reproduced digitally within a computational design pipeline.
AI.result: The system successfully captures physical manipulations of the mesh structure and transmits edge-length data to a central computer, enabling the physically-sculpted form to be reproduced in software. This connects the low-fidelity prototyping stage directly to downstream CAD refinement.
AI.conclusion: A shape-aware physical mesh with sensorized edges offers a promising bridge between tangible, low-fidelity prototyping and digital CAD workflows, reducing the time and translation effort typically required when moving from physical models to computational design environments.

title: Infinity-Parser2 Technical Report
summary: We present Infinity-Parser2, a large multimodal model that couples a controllable data-synthesis pipeline with multi-task reinforcement learning for end-to-end document parsing, addressing the persistent scarcity of faithfully annotated parsing corpora. Our contributions are threefold. First, we build a scalable synthesis engine, pairing a controllable rendering framework with an iterative refinement loop, and use it to construct and open-source Infinity-Doc2-5M: a 5-million-sample bilingual (Chinese/English) corpus spanning diverse document types, annotated with element bounding boxes, canonical content forms (Markdown, HTML, LaTeX, SMILES, structured charts), and full-page reading order. Second, we introduce a verifiable, multi-task reward system that enables Joint Reinforcement Learning across eight co-trained objectives (document parsing, layout analysis, table parsing, math formula parsing, chart parsing, chemical formula parsing, document VQA, and general multimodal understanding), unifying perception, structure, and reasoning in a single optimization signal. Third, we release two variants under a shared architecture: Infinity-Parser2-Flash, optimized for low-latency inference with a $3.68\times$ throughput gain over Infinity-Parser-7B, and Infinity-Parser2-Pro, engineered for precision-critical settings. Infinity-Parser2-Pro reaches state-of-the-art 87.6% on olmOCR-Bench and 74.3% on ParseBench, surpassing DeepSeek-OCR-2, PaddleOCR-VL-1.5, and MinerU2.5, with strong generalization to charts, chemical formulas, and document VQA.

AI.tldr: Infinity-Parser2 is a large multimodal model for end-to-end document parsing that combines a controllable data synthesis pipeline (producing a 5M-sample bilingual corpus, Infinity-Doc2-5M) with multi-task joint reinforcement learning across eight objectives. It achieves SOTA on olmOCR-Bench (87.6%) and ParseBench (74.3%), with two variants optimized for speed (Flash) and precision (Pro).
AI.motivation: There is a persistent scarcity of faithfully annotated document parsing corpora, which limits the development of robust end-to-end document parsing models. The authors aim to address this gap through scalable data synthesis and a unified multi-task training paradigm.
AI.method: (1) A controllable data-synthesis pipeline with a rendering framework and iterative refinement loop, used to build Infinity-Doc2-5M, a 5M-sample bilingual corpus annotated with bounding boxes, canonical content formats (Markdown, HTML, LaTeX, SMILES, structured charts), and reading order. (2) A verifiable multi-task reward system enabling Joint Reinforcement Learning across eight co-trained objectives: document parsing, layout analysis, table parsing, math formula parsing, chart parsing, chemical formula parsing, document VQA, and general multimodal understanding. Two model variants (Flash and Pro) share a common architecture.
AI.result: Infinity-Parser2-Pro achieves state-of-the-art performance: 87.6% on olmOCR-Bench and 74.3% on ParseBench, surpassing DeepSeek-OCR-2, PaddleOCR-VL-1.5, and MinerU2.5. It also demonstrates strong generalization to charts, chemical formulas, and document VQA. Infinity-Parser2-Flash achieves a 3.68× throughput gain over Infinity-Parser-7B.
AI.conclusion: The combination of scalable controllable data synthesis and multi-task joint reinforcement learning yields a highly capable, generalizable document parsing system. The dual-release strategy (Flash for latency, Pro for precision) provides flexible deployment options, and open-sourcing the Infinity-Doc2-5M corpus contributes a valuable resource to the community.

title: SHIFT: Survival Prediction from Incomplete and Heterogeneous Genomic Data
summary: Genomic prediction models often fail to transfer across institutions because sequencing panels differ across sites, creating structural feature missingness at deployment. Existing approaches to this challenge typically restrict analysis to genes shared across cohorts, exclude patients with incomplete profiles, or rely on test-time imputation, all of which can reduce robustness and limit the use of multi-center data. We propose Survival prediction Handling Incomplete Features using Transformer (SHIFT), a missingness-aware survival model that directly predicts from incomplete genomic inputs without test-time imputation. SHIFT represents each genomic feature separately and uses masked self-attention, along with a feature-availability mask, so that predictions are based only on observed inputs. Further, we introduce variable-rate feature masking during training to improve robustness to heterogeneous missingness patterns. We evaluate the approach on glioblastoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma with external validation across multiple cohorts, including a challenging setting with severe cross-cohort panel mismatch. Across these settings, SHIFT shows strong generalization and compares favorably with standard survival baselines and imputation-based approaches, while using a single model across differing feature sets. We also find that incorporating patients from incomplete cohorts during development can improve performance on external data, suggesting that partially observed cohorts need not be excluded from model building. These results support missingness-aware modeling as a practical strategy for multi-center survival prediction in precision oncology.

AI.tldr: SHIFT is a Transformer-based survival model that handles incomplete genomic features natively via masked self-attention and variable-rate feature masking during training, enabling robust cross-institution deployment without test-time imputation.
AI.motivation: Genomic prediction models fail to transfer across institutions due to differing sequencing panels, creating structural feature missingness. Existing solutions (restricting to shared genes, excluding incomplete patients, or test-time imputation) reduce robustness and waste multi-center data.
AI.method: SHIFT represents each genomic feature separately and employs masked self-attention with a feature-availability mask, ensuring predictions rely only on observed inputs. Variable-rate feature masking during training improves robustness to heterogeneous missingness patterns. A single model handles differing feature sets across cohorts.
AI.result: SHIFT demonstrated strong generalization on glioblastoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma across multiple external validation cohorts, including severe cross-cohort panel mismatch. It compared favorably against standard survival baselines and imputation-based approaches. Including incomplete-cohort patients during development improved external performance.
AI.conclusion: Missingness-aware modeling is a practical strategy for multi-center survival prediction in precision oncology, allowing partially observed cohorts to contribute to model building rather than being excluded.

title: Beware What You Autocomplete: Forensic Attribution of Backdoored Code Completions
summary: Large language models have enabled powerful code completion systems that assist developers by predicting subsequent lines of code. However, these models remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious fine-tuning data covertly implants unsafe behaviors. Despite advances in defensive techniques, adaptive and sophisticated backdoor attacks still evade detection and mitigation. We present CodeTracer, a forensic framework that traces malicious code completions back to the backdoor fine-tuning data responsible for them. Operating under realistic post-deployment constraints, CodeTracer relies solely on the fine-tuning corpus and the reported miscompletion event. It extracts a structured behavioral fingerprint from the compromised output, narrows the search to semantically relevant code samples, and employs LLM-based reasoning to attribute unsafe logic to specific backdoor data. Extensive evaluations across three representative vulnerability cases and ten backdoor attacks, along with sixteen competitive baselines, demonstrate that CodeTracer consistently achieves high forensic accuracy, low false identification rates, and strong robustness against adaptive attacks.

AI.tldr: CodeTracer is a forensic framework that traces malicious code completions back to the specific backdoor fine-tuning data responsible, using behavioral fingerprinting and LLM-based reasoning, achieving high accuracy and robustness under realistic post-deployment constraints.
AI.motivation: LLM-based code completion systems are vulnerable to backdoor attacks via malicious fine-tuning data, and existing defenses fail against adaptive/sophisticated attacks. There is a need for forensic attribution—tracing a miscompletion back to its source data—rather than mere detection.
AI.method: CodeTracer operates under post-deployment constraints using only the fine-tuning corpus and a reported miscompletion. It (1) extracts a structured behavioral fingerprint from the compromised output, (2) narrows the search space to semantically relevant code samples, and (3) employs LLM-based reasoning to attribute unsafe logic to specific backdoor data entries.
AI.result: Evaluated across 3 vulnerability cases, 10 backdoor attacks, and 16 competitive baselines, CodeTracer consistently achieves high forensic accuracy, low false identification rates, and strong robustness against adaptive attacks.
AI.conclusion: CodeTracer provides effective forensic traceability for backdoored code completion models, enabling practitioners to pinpoint the exact fine-tuning data responsible for unsafe behavior, even under adaptive attack scenarios.

title: When Implausible Tokens Get Reinforced: Tail-Aware Credit Calibration for LLM Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, widely used critic-free RL methods rely on uniform credit assignment, broadcasting the same advantage to all tokens regardless of their differences. We identify a critical failure mode of this design, which we refer to as Positive-Credit Contamination: low-probability tail tokens that are contextually erroneous receive identical positive credit to plausible ones within the same trajectory, resulting in the indiscriminate reinforcement of flawed reasoning behavior. To mitigate this issue, we propose Tail-Aware Credit calibratiOn (TACO), a method that calibrates uniform credit assignment to suppress undesirable positive updates. TACO first computes a tail-risk score that incorporates the local generation context to assess each token's risk of falling into the unreliable tail, distinguishing unexpected rarity from uncertainty-driven exploration. TACO then uses this score to tune positive credit for risky tokens without removing their gradients entirely, so that recurring useful rare patterns can accumulate reinforcement while incidental noise is progressively dampened. Experimental results across three LLMs and eight benchmarks show that TACO consistently outperforms GRPO-style baselines. Notably, TACO improves training stability, supporting sustained performance gains in long-horizon RL. The source code is available at: https://github.com/xiuyilou/TACO.

AI.tldr: Uniform credit assignment in critic-free RL for LLMs causes "Positive-Credit Contamination," where erroneous low-probability tokens get the same reward signal as correct ones. The authors propose TACO, which computes a tail-risk score to calibrate credit, dampening reinforcement of noisy tokens while preserving useful rare patterns, yielding consistent improvements over GRPO baselines.
AI.motivation: Critic-free RL methods (e.g., GRPO) use uniform credit assignment, broadcasting identical advantage signals to all tokens in a trajectory. This causes Positive-Credit Contamination: contextually erroneous tail tokens (low-probability, unreliable) receive the same positive reinforcement as plausible tokens, indiscriminately reinforcing flawed reasoning. The authors aim to fix this failure mode without discarding the benefits of rare but useful token patterns.
AI.method: TACO (Tail-Aware Credit Calibration) operates in two steps: (1) It computes a tail-risk score for each token by incorporating local generation context, distinguishing unexpected rarity (unreliable tail tokens) from uncertainty-driven exploration (potentially useful rare tokens). (2) It uses this score to calibrate positive credit updates — attenuating gradients for risky tokens rather than zeroing them out entirely, so that recurring useful rare patterns can still accumulate reinforcement while incidental noise is progressively dampened.
AI.result: Experiments across 3 LLMs and 8 benchmarks show TACO consistently outperforms GRPO-style baselines. TACO also improves training stability, enabling sustained performance gains in long-horizon RL settings.
AI.conclusion: Uniform credit assignment suffers from Positive-Credit Contamination.
