TACO effectively addresses this via context-aware tail-risk calibration, selectively dampening noisy token reinforcement. The method is lightweight, stabilizes RL training, and yields consistent gains across diverse models and benchmarks.

title: VectorizationLLM: Smart Vectorization Based AI Assistant
summary: VectorizationLLM is a specialized Large Language Model based on Google open-weight LLMs. The model is designed to assist students to learn smart vectorization, time/wave vector analysis, piecewise functions, Fourier analysis, and differential equations in MATLAB. The course application is CTEC 247: Applied Computational Analysis II by the Department of Electrical & Computer Engineering Technology at New York Institute of Technology Old Westbury. The LLM model is designed to be an instructive assistant, providing detailed explanations of concepts with examples from in-class notes without providing direct answers to questions. The model is designed with a RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) knowledge base and system prompt architecture. Examples in both code, text, and images are provided in the LLM responses.

AI.tldr: VectorizationLLM is a specialized LLM built on Google open-weight models, equipped with RAG and system prompts, designed to help students learn MATLAB vectorization, Fourier analysis, and differential equations by providing instructive explanations and examples without giving direct answers.
AI.motivation: To create an instructive AI assistant for the CTEC 247 course at NYIT that supports student learning of complex computational analysis topics in MATLAB without simply handing out answers, thereby fostering deeper understanding.
AI.method: The model is built upon Google open-weight LLMs and augmented with a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) knowledge base, system prompt architecture, and in-class notes. It delivers responses that include code examples, text explanations, and images, while explicitly avoiding providing direct answers to assignment questions.
AI.result: The system produces multimodal responses (code, text, images) that explain concepts related to smart vectorization, time/wave vector analysis, piecewise functions, Fourier analysis, and differential equations within the MATLAB environment, guiding students through in-class examples without giving direct solutions.
AI.conclusion: VectorizationLLM demonstrates a domain-specific educational application of LLMs enhanced with RAG and prompt engineering, tailored for engineering technology education where guided learning rather than answer-provision is the pedagogical goal.

title: Jet-Long: Efficient Long-Context Extension with Dynamic Bifocal RoPE
summary: Modern LLMs are increasingly deployed in long-context applications such as retrieval-augmented generation, repository-level coding, and agentic workflows whose accumulated reasoning and tool traces routinely push the input an order of magnitude past the pretraining window, making zero-shot context extension the dominant deployment path for open-weight checkpoints. Most existing zero-shot methods fix a single rescaling factor up front, so an aggressive factor sacrifices short-context fidelity while a conservative one breaks down at long contexts. We propose Jet-Long, a tuning-free zero-shot method that pairs a local RoPE-faithful window with a long-range window whose rescaling factor adapts dynamically to the current sequence length, recovering the base model exactly at short inputs while extrapolating cleanly at long ones. An inclusion-exclusion attention merge and an on-the-fly RoPE correction rotation make the bifocal construction essentially free at inference; fused into a single CuTe kernel, long-context prefill reaches up to $1.39\times$ FA2 throughput on H100 (approaching the Hopper-only FA4), and single-batch generation incurs $\le 4\%$ overhead at every length. On Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B up to 128K context, Jet-Long leads RULER by $+4.79$/$+2.18$/$+2.03$~pp over the strongest baseline at 1.7B/4B/8B, achieves the best overall accuracy on HELMET-RAG (a benchmark identified by HELMET as the most efficient predictor of downstream long-context performance) and attains the lowest PG-19 perplexity. Jet-Long also generalizes to hybrid attention architectures such as Jet-Nemotron for further long-context improvement without retraining, and remains hyperparameter-resilient for ease of deployment.

AI.tldr: Jet-Long is a tuning-free, zero-shot context extension method for LLMs that uses a bifocal RoPE strategy — a local faithful window combined with a dynamic long-range rescaling window — achieving strong short-context fidelity and long-context extrapolation with negligible inference overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing zero-shot context extension methods use a single fixed rescaling factor, creating a trade-off: aggressive factors degrade short-context performance, while conservative factors fail at long contexts. As LLMs are deployed in long-context scenarios (RAG, code, agents) far beyond pretraining windows, a method that performs well at both extremes without retraining is needed.
AI.method: Jet-Long employs a bifocal attention mechanism with two complementary windows: (1) a local window that remains RoPE-faithful (no rescaling), preserving exact base-model behavior at short sequences; (2) a long-range window with a rescaling factor that dynamically adapts to the current sequence length for smooth extrapolation. These are combined via an inclusion-exclusion attention merge with an on-the-fly RoPE correction rotation, all fused into a single CuTe kernel for efficiency.
AI.result: On Qwen3 models (1.7B/4B/8B) up to 128K context, Jet-Long outperforms the strongest baseline on RULER by +4.79/+2.18/+2.03 pp respectively. It achieves best overall accuracy on HELMET-RAG and lowest PG-19 perplexity. Long-context prefill reaches up to 1.39× FA2 throughput on H100 GPUs; single-batch generation incurs ≤4% overhead at all lengths. It also generalizes to hybrid attention architectures like Jet-Nemotron.
AI.conclusion: Jet-Long resolves the short/long context trade-off in zero-shot extension via dynamic bifocal rescaling, delivering SOTA long-context performance with minimal overhead. Its tuning-free nature, hyperparameter resilience, and compatibility with hybrid architectures make it practical for real-world deployment of open-weight LLMs.

title: Aleena: Alignment Agent for Research Software Engineering Collaborations
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. AgenticSE @ KDD '26: Agentic Software Engineering (SE 3.0): The Rise of AI Teammates, KDD 2026 Workshop
summary: Research software collaborations span meetings, informal chats, pull requests, and GitHub issues. A decision surfaced in a Slack thread, refined in a meeting, and implemented in a pull request can lose its original rationale across these artifacts, leaving domain researchers and research software engineers with divergent mental models of project intent, ownership, and scientific assumptions. We argue that alignment in research software engineering is a continuous lifecycle problem, and that agentic AI can support stakeholder alignment and project-state tracking without replacing human decision-making. We present Aleena, an open-source lifecycle alignment agent that uses GitHub as a shared collaboration surface, transforming multi-modal stakeholder interactions into structured project records that surface risks, track open questions, and preserve decision continuity. Grounded in university-based research software engineering center experiences, this paper presents the motivating problem, system design, prototype, and illustrative lifecycle scenarios for Aleena.

AI.tldr: Aleena is an open-source agentic AI system that addresses the fragmentation of decision rationale across research software collaboration channels (Slack, meetings, GitHub) by transforming multi-modal stakeholder interactions into structured project records for risk surfacing, question tracking, and decision continuity.
AI.motivation: Research software collaborations suffer from "alignment drift": decisions made across disparate channels (Slack threads, meetings, pull requests, informal chats) lose their original rationale, causing research software engineers and domain researchers to develop divergent mental models of project intent, ownership, and scientific assumptions. This is framed as a continuous lifecycle problem rather than a one-time documentation fix.
AI.method: The authors present Aleena, an open-source lifecycle alignment agent that leverages GitHub as a shared collaboration surface. It ingests multi-modal stakeholder interactions across communication channels and converts them into structured project records, surfacing risks, tracking open questions, and preserving decision continuity through the project lifecycle.
AI.result: The paper presents the system design, a working prototype, and illustrative lifecycle scenarios grounded in experiences from university-based research software engineering centers, demonstrating how agentic AI can support alignment without replacing human decision-making.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI can serve as a continuous alignment mechanism in research software engineering, preserving decision rationale and maintaining shared understanding across stakeholders without supplanting human judgment, as demonstrated through the Aleena prototype.

title: ICDAR 2026 HIPE-OCRepair Competition on LLM-Assisted OCR Post-Correction for Historical Documents
summary: We present the results of HIPE-OCRepair-2026, an ICDAR competition on LLM-assisted OCR post-correction of historical documents. OCR post-correction remains a long-standing challenge in digital heritage: large-scale collections of digitized documents are affected by legacy OCR errors, while re-digitization at scale remains impractical. Large language models (LLMs) offers a major opportunity to revisit this challenge, yet their effectiveness across languages, document types, and noise conditions - and their tendency to hallucinate - remains insufficiently understood. HIPE-OCRepair-2026 pursues two objectives: (i) to evaluate the capabilities of modern OCR post-correction systems, and (ii) to provide a reproducible evaluation framework anchored in the HIPE-OCRepair-2026 dataset, a harmonized multilingual resource consolidating existing and newly curated historical datasets. Participants were tasked with correcting noisy OCR transcripts from historical newspapers and printed works in English, French, and German (17th-20th century), working at the level of coherent transcription units (paragraphs or articles) without access to source images. The evaluation adopts a retrieval-oriented rather than diplomatic scoring approach, reflecting the practical use case of search and access over digitized collections. Four teams submitted systems ranging from zero-shot prompting to continued pre-training and fine-tuning, offering insights into the merits of different adaptation strategies. Results show that modern LLM-assisted systems can significantly improve OCR quality, but performance varies across datasets, languages, and noise levels. Over-correction on low-noise inputs emerges as a recurring challenge, highlighting the importance of evaluation beyond character error reduction. The dataset, scorer, and evaluation pipeline are publicly released to support future research.

AI.tldr: HIPE-OCRepair-2026 competition evaluates LLM-based OCR post-correction on historical documents (English, French, German, 17th–20th c.), finding LLMs significantly improve OCR quality but struggle with over-correction on low-noise inputs and exhibit performance variability across languages and datasets.
AI.motivation: Legacy OCR errors plague large-scale digitized historical collections, and re-digitization is impractical. LLMs offer a promising solution, but their cross-lingual, cross-domain effectiveness and hallucination tendencies remain poorly understood, motivating a structured competition and benchmark.
AI.method: The competition provides the HIPE-OCRepair-2026 dataset — a harmonized multilingual resource of historical newspapers and printed works with noisy OCR transcripts. Participants correct paragraph/article-level OCR output without access to source images, using approaches from zero-shot prompting to continued pre-training and fine-tuning. Evaluation uses a retrieval-oriented scoring metric rather than diplomatic transcription accuracy.
AI.result: Four teams participated. LLM-assisted systems substantially improved OCR quality, but performance varied across datasets, languages, and noise levels. A key finding is that models tend to over-correct low-noise inputs, underscoring limitations of character-error-rate-centric evaluation.
AI.conclusion: LLM-assisted post-correction is effective but not uniformly reliable; evaluation must account for over-correction and retrieval-oriented use cases. The publicly released dataset, scorer, and pipeline provide a reproducible foundation for future research.

title: Feedback Manipulation Regularization: Enabling Offline Agent Alignment for Imitation Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) research has increasingly shifted focus towards alignment, ensuring agents learn behaviors adhering to human values. While human demonstrations and feedback have proven crucial for alignment, existing approaches predominantly combine these signals using multi-stage pipelines designed for the contextual bandit framing of language generation. Yet little work explores how these complementary inputs can serve as a richer, interconnected signal for single-stage offline training in fully sequential decision-making environments. We propose Feedback Manipulation Regularization (FMR), an algorithm-agnostic method that harnesses evaluative feedback as a corrective signal to improve the alignment of imitation learning policies. We adapt Safety Gymnasium environments to be a principled testbed for alignment evaluation, demonstrating improved aptitude and up to a 98\% reduction in misalignment across a range of imitation learning algorithms. FMR remains robust in limited data regimes, even when learning from scarce aligned and uninformative noisy demonstrations.

AI.tldr: FMR is an algorithm-agnostic method that uses evaluative feedback to regularize and improve alignment of imitation learning policies in sequential decision-making settings, achieving up to 98% misalignment reduction on adapted Safety Gymnasium benchmarks while remaining robust under limited and noisy data.
AI.motivation: Current alignment approaches for RL predominantly combine human demonstrations and evaluative feedback through multi-stage pipelines designed for contextual bandit settings (e.g., language generation). Little work explores how these complementary signals can be jointly leveraged for single-stage offline training in fully sequential decision-making environments. The authors aim to fill this gap by using feedback as a corrective signal to improve imitation learning alignment.
AI.method: The authors propose Feedback Manipulation Regularization (FMR), an algorithm-agnostic approach that is applied on top of existing imitation learning algorithms. FMR harnesses evaluative feedback (e.g., human preferences, scores) as a corrective signal to regularize imitation learning policies, steering them toward aligned behavior during single-stage offline training. Safety Gymnasium environments are adapted as a principled testbed for alignment evaluation in sequential settings.
AI.result: FMR demonstrates improved aptitude and up to a 98% reduction in misalignment across a range of imitation learning algorithms on adapted Safety Gymnasium benchmarks. The method remains robust in limited data regimes, even when learning from scarce aligned demonstrations and uninformative noisy demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: Evaluative feedback can serve as an effective corrective signal to regularize imitation learning for alignment in fully sequential decision-making, without requiring multi-stage pipelines. FMR provides a simple, algorithm-agnostic mechanism that substantially reduces misalignment, offering a promising direction for single-stage offline alignment training beyond contextual bandit settings.

title: A Reliability Assessment of LALM Audio Judges for Full-Duplex Voice Agents
comment: 28 pages total (12 main body, 1 reference, 15 appendix). In main body: 2 diagrams, 3 table, 2 charts
summary: We report the empirical reliability of Gemini models as audio judges that score full-duplex agent conversations directly from the raw stereo waveform, tested across three models in the Gemini family: 2.5 Flash, 3.5 Flash, and 3.1 Pro. Our primary evidence base uses Gemini 2.5 Flash as the ground-truth model, validated against three calibrated human raters on 209 stereo sessions, scored on 8 production dimensions: 152 full-duplex conversations across 13 accent-and-condition strata, together with 57 adversarial defect-injected clips. The evidence for Gemini 2.5 Flash is consistent across three tests. (i) On 5 of 8 dimensions the LALM-human Spearman rho departs from the pairwise human-human rho by at most 0.07, and on 7 of 8 dimensions the two quantities 95 percent bootstrap confidence intervals overlap. (ii) The LALM agrees with the three-rater human mean within 1 point on 60 to 92 percent of sessions on 6 of 8 dimensions. (iii) On 45 of 48 (defect, dimension) cells the LALM is as sensitive as humans or better under Newcombe-Wilson 95 percent confidence intervals, though most of these are underpowered nulls rather than demonstrated parity. Rank-ordering ability transfers across the Gemini family: 3.5 Flash improves simple agreement to 8 of 8 dimensions, while 3.1 Pro rates several dimensions markedly lower than humans despite comparable rank correlation. A model swap should be re-validated on calibration specifically, not assumed from rank-correlation alone. We identify four areas where deployment requires care, and we estimate that human rating alone for our current evaluation cadence costs roughly two orders of magnitude more than the equivalent LALM workload. The data presented here provides a defensible empirical basis for deploying the LALM as a substitute or fourth rater on the dimensions where the evidence supports it.

AI.tldr: Gemini models, particularly 2.5 Flash, can serve as reliable audio judges (LALMs) for scoring full-duplex conversational quality directly from raw stereo audio, showing strong agreement with human raters on most evaluation dimensions, with evidence supporting deployment as a cost-effective substitute or supplementary rater.
AI.motivation: To empirically validate whether large audio-language models (LALMs) can reliably replace or augment costly human evaluation of full-duplex spoken agent conversations, addressing the two-order-of-magnitude cost disparity between human rating and automated LALM-based evaluation.
AI.method: Three Gemini family models (2.5 Flash, 3.5 Flash, 3.1 Pro) were tested as audio judges scoring raw stereo waveforms on 8 production dimensions. Gemini 2.5 Flash served as the ground-truth model, validated against 3 calibrated human raters on 209 stereo sessions comprising 152 full-duplex conversations (stratified across 13 accent-and-condition strata) and 57 adversarial defect-injected clips. Agreement was assessed via (i) Spearman rank correlation with bootstrap confidence intervals, (ii) exact agreement within 1 point of human mean, and (iii) sensitivity to injected defects using Newcombe-Wilson confidence intervals.
AI.result: Gemini 2.5 Flash showed strong human alignment: on 5/8 dimensions the LALM-human Spearman ρ differed from human-human ρ by ≤0.07; on 7/8 dimensions 95% bootstrap CIs overlapped with human-human CIs; on 6/8 dimensions the LALM agreed within 1 point of the human mean for 60–92% of sessions. On 45/48 defect-dimension cells the LALM matched or exceeded human sensitivity. Gemini 3.5 Flash achieved simple agreement on all 8 dimensions, while 3.1 Pro showed comparable rank correlation but systematically lower ratings, cautioning against assuming transferability from rank correlation alone.
AI.conclusion: The study provides defensible empirical evidence for deploying Gemini LALMs as a substitute or fourth rater on supported dimensions. However, model swaps require re-validation on calibration, not merely rank correlation, and four specific deployment pitfalls need care. LALM evaluation costs are roughly two orders of magnitude lower than equivalent human rating.

title: A Graph Neural Network Model for Real-Time Gesture Recognition Based on sEMG Signals
summary: For seemless control of advanced hand prostheses and augmented reality, accurate and immediate hand gestures recognition is essential. Surface electromyography (sEMG) signals obtained from the forearm are commonly employed for this purpose. In this paper, we present a novel approach for sEMG representation that utilizes graph networks which contain information about muscle activation patterns in the forearm. Based on these graph networks, we have developed a machine learning algorithm capable of real-time hand gesture recognition using a graph neural network. The algorithm's performance was evaluated using sEMG signals acquired from myoband, which has 8 electrodes placed around the forearm, involving 8 healthy subjects. The proposed method demonstrated an average classification accuracy of 99\%, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art techniques. The average time for both graph construction and prediction stood at 48ms utilizing a M1 pro CPU, rendering the approach well-suited for real-time applications.

AI.tldr: A novel graph network-based representation of forearm sEMG signals enables real-time hand gesture recognition with 99% classification accuracy using a graph neural network, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Accurate and immediate hand gesture recognition is essential for seamless control of advanced hand prostheses and augmented reality applications. Existing sEMG-based methods can benefit from improved representation of muscle activation patterns.
AI.method: The authors propose representing sEMG signals as graph networks that encode muscle activation patterns in the forearm. A graph neural network (GNN) is then trained for classification. Data was collected from 8 healthy subjects using a MyoBand (8 electrodes around the forearm).
AI.result: The method achieved 99% average classification accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art techniques. The combined graph construction and prediction time averaged 48ms on an M1 Pro CPU, confirming real-time capability.
AI.conclusion: Graph network representations of sEMG combined with GNNs offer a highly accurate and fast solution for real-time hand gesture recognition, suitable for prosthetic control and augmented reality.

title: Architecture Generalization with MetaNCA
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. To appear in the proceedings of the Artificial Life Conference (ALIFE 2026)
summary: Self-organization is an emergent property of life, driven by the collective behavior of individual components acting on local information. Biological neurons, through local interactions transmitted through synapses, are able to learn efficiently and can adapt their connections over an organism's lifespan. Motivated by these desirable properties of adaptability and local interaction, neural cellular automata (NCA) models have been successful at learning morphogenesis solely through local update rules, demonstrating stability over many updates and robustness to perturbations. In this work, we introduce Meta Neural Cellular Automata (MetaNCA), a framework that learns local rules which self-organize the weights of artificial neural networks. A learned rule network iteratively updates the weights of a task network using only local interactions on the computation graph. We propose a novel Weight Transformer architecture for the local rule network, which uses linear attention to aggregate signals from neighboring weights and hidden states. Once trained, the rule network generates task networks of diverse architectures without backpropagation. We show that MetaNCA generates weights for feedforward MLPs, CNNs, and ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-100, scaling to networks of 2 million parameters. We further show that MetaNCA generalizes to architectures not seen during meta-training, and that architectural diversity in the training phase strengthens this generalization.

AI.tldr: MetaNCA introduces a framework that uses neural cellular automata with a Weight Transformer architecture to self-organize neural network weights through purely local interactions, generating diverse network architectures without backpropagation and scaling to millions of parameters.
AI.motivation: Biological neural systems exhibit self-organization through local synaptic interactions, enabling lifelong adaptability. Existing neural cellular automata models have succeeded in morphogenesis tasks using local rules, but applying similar principles to self-organize artificial neural network weights — enabling learning without global optimization like backpropagation — remains an open challenge.
AI.method: The authors propose MetaNCA, which consists of (1) a learned rule network that iteratively updates the weights of a target task network using only local information on the computation graph, and (2) a novel Weight Transformer architecture employing linear attention to aggregate signals from neighboring weights and hidden states. The framework is meta-trained such that, after training, the rule network can generate weights for diverse architectures (MLPs, CNNs, ResNets) without any backpropagation at deployment.
AI.result: MetaNCA successfully generates weights for feedforward MLPs, CNNs, and ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-100, scaling to networks with 2 million parameters. The framework generalizes to architectures not encountered during meta-training, and architectural diversity during training improves this generalization capability.
AI.conclusion: MetaNCA demonstrates that purely local, self-organizing rules can effectively construct functional neural network weights at scale, bridging principles from biological self-organization and artificial neural network training, with promising generalization to unseen architectures.

title: TTHE: Test-Time Harness Evolution
summary: The behavior of an LLM agent is determined not only by the underlying model, but also by its harness: the executable program that constructs context, invokes tools, verifies intermediate results, and recovers from failures. Existing approaches optimize such harnesses before deployment, searching training or development data for a fixed agent workflow that is then frozen at test time. This limits adaptation when the test distribution, failure modes, or tool interactions differ from those seen during development. We ask whether the harness can instead be optimized during evaluation itself, using only the unlabeled execution traces the agent produces on the test inputs. We introduce Test-Time Harness Evolution (TTHE), which treats the executable harness as the state of test-time adaptation. During evaluation, TTHE maintains a population of candidate harnesses and refines them through an agentic proposer that reasons over their execution traces, without gold labels or task-specific supervision; a judge then commits an improved harness from execution-derived proxy signals, and the selected program persists to govern subsequent inputs. Crucially, TTHE does not update model weights, require gold labels, or train a separate adaptation model: solver, proposers, and judge are different roles and harnesses around the same frozen LLM, so all adaptation occurs through changes to the surrounding program. Across text-to-SQL, competitive programming, software engineering, data-science coding, and agentic tool-use tasks, TTHE improves fixed ReAct-style baseline harnesses, yielding persistent, inspectable improvements rather than a pre-searched workflow or per-query retries. These results recast test-time adaptation for LLM agents as evolution over executable control programs and identify execution-derived proxy reliability as a central challenge for robust unsupervised agent improvement.

AI.tldr: TTHE evolves LLM agent harnesses (executable control programs) at test time using execution traces as feedback, without model weight updates or gold labels, achieving persistent improvements across diverse coding and agentic tasks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent systems optimize harnesses pre-deployment, freezing workflows that cannot adapt when test distributions, failure modes, or tool interactions diverge from development data. This static approach limits robustness in real-world deployment.
AI.method: TTHE maintains a population of candidate harnesses during evaluation. An agentic proposer reasons over unlabeled execution traces to generate improved harnesses; a judge selects the best candidate using execution-derived proxy signals (e.g., runtime success, output consistency). The winning harness persists for subsequent test inputs. All components—solver, proposer, and judge—are different roles/harnesses around the same frozen LLM.
AI.result: TTHE improves over fixed ReAct-style baselines across text-to-SQL, competitive programming, software engineering, data-science coding, and agentic tool-use benchmarks, yielding inspectable and persistent gains without per-query retries or pre-searched workflows.
AI.conclusion: Test-time adaptation for LLM agents can be effectively reframed as evolution over executable control programs. Execution-derived proxy reliability emerges as the central challenge for robust unsupervised agent improvement.

title: ProjAgent: Procedural Similarity Retrieval for Repository-Level Code Generation
summary: Repository-level code generation requires implementing target functions while accounting for complex cross-file dependencies and project-specific conventions. Existing retrieval methods predominantly rely on lexical, structural, or semantic similarity, often overlooking repository functions that implement similar procedural logic despite differing in identifiers or application domains. We propose ProjAgent, a repository-level code generation system that introduces procedural similarity as an explicit retrieval signal. ProjAgent decomposes the target function into intermediate reasoning steps and employs an agentic workflow to retrieve repository functions that exhibit similar procedural behavior at each step. The retrieved procedural context is integrated with conventional semantic retrieval to construct a richer repository context for code generation. ProjAgent further incorporates a conservative static-analysis feedback loop that iteratively repairs generated code using compiler and static-analysis feedback. Evaluated on REPOCOD, ProjAgent achieves 41.14% Pass@1, outperforming existing retrieval-based baselines. These results demonstrate that procedural similarity is an effective and previously unexplored retrieval dimension for repository-level code generation.

AI.tldr: ProjAgent introduces procedural similarity as a novel retrieval signal for repository-level code generation. It decomposes target functions into reasoning steps, retrieves functions with similar procedural behavior at each step, and uses a static-analysis feedback loop to repair generated code. It achieves 41.14% Pass@1 on REPOCOD, outperforming existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval methods for repository-level code generation rely on lexical, structural, or semantic similarity, but they often miss repository functions that implement similar procedural logic — functions that solve problems similarly despite differing in naming or domain. This unexplored "procedural similarity" dimension represents a gap in current retrieval-augmented code generation approaches.
AI.method: ProjAgent operates in two main stages: (1) It decomposes the target function into intermediate reasoning steps and uses an agentic workflow to retrieve repository functions exhibiting similar procedural behavior at each step. These procedurally similar functions are combined with conventional semantic retrieval results to form a richer context. (2) A conservative static-analysis feedback loop iteratively repairs the generated code using compiler and static-analysis diagnostics.
AI.result: ProjAgent achieves 41.14% Pass@1 on the REPOCOD benchmark, outperforming existing retrieval-based baselines. The ablation and comparative results demonstrate that procedural similarity is an effective, previously unexplored retrieval dimension for repository-level code generation.
AI.conclusion: Procedural similarity — matching functions based on how they solve problems step-by-step rather than surface-level features — is a valuable and underexploited retrieval signal. Combining it with semantic retrieval and static-analysis feedback yields significant gains in repository-level code generation performance.

title: LEXIC: Lightweight Eye-tracking eXtension via Injected Complexity
summary: On the recent EyeBench benchmark, predicting reading comprehension from eye movements exposes a stark gap: text-aware models using pretrained language models reach 56--63% AUROC, while gaze-only models operate at chance. We ask how far a gaze-only model can be pushed by lightweight, language-model-free conditioning. Building on the EyeBench AhnCNN baseline, LEXIC-Base, we propose two mechanisms to inject three precomputed word-level difficulty signals, GPT-2 surprisal, word frequency, and word length, into the per-fixation input: direct concatenation, LEXIC-Concat, and a residual mechanism, LEXIC-Res, where a small head predicts typical-reader gaze response and the encoder is conditioned on the deviation. On the OneStop reading comprehension task, with K=5 seed-ensemble training across ten folds, both mechanisms produce statistically consistent AUROC gains on Unseen Text, +1.8 to +2.2 percentage points, Wilcoxon p <= 0.065. LEXIC-Concat additionally lifts Unseen Reader by +2.9 percentage points, p = 0.010. We trace an architectural boundary in LEXIC-Res on Unseen Reader, +1.8 percentage points, p = 0.19, to the prediction head being calibrated to training readers, transferring imperfectly to out-of-distribution readers.

AI.tldr: Gaze-only models for reading comprehension prediction operate at chance on EyeBench. The authors propose LEXIC, which injects word-level difficulty signals (GPT-2 surprisal, frequency, length) into a fixation-based CNN via concatenation (LEXIC-Concat) or residual deviation conditioning (LEXIC-Res). Both yield statistically consistent AUROC gains (+1.8–2.2pp) on Unseen Text; LEXIC-Concat also improves Unseen Reader (+2.9pp). LEXIC-Res underperforms on Unseen Reader due to prediction head miscalibration across readers.
AI.motivation: EyeBench reveals a large performance gap between text-aware models (56–63% AUROC) and gaze-only models (chance-level) for reading comprehension prediction. The work investigates whether lightweight, language-model-free conditioning with word-level difficulty signals can meaningfully push gaze-only model performance without relying on pretrained language models.
AI.method: Building on the EyeBench AhnCNN (LEXIC-Base), two conditioning mechanisms are proposed: (1) LEXIC-Concat — direct concatenation of three per-fixation word-level difficulty signals (GPT-2 surprisal, word frequency, word length) into the input; (2) LEXIC-Res — a residual approach where a small prediction head estimates typical-reader gaze response and the encoder is conditioned on the deviation from that prediction. Evaluation uses K=5 seed-ensemble training across ten folds on the OneStop reading comprehension task.
AI.result: Both LEXIC-Concat and LEXIC-Res achieve statistically consistent AUROC improvements on Unseen Text: +1.8 to +2.2 percentage points (Wilcoxon p ≤ 0.065). LEXIC-Concat additionally yields +2.9 pp on Unseen Reader (p = 0.010). LEXIC-Res shows a weaker +1.8 pp gain on Unseen Reader (p = 0.19), traced to the prediction head being calibrated to training readers and transferring poorly to out-of-distribution readers.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight word-level difficulty signals can meaningfully improve gaze-only models for reading comprehension prediction without language model integration. However, reader-specific calibration in residual architectures introduces brittleness under reader distribution shift, marking an architectural boundary that warrants further investigation.

title: Hallucination Self-Play: Bootstrapping Reinforced Detector via Evolved Generator
comment: Accepted to COLM 2026. Camera-ready version to appear
summary: Identifying faithfulness hallucinations in LLM-generated outputs remains challenging due to the scarcity of high-quality annotated data. Recent work relies on advanced LLMs to synthesize training data, including rationales, labels, and hallucinated claims. However, these methods treat the generator as a static component, limiting iterative improvement of the detector. To address this limitation, we introduce Hallucination Self-Play (HSP), a novel framework that enables the detector to bootstrap with an evolved generator. HSP involves two roles initialized from the same base model, a detector that assesses the faithfulness of model outputs, and a generator that produces increasingly hard-to-detect hallucinated responses. Specifically, the detector is first fine-tuned on human-labeled data and then employed as a reward model to train the generator via reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF). In turn, the evolved generator synthesizes hallucination data to further optimize the detector through rule-based reinforcement learning. Experiments on RAGTruth benchmark and two model families demonstrate that the proposed framework can progressively enhance a small LLM to match or even outperform advanced LLMs without external supervision. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Hallucination-Self-Play-50B5 .

AI.tldr: Hallucination Self-Play (HSP) is a framework where a detector and generator — initialized from the same base model — iteratively improve each other: the detector serves as a reward model to train the generator via RLAIF to produce harder hallucinations, and the generator in turn synthesizes data to refine the detector via rule-based RL, progressively boosting a small LLM to match or surpass larger LLMs without external supervision.
AI.motivation: Detecting faithfulness hallucinations in LLM outputs is hindered by scarce high-quality annotated data. Existing synthetic data approaches treat the generator as static, preventing iterative co-improvement of the detector. There is a need for a bootstrapping framework where detector and generator evolve jointly.
AI.method: HSP initializes both a detector and a generator from the same base LLM. The detector is first fine-tuned on human-labeled faithfulness data, then used as a reward model to train the generator via reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), encouraging generation of increasingly deceptive hallucinations. The evolved generator then synthesizes hallucination data, which is used to further optimize the detector through rule-based reinforcement learning. This self-play loop repeats iteratively.
AI.result: Experiments on the RAGTruth benchmark with two model families show that HSP progressively enhances a small LLM-based detector to match or even outperform advanced LLMs, without requiring external supervision beyond the initial human-labeled seed data.
AI.conclusion: HSP demonstrates that iterative self-play between a hallucination detector and generator enables small LLMs to achieve strong faithfulness detection performance, rivaling much larger models through mutual bootstrapping.

title: Agentic AI and Retrieval-Augmented Models in Straight-Through Underwriting
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to reshape actuarial practice, particularly in domains that require reasoning over unstructured documents, heterogeneous data sources, and regulated decision workflows. Actuaries now face a design space that ranges from traditional rule-based automation to large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and multi-agent ``agentic'' systems that plan, retrieve, call tools, and reflect. This paper examines how these emerging architectures can support actuarial priorities such as transparency, auditability, and human-in-the-loop governance, with a focus on straight-through decision processes. To make these ideas concrete, we develop and analyze an agentic AI framework for straight-through underwriting of small commercial Business Owner Policies (BOPs). We construct a synthetic but realistic experimental environment and compare three underwriting pipelines: (i) a single-LLM baseline, (ii) a naive RAG system, and (iii) a multi-agent ``Agentic RAG'' pipeline that combines targeted retrieval, third-party data checks, and explicit multi-step rule evaluation. The agentic system performs best overall, with the largest gains in multi-step and missing-information scenarios, where structured retrieval and reflection help the model avoid unsupported straight-through decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper explores how agentic AI architectures—specifically multi-agent systems combining LLMs, RAG, and tool use—can support actuarial straight-through underwriting, demonstrating through a synthetic BOP experiment that an "Agentic RAG" pipeline outperforms single-LLM and naive RAG baselines, especially in multi-step and missing-information scenarios.
AI.motivation: AI is reshaping actuarial practice, but actuaries must navigate a complex design space spanning rule-based automation to LLMs, RAG, and agentic systems. The paper is motivated by the need to identify architectures that satisfy core actuarial requirements—transparency, auditability, and human-in-the-loop governance—within straight-through decision processes, a domain where unstructured documents, heterogeneous data, and regulatory constraints converge.
AI.method: The authors construct a synthetic but realistic experimental environment for straight-through underwriting of small commercial Business Owner Policies (BOPs). They compare three underwriting pipelines: (i) a single-LLM baseline, (ii) a naive RAG system, and (iii) a multi-agent "Agentic RAG" pipeline that integrates targeted retrieval, third-party data checks, and explicit multi-step rule evaluation. Performance is evaluated with emphasis on multi-step reasoning and handling of missing information.
AI.result: The agentic system achieves the best overall performance. The largest gains are observed in multi-step and missing-information scenarios, where structured retrieval and reflection mechanisms prevent the model from making unsupported straight-through decisions.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI architectures that combine retrieval, tool use, planning, and reflection offer a promising path for actuarial straight-through processing, aligning with the profession's demands for transparency, auditability, and governed decision-making. The multi-agent approach materially reduces the risk of erroneous unsupported decisions compared to simpler LLM or naive RAG pipelines.

title: LiST: Lipschitz Scaling Training for Robust and Calibrated Neural Networks
summary: While accuracy, robustness, and calibration are all essential for reliable neural networks, they are often studied separately; developing models that satisfy all three simultaneously remains a central challenge. Lipschitz-constrained models guarantee robustness by design, yet the manual selection of the Lipschitz constraint L governs the resulting accuracy-robustness trade-off, and their calibration properties remain largely underexplored. In this work, we highlight a theoretical and empirical link between the enforced Lipschitz constraint and Temperature Scaling, a state-of-the-art calibration method. Specifically, we find that for a given training scheme, there exists a non-trivial value L* that yields an out-of-the-box calibrated network, and that calibration acts as a principled criterion to select a well-defined operating point on the accuracy-robustness Pareto front. Leveraging these insights, we introduce Lipschitz Scaling Training (LiST), a novel training paradigm that iteratively adjusts the global Lipschitz constant to reach this operating point. Through a margin parameter in the training loss, LiST further enables the construction of a fully calibrated Pareto front, allowing users to navigate the accuracy-robustness trade-off while remaining calibrated throughout. At convergence, LiST also enables the reintegration of calibration data into training, improving sample efficiency without sacrificing calibration. We validate LiST on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet, demonstrating competitive accuracy and robustness against constrained and unconstrained baselines, while remaining calibrated out of the box. Code is available at GitHub.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a theoretical link between Lipschitz constraints and Temperature Scaling calibration, showing that a specific Lipschitz constant L* yields naturally calibrated networks. Building on this, the authors propose LiST, a training method that iteratively adjusts the Lipschitz constant to achieve calibration automatically while navigating the accuracy-robustness Pareto front.
AI.motivation: Neural networks need accuracy, robustness, and calibration simultaneously, but these are typically studied in isolation. Lipschitz-constrained models provide certified robustness, yet choosing the Lipschitz constant involves a manual accuracy-robustness trade-off, and calibration of such models is underexplored. There is no principled criterion for selecting the operating point on the accuracy-robustness Pareto front.
AI.method: The authors first prove a theoretical connection between the enforced Lipschitz constant and Temperature Scaling, showing that an optimal L* exists for calibrated predictions. They then propose Lipschitz Scaling Training (LiST), which iteratively adjusts the global Lipschitz constant during training to converge to L*. A margin parameter in the loss enables constructing a fully calibrated Pareto front. Post-convergence, calibration data can be reintegrated into training to improve sample efficiency without losing calibration.
AI.result: LiST is validated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, achieving competitive accuracy and robustness against both constrained and unconstrained baselines while remaining calibrated out-of-the-box. The method successfully constructs calibrated Pareto fronts and demonstrates improved sample efficiency through calibration data reintegration.
AI.conclusion: Calibration serves as a principled, well-defined criterion for selecting the Lipschitz constant in Lipschitz-constrained networks. LiST enables simultaneous optimization of accuracy, robustness, and calibration, eliminating the need for post-hoc calibration methods while giving users explicit control over the accuracy-robustness trade-off in a calibrated setting.

title: zkComposer: Decomposing Proof Construction to Scale zkML
summary: Zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) enables a server to perform verifiable inference while keeping model parameters private from the client. However, existing zkML systems incur prohibitive proof-generation costs. We observe that proof generation exhibits limited parallelism; that is, prover time does not decrease significantly as the number of threads increases. This limitation is because existing systems rely on monolithic proof computation, constructing a single proof for the entire machine learning model. We introduce zkComposer, a modular proof-construction framework that unlocks an additional dimension of parallelism, in addition to the parallelism in existing proof kernels. zkComposer decomposes the zkML proof of correct inference into independent sub-proofs, each covering a subset of the computation for inference e.g., each independent sub-proof can cover a subset of contiguous layers in the ML model. Adjacent sub-proofs are cryptographically linked through shared commitments to the activations from the boundary layer. zkComposer provides the same guarantees as the monolithic proof without requiring additional linking proofs or changes to the underlying cryptographic primitives. We implement zkComposer and evaluate it on three CNNs and GPT-2. We show that, on CNN workloads, zkComposer reduces prover time and response time by up to 3.25x relative to zkCNN [1]. On GPT-2, zkComposer reduces these times by up to 4.83x relative to zkGPT [2], when partitioning along the model layers. When partitioning across both model layers and input sequences in GPT-2, we show that zkComposer reduces prover time and response time by up to 6.84x relative to zkGPT [2].

AI.tldr: zkComposer introduces a modular proof-construction framework for zero-knowledge machine learning that decomposes monolithic proofs into independent sub-proofs linked via shared commitments, achieving up to 6.84× speedup in prover time over existing zkML systems.
AI.motivation: Existing zkML systems suffer from prohibitive proof-generation costs. The key observation is that proof generation exhibits limited parallelism — simply adding more threads does not significantly reduce prover time — because these systems rely on monolithic proof computation, constructing a single proof for the entire ML model.
AI.method: zkComposer decomposes the zkML proof of correct inference into independent sub-proofs, each covering a subset of the computation (e.g., contiguous layers). Adjacent sub-proofs are cryptographically linked through shared commitments to activations at boundary layers. Critically, this requires no additional linking proofs or changes to underlying cryptographic primitives while preserving the same guarantees as monolithic proofs. Partitioning can be done along model layers and, for models like GPT-2, across both layers and input sequences.
AI.result: On CNN workloads, zkComposer reduces prover time and response time by up to 3.25× relative to zkCNN. On GPT-2 with layer-wise partitioning, it achieves up to 4.83× reduction relative to zkGPT. With partitioning across both model layers and input sequences in GPT-2, the reduction reaches up to 6.84× relative to zkGPT.
AI.conclusion: zkComposer demonstrates that modular, decomposed proof construction unlocks substantial parallelism in zkML, overcoming the scalability bottleneck of monolithic proofs without sacrificing cryptographic guarantees or requiring new primitives.

title: Simulating the Resident: Generating Executable Smart Home Schedules via LLM Personas
comment: Published in the Proc. 1st Symposium on Artificial Intelligence throughout the Human-Centered Design Process (https://dl.gi.de/handle/20.500.12116/48536). Winner of the Best Paper Award
summary: Smart homes have emerged as an important domain for HCI research, including work on usable security and privacy. Ideally, studies in these areas draw on datasets collected in real homes with real residents, capturing authentic device interactions, network traffic, and daily routines. However, creating such datasets is slow, expensive, and raises significant privacy concerns, as it requires long-term observation of people in their most private spaces. We propose using LLMs to generate diverse resident personas that interact with a simulated smart home, producing behaviorally grounded interaction schedules that can be executed on physical testbeds. We present (1) a design framework configuring simulated households across five socio-technical dimensions, (2) a multi-stage LLM pipeline that produces structured, executable device interaction schedules, and (3) a proof of concept demonstrating feasibility. As a work in progress, we aim to support scalable, privacy-conscious smart-home experimentation without relying on intrusive real-world data collection.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using LLMs to generate diverse resident personas and simulated device interaction schedules for smart home testbeds, enabling scalable, privacy-conscious experimentation without intrusive real-world data collection.
AI.motivation: Collecting real-world smart home datasets is slow, expensive, and raises significant privacy concerns due to long-term observation of residents in their most private spaces. There is a need for scalable, privacy-preserving alternatives that still capture authentic device interactions and daily routines for HCI usable security and privacy research.
AI.method: The authors propose three contributions: (1) a design framework that configures simulated households across five socio-technical dimensions, (2) a multi-stage LLM pipeline that generates structured, executable device interaction schedules from resident personas, and (3) a proof-of-concept implementation demonstrating feasibility on physical testbeds.
AI.result: The proof of concept demonstrates that the LLM-driven pipeline can successfully produce behaviorally grounded, structured device interaction schedules executable on physical smart home testbeds, validating the feasibility of the approach.
AI.conclusion: As a work in progress, the approach shows promise in supporting scalable, privacy-conscious smart-home experimentation, potentially eliminating reliance on intrusive real-world data collection while maintaining behavioral authenticity.

title: Can We Trust LLM's Logic? Quantifying Uncertainty, Coherence, and Robustness via a Graph-Based Framework
summary: Large-Language Models (LLMs) can be prone to flawed and unfaithful reasoning that decoding strategies like Self-Consistency (SC) fail to detect as they evaluate only final-answer agreement while ignoring the logical validity of intermediate steps. This raises three fundamental questions: How can we reliably quantify uncertainty in LLM reasoning? Can semantic, structural, and causal awareness select more faithful reasoning compared to naïve majority voting? and How robust is reasoning topology under adversarial conditions? To address these questions, we introduce GRAPHEVAL, a graph-based reasoning framework that re-frames uncertainty quantification (UQ) as a holistic reasoning fidelity problem. We propose a novel UQ metric, Graph Reasoning Coherence Score (GRCS), that quantifies semantic-structural consensus of the reasoning space and captures pathological mode collapse and confident hallucinations. We find that GRCS is the only metric that is consistently negatively correlated with reasoning faithfulness across both more capable and smaller models. Additionally, we introduce Graph Self-Consistency (GSC), a medoid-based decoding strategy that trades nominal accuracy for reasoning fidelity, exposing the degree to which SC is inflated by unfaithful lucky guesses in smaller models, while preserving or improving accuracy in more capable ones. Finally, through adversarial medoid ablation, we demonstrate that the GSC-selected path acts as a "load-bearing path" and forcing models away from it degrades reasoning faithfulness and, in targeted cases, causes drops in accuracy.

AI.tldr: GRAPHEVAL introduces a graph-based framework for evaluating LLM reasoning faithfulness via a novel metric (GRCS) and a medoid-based decoding strategy (GSC), showing that majority voting can be inflated by unfaithful reasoning and that medoid-selected paths are structurally load-bearing.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit flawed, unfaithful reasoning that Self-Consistency (SC) fails to detect because SC only checks final-answer agreement, ignoring the logical validity of intermediate reasoning steps. This creates a need for uncertainty quantification methods that assess reasoning fidelity holistically, accounting for semantic, structural, and causal dimensions of the reasoning process.
AI.method: The authors propose GRAPHEVAL, which constructs a reasoning graph from sampled chain-of-thought outputs. They introduce the Graph Reasoning Coherence Score (GRCS), a UQ metric quantifying semantic-structural consensus across the reasoning space, and Graph Self-Consistency (GSC), a medoid-based decoding strategy that selects the reasoning path most central to the reasoning graph, prioritizing faithfulness over nominal accuracy.
AI.result: GRCS is the only metric consistently negatively correlated with reasoning faithfulness across both large and small models. GSC exposes that SC accuracy is inflated by unfaithful lucky guesses in smaller models, while preserving or improving accuracy in more capable models. Adversarial medoid ablation shows that forcing models away from the GSC-selected path degrades faithfulness and can reduce accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning faithfulness can be better assessed through graph-based structural and semantic coherence rather than final-answer voting alone. The medoid path serves as a load-bearing reasoning structure, and GSC offers a more faithful alternative to SC, particularly valuable for smaller models where unfaithful reasoning inflates perceived performance.

title: Token-Flow Firewall: Semantic Runtime Auditing for Persistent AI Agents
summary: Persistent AI agents extend large language models (LLMs) beyond single-turn interaction into long-lived software systems. Unlike traditional chat assistants, unsafe content in these agents can propagate through persistent state, reusable skills, and tool-mediated interactions, creating a substantially larger semantic attack surface. We observe that most security-critical interactions in such agents are transmitted through natural-language token flows, including memory updates, tool arguments, retrieved files, and inter-component communications. This observation enables a new security formulation: unsafe behavior can be intercepted as risky semantic flows before reaching privileged runtime sinks. Based on this insight, we propose TokenWall, a runtime defense framework that acts as a semantic firewall over agent token flows. TokenWall performs boundary-aware semantic auditing over these flows, constructing structured source-sink audit records, applying lightweight local inspection before execution, and selectively escalating ambiguous high-risk cases to stronger arbitration modules. Unlike prior approaches that rely on sparse auditing or remote large-model oversight, TokenWall enables full-coverage pre-execution mediation while reducing remote arbitration and latency. Experiments on CIK-Bench show that TokenWall reduces attack success rate to 12.5% while maintaining a 97.4% benign executable pass rate without human confirmation. TokenWall further introduces only 0.69 seconds of additional latency on benign cases, demonstrating that semantic runtime containment can achieve a practical security-utility trade-off for persistent AI agents.

AI.tldr: TokenWall is a runtime semantic firewall for persistent AI agents that intercepts unsafe natural-language token flows before they reach privileged sinks, reducing attack success rate to 12.5% with only 0.69s added latency and a 97.4% benign pass rate.
AI.motivation: Persistent AI agents have an expanded semantic attack surface because unsafe content propagates through persistent state, reusable skills, and tool interactions — all transmitted via natural-language token flows. Existing defenses rely on sparse auditing or remote large-model oversight, which are insufficient for full-coverage protection.
AI.method: TokenWall operates as a semantic firewall over agent token flows with three key mechanisms: (1) boundary-aware semantic auditing that constructs structured source-sink audit records, (2) lightweight local inspection before execution, and (3) selective escalation of ambiguous high-risk cases to stronger arbitration modules. This enables full-coverage pre-execution mediation.
AI.result: On CIK-Bench, TokenWall achieves a 12.5% attack success rate while maintaining a 97.4% benign executable pass rate without human confirmation. It introduces only 0.69 seconds of additional latency on benign cases.
AI.conclusion: Semantic runtime containment via TokenWall demonstrates a practical security-utility trade-off for persistent AI agents, enabling effective defense without prohibitive latency or excessive false positives.

title: path_boost: A Python Package for Interpretable Graph-Level Prediction using Path-Based Gradient Boosting
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Code available at https://github.com/Claudio-Me/extended_path_boost and on PyPI (path-boost)
summary: We present path_boost, a Python package for interpretable supervised learning on graph-structured input data. The package implements PathBoost, a gradient boosting algorithm that automatically discovers predictive labeled paths within graphs during the learning process. Unlike graph neural networks, which are generally difficult to interpret, PathBoost produces an additive prediction model over path-based features that explicitly reveals which substructures drive predictions. To avoid an exhaustive enumeration of all possible paths, the algorithm iteratively selects and extends paths during learning based on their predictive power, using boosting to combine weak learners into a strong ensemble. The package supports both regression and binary classification. Key features include compatibility with scikit-learn workflows, support for custom base learners and selectors, automatic starting node selection, parallel training across anchor nodes, and built-in variable importance computation. We demonstrate PathBoost on molecular property prediction of transition metal compounds, where atoms serve as nodes and bonds as edges, and further benchmark PathBoost against an established graph neural network and a graph kernel method across six molecular datasets. The package is available on PyPI and GitHub under an open-source license.

AI.tldr: PathBoost is a Python package implementing a gradient boosting algorithm that discovers predictive labeled paths in graphs, producing interpretable additive models as an alternative to black-box graph neural networks.
AI.motivation: Graph neural networks (GNNs) achieve strong predictive performance on graph-structured data but are notoriously difficult to interpret. There is a need for graph learning methods that maintain predictive power while explicitly revealing which substructures (paths) drive predictions, avoiding exhaustive path enumeration.
AI.method: PathBoost uses gradient boosting to iteratively select and extend labeled paths in graphs based on their predictive power, combining weak path-based learners into a strong ensemble. The algorithm automatically selects starting nodes, supports parallel training across anchor nodes, and produces an additive model over discovered path features.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated on molecular property prediction of transition metal compounds and benchmarked against an established GNN and a graph kernel method across six molecular datasets, showing competitive performance with built-in interpretability.
AI.conclusion: PathBoost provides an effective, interpretable alternative to GNNs for supervised learning on graphs, with a user-friendly scikit-learn-compatible interface available as an open-source package on PyPI and GitHub.

title: Different Teachers, Different Capabilities: Sub-1B On-Device Distillation for Structured Text Enrichment
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. has a same-size non-reasoning-teacher control, a three-judge LLM-as-a-judge panel with a negative control, full-source faithfulness grading, and a per-field routing analysis
summary: High-volume structured extraction pays a large model's latency on every item, so distilling the task into a small on-device model is attractive: comparable output at a fraction of the time and cost. We measure what that distillation actually delivers, per sub-task. Each news article is mapped to one JSON object with a short summary and five categorical labels. We distill an 8B reasoning teacher (deepseek-r1:8b) into a 0.6B student (Qwen3-0.6B; QLoRA, three seeds), and add two teacher controls: a same-size non-reasoning teacher and a larger managed pipeline. A blinded, reference-free, three-judge panel scores every arm against the full article, alongside two non-distillation baselines, few-shot prompting and constrained decoding. The student runs at about 0.8 s per article against the teacher's 39 s, and recovers 58% of the base-to-teacher gap on summary quality, beating its primary baseline (constrained decoding) by +16.8 points and few-shot prompting by a secondary +4.9. A same-size non-reasoning teacher trains a student no better than the untuned base, so the summary gain follows from the teacher's reasoning nature rather than its scale. Capabilities then split by teacher: the reasoning teacher transfers writing quality and the managed pipeline transfers label diversity, while a same-size instruction teacher's students stay more grounded on the 22 short, thin-source articles in the 93-item test set (74 versus 55 faithful), where the reasoning-lineage student fabricates. That grounding difference is a consistent ordering rather than a significant aggregate effect, and the subgroup is small, so we report it as a direction. Because no single engine wins every field, the deliverable is a per-field routing map for on-device enrichment.

AI.tldr: Distilling an 8B reasoning LLM into a 0.6B on-device model for structured news extraction recovers 58% of the quality gap, with the reasoning teacher transferring writing quality while a managed pipeline transfers label diversity. A per-field routing map is proposed since no single engine excels across all sub-tasks.
AI.motivation: High-volume structured extraction from text is costly when using large models due to latency (~39s per article). Distilling into small on-device models promises comparable output at reduced time/cost, but the authors note it's unclear what distillation actually delivers per sub-task, motivating a granular, multi-dimensional evaluation.
AI.method: An 8B reasoning teacher (deepseek-r1:8b) is distilled via QLoRA into a 0.6B student (Qwen3-0.6B, three seeds). The task: map each news article to a JSON object with a summary and five categorical labels. Two teacher controls are added: a same-size non-reasoning teacher and a larger managed pipeline. Two non-distillation baselines (few-shot prompting, constrained decoding) are included. A blinded, reference-free, three-judge panel scores all arms against the full article across 93 test items (22 thin-source).
AI.result: The student runs at ~0.8s/article vs. the teacher's 39s, recovering 58% of the base-to-teacher gap on summary quality. It beats constrained decoding by +16.8 points and few-shot prompting by +4.9. The same-size non-reasoning teacher yields no improvement over the untuned base, indicating the reasoning nature—not scale—drives the gain. The reasoning teacher transfers writing quality; the managed pipeline transfers label diversity. The instruction-teacher student is more grounded on thin-source articles (74 vs. 55 faithful), but this is a consistent ordering, not a significant aggregate effect.
AI.conclusion: Distillation delivers substantial but uneven gains across sub-tasks. Since no single engine excels on every field (summary quality, label diversity, grounding), the practical deliverable is a per-field routing map for on-device enrichment, guiding which model to use for which sub-task.

title: Prompt Compression via Activation Aggregation
summary: Large language models process prompts by propagating activations through dozens of layers before generating a response. We ask whether the task-relevant information contained in an instruction prompt can be compressed into a single activation vector and re-injected into the model, replacing the original token sequence? We show this is achievable using a learned weighted sum of activations extracted at an intermediate layer and injected at an early layer of the target LLM. The compressed vector preserves task-relevant information, incurring an accuracy drop of under $2\%$ relative to full prompt processing. Beyond its practical implications, including reducing per-query computation for fixed instruction prompts without reprocessing the original token sequence, our analysis reveals structure in the activation space of LLMs: (i) mid-layer representations transfer meaningfully to early layers, suggesting a degree of cross-layer compatibility in how information is encoded; (ii) a single activation vector encodes a quantifiable and recoverable amount of semantic information; (iii) a weighted sum of activations is a robust representation compressor.

AI.tldr: LLM instruction prompts can be compressed into a single activation vector via a learned weighted sum from mid-layer activations and re-injected at an early layer, preserving task performance within 2% of full prompt processing.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether task-relevant information in instruction prompts can be distilled into a compact activation vector, eliminating the need to reprocess long token sequences for fixed instructions, and uncover structural properties of LLM activation spaces.
AI.method: Extract activations at an intermediate layer of the target LLM, compute a learned weighted sum to form a single compressed vector, and inject this vector at an early layer to replace the original token sequence.
AI.result: The compressed vector preserves task-relevant information with less than 2% accuracy degradation versus full prompt processing. Analysis reveals cross-layer compatibility of mid-to-early layer representations, quantifiable semantic information in single vectors, and robustness of weighted-sum compression.
AI.conclusion: Prompt compression into a single activation vector is both feasible and efficient, offering practical compute savings for fixed-instruction scenarios while exposing meaningful structure in LLM activation spaces.

title: INTENT: An LSTM Framework for Vehicle Intention Prediction in Intersection Scenarios with Comprehensive Ablation Analysis
summary: Vehicle intention prediction is a pivotal aspect in the agility and safety of autonomous vehicles in all driving scenarios; if genuine enhancement of autonomous vehicles are required, we need to make them adopt human interpretation of driver's intention especially in cases that require a lot of human interaction as well as complex driving behaviors like the ones at intersections, roundabouts and emergency cases such as sudden stops where vehicle intention prediction helps in taking the correct evasive action within a real time period where every second of action makes an impact and can prevent a catastrophe from taking place. In the worst case, it helps minimize the damage and make safety a priority. Intention prediction can also be used to enhance trajectory prediction (intention conditioned trajectory prediction). In this study, The INTENT framework is proposed using LSTM model to predict the vehicle's intention at intersections 2 seconds ahead of the event occurrence to predict whether the cars in intersections are going straight, turning left, or turning right. Various model experiments and ablation study are thoroughly tested on InD dataset achieving 99.71% accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes INTENT, an LSTM-based framework for predicting vehicle intentions (going straight, turning left, or turning right) at intersections 2 seconds ahead, achieving 99.71% accuracy on the InD dataset.
AI.motivation: Autonomous vehicles need human-like interpretation of driver intention, especially in complex, interactive scenarios (intersections, roundabouts, emergency stops), to enable timely evasive actions, enhance safety, and improve trajectory prediction through intention-conditioned models.
AI.method: The INTENT framework employs an LSTM model to classify vehicle intention at intersections into three categories: going straight, turning left, or turning right. The model predicts intention 2 seconds before the event occurs. Experiments and ablation studies are conducted on the InD dataset.
AI.result: The proposed INTENT framework achieves 99.71% accuracy on the InD dataset, with comprehensive model experiments and ablation studies validating the approach.
AI.conclusion: The INTENT framework demonstrates highly accurate vehicle intention prediction at intersections, underscoring its potential to improve autonomous vehicle safety and enable intention-conditioned trajectory prediction in complex driving environments.

title: Towards Efficient Large Language Model Serving: A Survey on System-Aware KV Cache Optimization
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 as a Findings paper
summary: Despite the rapid advancements of large language models (LLMs), LLM serving systems remain memory-intensive and costly. The key-value (KV) cache, which stores KV tensors during autoregressive decoding, is crucial for enabling low-latency, high-throughput LLM inference serving. In this survey, we focus on system-aware KV infrastructure for serving LLMs (abbreviated as sKis). We revisit recent work from a system behavior perspective, organizing existing efforts into three dimensions: execution and scheduling (temporal), placement and migration (spatial), and representation and retention (structural). Furthermore, we analyze cross-behavior co-design affinity and behavior-objective links, highlighting future opportunities. Our work systematizes a rapidly evolving area, providing a foundation for understanding and innovating KV cache designs in modern LLM serving infrastructure.

AI.tldr: A survey systematizing KV cache infrastructure for LLM serving across three dimensions: temporal (execution/scheduling), spatial (placement/migration), and structural (representation/retention), with analysis of cross-behavior co-design and future opportunities.
AI.motivation: LLM serving systems are memory-intensive and costly, with the KV cache being a critical bottleneck. Despite rapid LLM advancements, there is no unified framework for understanding KV cache designs from a systems perspective, motivating this survey to organize and systematize the rapidly evolving landscape.
AI.method: The authors propose a taxonomy organizing KV cache infrastructure work into three behavioral dimensions: (1) temporal — execution and scheduling; (2) spatial — placement and migration; (3) structural — representation and retention. They also analyze cross-behavior co-design affinities and behavior-objective links.
AI.result: The survey provides a structured overview of existing system-aware KV cache approaches, revealing design patterns, trade-offs, and interconnections across the three dimensions, and identifies gaps and opportunities for future research.
AI.conclusion: The sKis taxonomy offers a foundational framework for understanding and innovating KV cache designs, highlighting that future gains will come from cross-dimensional co-design rather than isolated optimizations.

title: Drift-Aware Temporal Graph Rewiring (DATGR) for Adaptive Semantic Modeling in Biomedical Text
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Published in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Conference on Artificial Intelligence (CAI 2026)
summary: Biomedical language evolves rapidly as new discoveries emerge, causing traditional text models to lose semantic fidelity over time. Static embeddings and co-occurrence graphs cannot capture such evolution, leading to performance degradation in retrieval and knowledge discovery tasks. This paper introduces a Drift-Aware Temporal Graph Rewiring (DATGR) framework that models concept evolution by dynamically updating co-occurrence edges based on estimated semantic drift. Instead of retraining embeddings for each time slice, DATGR performs lightweight, feedback-driven rewiring using a logistic update rule applied to edge weights. Evaluated on the Biomedical Multi-Relation Corpus (BIOMRC), the method achieved a mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) improvement of approximately 0.066 absolute difference (0.699 vs. 0.633) over a static baseline. Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) remained comparable (0.738 vs. 0.744), showing that drift-aware adaptation enhances link-prediction recall without a loss in precision. These results demonstrate that edge-level adaptation effectively captures temporal semantic change in evolving biomedical text while remaining computationally efficient and interpretable.

AI.tldr: DATGR dynamically rewires co-occurrence graph edges using a logistic update rule to track semantic drift in biomedical text, improving link-prediction AUROC by ~0.066 over static baselines while maintaining AUPRC.
AI.motivation: Biomedical language evolves rapidly, causing static embeddings and co-occurrence graphs to lose semantic fidelity over time. Retraining embeddings for each time slice is computationally expensive, motivating a lightweight, edge-level adaptation mechanism that captures temporal semantic shifts without full retraining.
AI.method: The DATGR framework models concept evolution by dynamically updating co-occurrence edge weights using a logistic update rule driven by estimated semantic drift. This feedback-driven rewiring avoids retraining embeddings per time slice, enabling efficient temporal graph adaptation.
AI.result: On the BIOMRC corpus, DATGR achieved a mean AUROC of 0.699 versus 0.633 for the static baseline (≈0.066 absolute improvement). AUPRC remained comparable (0.738 vs. 0.744), indicating enhanced recall without precision loss.
AI.conclusion: Edge-level, drift-aware adaptation effectively captures temporal semantic change in evolving biomedical text, offering a computationally efficient and interpretable alternative to full retraining while improving link-prediction performance.

title: CommuniWave:A Machine Learning Model for Quantifying the Degree of Temporary Informal Behavior in Urban Communities
summary: For urban managers and designers, improving the functional attributes of urban communities to enhance territorial resilience in the face of complexity and uncertainty is crucial. Currently, community planning often follows a top-down approach and lacks effective metrics to quantify informal behaviors of residents, leading to frequent conflicts with original plans. This study introduces CommuniWave, a machine learning model designed to efficiently detect and quantify the Degree of Informal Behavior (DIB) in urban communities. The model integrates a Behavior Capture Net (BCN) based on mmaction2, a self-developed YOLOv10 model (YLX), and a Behavior Eval Model (BEM) using random forest. Ultimately, by generating DIB fluctuation charts from street videos, the model facilitates dynamic monitoring, supporting urban managers in making refined decisions to enhance the overall resilience of communities.

AI.tldr: CommuniWave is a machine learning model that detects and quantifies informal resident behaviors (Degree of Informal Behavior, DIB) in urban communities using street video analysis, enabling dynamic monitoring for refined urban management and enhanced community resilience.
AI.motivation: Current top-down community planning lacks effective metrics to quantify residents' informal behaviors, causing frequent conflicts between actual usage patterns and original plans. Urban managers require data-driven tools to monitor these behaviors and improve territorial resilience under complexity and uncertainty.
