AI.method: CommuniWave integrates three components: (1) a Behavior Capture Net (BCN) based on mmaction2 for action recognition from street videos, (2) a self-developed YOLOv10 variant (YLX) for object detection, and (3) a Behavior Eval Model (BEM) using random forest to compute the Degree of Informal Behavior (DIB). The system ultimately generates DIB fluctuation charts for dynamic monitoring.
AI.result: The model produces DIB fluctuation charts derived from street video data, enabling the quantification and visualization of informal behaviors over time, which supports refined decision-making by urban managers.
AI.conclusion: CommuniWave provides a bottom-up, data-driven approach to quantifying informal resident behaviors, bridging the gap between planned design and actual community usage, and ultimately strengthening urban community resilience through dynamic, evidence-based management.

title: Deep Learning Method for Stationary Distribution of Reflected Brownian Motion
summary: The stationary distribution of reflected Brownian motion (RBM) plays an important role in the analysis of high-dimensional stochastic systems, yet closed-form solutions are known only for a few special cases. Computing important performance metrics, such as tail probabilities, is even more intractable, despite their practical relevance. In this paper, we develop a deep learning approach that accurately and efficiently learns the Laplace transform of high-dimensional RBMs based on the basic adjoint relationship (BAR). Our framework combines a careful design of the loss function, training data sampling procedure, and neural network architecture. We evaluate the proposed method on RBM instances with known ground-truth tail probabilities and demonstrate near-perfect prediction in high-dimensional settings, highlighting its potential as a general tool for analyzing stochastic systems beyond analytically tractable regimes. Our code can be found at https://github.com/zhangz73/NN4MGF.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework is proposed to learn the Laplace transform of high-dimensional reflected Brownian motion (RBM) using the basic adjoint relationship (BAR), achieving near-perfect prediction of tail probabilities where closed-form solutions are unavailable.
AI.motivation: The stationary distribution of RBM is critical for analyzing high-dimensional stochastic systems (e.g., queueing networks), but closed-form solutions exist only in rare special cases. Computing performance metrics like tail probabilities remains computationally intractable despite their practical importance.
AI.method: The authors develop a deep learning approach that learns the Laplace transform (moment generating function) of high-dimensional RBMs. The framework leverages the basic adjoint relationship (BAR) — a PDE characterization of the stationary distribution — to construct the loss function. Key contributions include careful design of the loss function formulation, a tailored training data sampling procedure, and a specific neural network architecture suited to the problem.
AI.result: The method was evaluated on RBM instances with known ground-truth tail probabilities and demonstrated near-perfect prediction accuracy in high-dimensional settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach shows strong potential as a general-purpose tool for analyzing stochastic systems beyond analytically tractable regimes. Code is publicly available.

title: Stochastic Order Learning: An Approach to Rank Estimation Using Noisy Data
summary: Rank estimation under label noise poses a fundamental challenge, as ordinal annotations often exhibit structured uncertainty rather than simple label corruption. In this paper, we reformulate rank estimation with noisy ordinal labels as a stochastic ordering problem, in which each instance is inherently associated with multiple plausible ranks instead of a single deterministic label. Based on this view, we propose stochastic order learning (SOL), a learning framework that captures ordinal label uncertainty and learns an embedding space through two complementary objectives: a discriminative loss that structures instance--centroid interactions and a stochastic order loss that enforces probabilistic ordering relations between instances. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that SOL enables reliable rank estimation under various types and levels of label noise. The source code is available at https://github.com/cwlee00/SOL.

AI.tldr: SOL reformulates noisy ordinal label learning as a stochastic ordering problem, using discriminative and stochastic order losses to capture label uncertainty, achieving reliable rank estimation under diverse noise conditions.
AI.motivation: Traditional rank estimation treats ordinal label noise as simple corruption, whereas real-world ordinal annotations exhibit structured uncertainty with multiple plausible ranks per instance. A framework that explicitly models this stochastic nature is needed.
AI.method: Stochastic Order Learning (SOL) with two complementary objectives: (1) a discriminative loss structuring instance–centroid interactions in embedding space, and (2) a stochastic order loss enforcing probabilistic ordering relations between instances.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse datasets show SOL reliably estimates ranks under various types and levels of label noise.
AI.conclusion: Framing noisy rank estimation as stochastic ordering, rather than label corruption correction, effectively captures ordinal uncertainty and yields robust ranking performance.

title: Contrastive Order Learning: A General Framework for Ordinal Regression
summary: We propose contrastive order learning (ConOrd), a contrastive learning framework for ordinal regression that integrates the strengths of contrastive learning and order learning. While contrastive learning effectively leverages all samples in a batch, it typically ignores the inherent ordering among rank labels. Conversely, order learning explicitly models label ordinality but often relies on local, margin-based comparisons, limiting its ability to capture global ordinal structure. ConOrd addresses these limitations by introducing a contrastive order loss with soft affinity and disparity weights based on rank differences, enabling fine-grained modeling of ordinal relationships across all sample pairs within a batch. Extensive experiments on a range of ordinal regression tasks, including facial age estimation, blind image quality assessment, and blind video quality assessment, demonstrate that ConOrd consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizes well across diverse ordinal regression scenarios. The source code is available at https://github.com/cwlee00/ConOrd.

AI.tldr: ConOrd proposes a contrastive learning framework for ordinal regression that uses soft affinity/disparity weights based on rank differences, enabling fine-grained modeling of ordinal relationships across all sample pairs in a batch, achieving SOTA on age estimation and blind quality assessment tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing contrastive learning methods ignore label ordering, while order learning methods rely on local margin-based comparisons and fail to capture global ordinal structure. ConOrd bridges this gap by integrating both paradigms.
AI.method: ConOrd introduces a contrastive order loss that assigns soft affinity and disparity weights proportional to rank differences between sample pairs. This allows all pairs in a batch to contribute to the loss with graded intensity, capturing both fine-grained local and global ordinal relationships simultaneously.
AI.result: ConOrd achieves state-of-the-art performance across facial age estimation, blind image quality assessment, and blind video quality assessment benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization across diverse ordinal regression scenarios.
AI.conclusion: By unifying contrastive learning with order learning through soft, rank-difference-based weighting, ConOrd effectively captures the full spectrum of ordinal relationships and sets a new SOTA for ordinal regression tasks.

title: DeepPySR -- A Symbolic Regression Framework with Dynamic Pruning, Pareto Selection, and Hierarchical Composition for Real-World Scientific Discovery
summary: Symbolic regression (SR) discovers analytical equations from data, yielding glass-box models with directly interpretable formulas, unlike black-box methods that rely on unstable post-hoc tools such as SHAP or LIME. This transparency is crucial in clinical medicine and social science, but SR faces three challenges: high-dimensional inputs, principled selection of Pareto-front formulae, and data irregularities such as multicollinearity and class imbalance. We introduce DeepPySR, which addresses these issues with a dynamic variable-pruning schedule to remove irrelevant features during search, an exponential Pareto selection criterion that eliminates trade-offs between accuracy and complexity, and a multi-layer architecture for hierarchical symbolic composition. On four Feynman physics benchmarks and seven biomedical and social-science datasets, DeepPySR outperforms PySR and baselines on body fat (R$^2$: 0.794 vs.\ 0.702), heart disease (F1: 0.898 vs.\ 0.787), student performance (R$^2$: 0.964 vs.\ 0.948), and Raine BMI (R$^2$: 0.525 vs.\ 0.370), producing interpretable formulas aligned with domain risk factors.

AI.tldr: DeepPySR enhances symbolic regression with dynamic variable pruning, an exponential Pareto selection criterion, and multi-layer hierarchical composition, outperforming PySR on physics benchmarks and biomedical/social-science datasets.
AI.motivation: Symbolic regression provides interpretable glass-box models crucial for high-stakes domains like clinical medicine and social science, but existing methods struggle with high-dimensional inputs, principled Pareto-front formula selection, and data irregularities such as multicollinearity and class imbalance.
AI.method: DeepPySR introduces three key innovations: (1) a dynamic variable-pruning schedule that removes irrelevant features during the search process; (2) an exponential Pareto selection criterion that resolves accuracy-complexity trade-offs without manual balancing; and (3) a multi-layer architecture enabling hierarchical symbolic composition of formulas.
AI.result: DeepPySR outperforms PySR and other baselines across four Feynman physics benchmarks and seven biomedical/social-science datasets: body fat (R²: 0.794 vs. 0.702), heart disease (F1: 0.898 vs. 0.787), student performance (R²: 0.964 vs. 0.948), and Raine BMI (R²: 0.525 vs. 0.370), producing interpretable formulas consistent with known domain risk factors.
AI.conclusion: DeepPySR successfully addresses key limitations of existing symbolic regression methods, delivering both superior predictive performance and interpretable, domain-aligned formulas across diverse scientific benchmarks.

title: Ensemble Diversity Optimization for Subjective Supervision
summary: Subjective NLP tasks often exhibit systematic annotator disagreement, requiring models that represent uncertainty rather than collapse it. We introduce Ensemble Diversity Optimization (EDO), a prediction-space framework that jointly optimizes ensemble weights, effective cardinality, and calibration through a unified differentiable objective. EDO learns ensemble composition and size end-to-end via Gumbel-Softmax relaxation and incorporates a signed diversity regularizer, tuned on validation data, to steer optimization toward either preserving or suppressing disagreement. This regularization prevents ensemble collapse and enables controlled navigation of the utility-calibration trade-off. The framework integrates a soft F1 surrogate, class-weighted cross-entropy to address imbalance, and reliability-weighted diversity to regulate intra-ensemble variability. Experiments on four subjective text-classification benchmarks (ArMIS, ConvAbuse, HS-Brexit, MD-Agreement) show that EDO substantially improves probabilistic calibration, reducing cross-entropy (40-78% depending on baseline) and lowering Brier scores relative to Soft-CE, Soft-MD, Top-5 Voting, and WEL, while maintaining competitive F1 and better alignment with annotator distributions. These results demonstrate that jointly optimizing ensemble structure with a signed diversity regularizer provides an efficient, model-agnostic approach for modeling human subjectivity in supervised learning.

AI.tldr: EDO is a prediction-space framework that jointly optimizes ensemble weights, size, and calibration via Gumbel-Softmax and a signed diversity regularizer, improving probabilistic calibration on subjective NLP tasks while preserving F1 performance.
AI.motivation: Subjective NLP tasks exhibit systematic annotator disagreement, necessitating models that represent uncertainty rather than collapsing it into a single ground-truth. Existing ensemble methods often suffer from ensemble collapse or poor calibration on such data.
AI.method: EDO jointly optimizes ensemble weights, effective cardinality, and calibration through a unified differentiable objective. It uses Gumbel-Softmax relaxation for end-to-end learning of ensemble composition/size, a signed diversity regularizer (tuned on validation data) to steer toward preserving or suppressing disagreement, a soft F1 surrogate, class-weighted cross-entropy for imbalance, and reliability-weighted diversity to regulate intra-ensemble variability.
AI.result: On ArMIS, ConvAbuse, HS-Brexit, and MD-Agreement benchmarks, EDO reduces cross-entropy by 40–78% (depending on baseline) and lowers Brier scores compared to Soft-CE, Soft-MD, Top-5 Voting, and WEL, while maintaining competitive F1 and better alignment with annotator distributions.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing ensemble structure with a signed diversity regularizer offers an efficient, model-agnostic approach for modeling human subjectivity in supervised learning, effectively navigating the utility-calibration trade-off.

title: Spectral Analysis of Dueling Q-Learning
summary: Q-learning is a fundamental algorithm in reinforcement learning (RL) for solving discounted Markov decision processes (MDPs) when the transition kernel is unknown. The deep Q-network (DQN) extends Q-learning by using a deep neural network for Q-function approximation, which makes Q-learning applicable to more practical high-dimensional problems. Dueling Q-learning decomposes the Q-function into a value function and an advantage function and learns the two components jointly, which can improve learning efficiency. However, the theoretical understanding of dueling Q-learning is still limited. Recent work has initiated an analysis of tabular dueling Q-learning, but existing guarantees focus on a regularized formulation and leave the pure tabular update less completely understood. This paper strengthens that line of analysis by adding a direct interpretation of the centered tabular decomposition and by establishing convergence guarantees for the unregularized, unprojected constant step-size recursion. In particular, we derive an exact switching linear system representation for deterministic dueling Q-learning and a finite-time error bound in expectation for the sampled stochastic version. The analysis clarifies how the value and advantage updates act as different gains on the action-common (value function) and action-differential (advantage function) components of the Q-function.

AI.tldr: This paper provides convergence guarantees for unregularized, unprojected dueling Q-learning with constant step-size, deriving an exact switching linear system representation and a finite-time error bound for the stochastic version.
AI.motivation: Dueling Q-learning improves learning efficiency by decomposing the Q-function into value and advantage functions, but theoretical understanding is limited—existing analyses only cover regularized formulations, leaving the pure tabular update less understood.
AI.method: The authors derive an exact switching linear system representation for deterministic dueling Q-learning and establish a finite-time error bound in expectation for the sampled stochastic version, using centered tabular decomposition with constant step-size recursion.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that value and advantage updates act as different gains on the action-common (value function) and action-differential (advantage function) components of the Q-function, providing convergence guarantees for the unregularized case.
AI.conclusion: The paper strengthens the theoretical foundation of dueling Q-learning by addressing the gap in understanding of pure tabular updates without regularization or projection.

title: Eigenvalue Calibration for Semantic Embeddings of Large Language Models
summary: Uncertainty quantification is central to the reliable deployment of large language models (LLMs), and eigenvalues of semantic embeddings have recently emerged as a key tool in state-of-the-art methods. However, conventional calibration results developed for classification probabilities cannot be directly transferred to eigenvalues. We address this gap by proposing a novel framework for calibrating the eigenvalues of semantic embeddings. We interpret LLMs combined with semantic embeddings of their generated answers as density matrix predictors, and we propose a novel approach to calibrate density matrix predictors by applying temperature scaling to their eigenvalues. We establish entropy-risk equivalence under calibration, derive a central calibration inequality specific to eigenvalues, and prove that temperature-scaled eigenvalues optimize calibration when minimizing proper score risks. Experiments on a variety of real-world settings show that current LLMs are systematically overconfident, and validate our theoretical findings. Together, these results advance the foundations and practice of uncertainty quantification for semantic embeddings.

AI.tldr: A framework for calibrating eigenvalues of semantic embeddings from LLMs using temperature scaling, with theoretical guarantees (entropy-risk equivalence, calibration inequality, optimality under proper scores) and empirical validation showing systematic overconfidence in current LLMs.
AI.motivation: Eigenvalues of semantic embeddings are increasingly used for uncertainty quantification in LLMs, but existing calibration techniques designed for classification probabilities cannot be directly applied to eigenvalue settings. This creates a gap in ensuring reliable confidence estimates from LLM semantic embeddings.
AI.method: The authors reinterpret LLMs with semantic embeddings as density matrix predictors. They propose temperature scaling applied specifically to eigenvalues of these density matrices. The framework derives three key theoretical results: (1) entropy-risk equivalence under calibration, (2) a central calibration inequality for eigenvalues, and (3) a proof that temperature-scaled eigenvalues are optimal for calibration when minimizing proper score risks.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse real-world settings reveal that current LLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence. The temperature-scaled eigenvalue calibration method validates the theoretical findings, demonstrating improved calibration of semantic embedding-based uncertainty estimates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework advances both the theoretical foundations and practical methodology for uncertainty quantification in semantic embeddings, bridging the gap between classical calibration theory and modern LLM embedding-based approaches.

title: Beyond Backpropagation: Monte Carlo Method Can Train Deep Neural Networks
summary: Backpropagation (BP) dominates deep learning training, but its reliance on gradients brings inherent troubles -- vanishing and exploding gradients. The pursuit of gradient-free methods has long been a goal in the field of artificial intelligence. This paper shows that indeed the simplest Monte Carlo algorithm implemented on a single GPU -- randomly mutate a parameter, keep it if the loss decreases, otherwise retry -- can practically train deep networks. This gradient-free method does not even need common techniques such as batch normalization or residual connections to directly train sufficiently deep networks. More remarkably, its flexibility extends to several nontrivial scenarios: it enables pure pruning training, supports discrete weights, accommodates unconventional transfer functions such as Gaussian, and reveals the substantial redundancy of deep networks. We have demonstrated its feasibility on deep networks with more than 20 layers, single-hidden-layer wide networks with up to 16,384 hidden neurons, and even a simple Transformer architecture trained on both image classification (MNIST) and character-level language modeling (Tiny Shakespeare). This simple gradient-free method may offer a complementary perspective for understanding the self-organization and learning mechanisms of neural networks, and also provides an alternative route for building physically inspired deep learning systems.

AI.tldr: A simple random-mutation Monte Carlo algorithm, without gradients, can effectively train deep networks (20+ layers, wide networks, Transformers) on MNIST and Tiny Shakespeare, and supports pruning, discrete weights, and unconventional transfer functions.
AI.motivation: Backpropagation suffers from vanishing/exploding gradients. The authors pursue a long-standing goal of gradient-free deep learning training to overcome these limitations and explore alternative learning mechanisms.
AI.method: A gradient-free Monte Carlo method: randomly mutate a parameter, keep the mutation if loss decreases, otherwise retry. Implemented on a single GPU, with no batch normalization or residual connections required. Extended to pruning, discrete weights, and non-standard activation functions (e.g., Gaussian).
AI.result: Successfully trained deep networks with 20+ layers, wide networks with up to 16,384 hidden neurons, and a simple Transformer on MNIST image classification and Tiny Shakespeare character-level language modeling. Demonstrated flexibility across pruning, discrete weights, and unconventional transfer functions, while revealing substantial network redundancy.
AI.conclusion: This gradient-free Monte Carlo approach offers a complementary perspective on neural network self-organization and learning, and provides an alternative pathway for physically inspired deep learning systems.

title: Frequency-Domain Multi-Modality Transportation Modeling
summary: Multi-modality transportation refers to urban systems composed of multiple transportation modes, such as traffic flow and public transit, whose dynamics are coupled by shared temporal patterns. Accurate multi-modality transportation forecasting remains challenging because (1) different modalities exhibit distinct spectral characteristics and (2) interact unevenly across frequencies, whereas most existing methods operate primarily in the time domain or rely on coarse feature fusion. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight yet effective Frequency-Domain Multi-Modality modeling (FreMo) that explicitly exploits the frequency domain to enable adaptive and selective cross-modality synergy. FreMo disentangles modality-wise spectral refinement from cross-modality synergy and supports plug-and-play integration with general time series backbones. Specifically, FreMo introduces a Modality-Wise Frequency Filter (MFF) to adaptively refine spectral components within each modality, emphasizing informative frequencies while suppressing noise. FreMo further incorporates a Frequency-Guided Synergy Integrator (FSI) that selectively aggregates information across modalities based on their relative contribution at each frequency, facilitating effective cross-modality knowledge sharing while mitigating negative transfer. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that FreMo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with superior performance and generalization across diverse forecasting scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/beginner-sketch/FreMo.

AI.tldr: FreMo is a lightweight frequency-domain framework for multi-modality transportation forecasting that disentangles per-modality spectral refinement from cross-modality synergy via a Modality-Wise Frequency Filter (MFF) and a Frequency-Guided Synergy Integrator (FSI), achieving SOTA performance with plug-and-play compatibility.
AI.motivation: Multi-modality transportation forecasting is challenging because different modalities (e.g., traffic flow, public transit) exhibit distinct spectral characteristics and interact unevenly across frequencies. Existing methods primarily operate in the time domain or use coarse feature fusion, failing to capture these nuanced frequency-domain interactions.
AI.method: FreMo operates in the frequency domain with two core components: (1) Modality-Wise Frequency Filter (MFF) that adaptively refines spectral components within each modality by emphasizing informative frequencies and suppressing noise; (2) Frequency-Guided Synergy Integrator (FSI) that selectively aggregates cross-modality information based on relative contribution at each frequency, enabling effective knowledge sharing while mitigating negative transfer. The framework supports plug-and-play integration with general time series backbones.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that FreMo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving superior performance and strong generalization across diverse forecasting scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Explicit frequency-domain modeling with adaptive, frequency-selective cross-modality synergy provides a lightweight yet highly effective approach for multi-modality transportation forecasting, surpassing time-domain and coarse fusion methods.

title: CAAD: Causality-Aware Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Multi-Scale Alignment and Structural Causal Consistency
summary:
The operational integrity of complex industrial systems relies on precise anomaly detection and diagnosis. The vast majority of existing methods narrowly focus on capturing temporal similarities of representations, often overlooking the disruption of internal causal relationships, which characterizes system failures and latent anomalies. In this paper, we propose a novel framework (CAAD) that reframes anomaly detection as the continuous verification of Granger causality consistency through exogenous variables.
  Specifically, the CAAD framework models exogenous time-series variables as residuals, identifying anomalies as significant deviations caused by external interventions. The proposed framework leverages multi-scale alignment to internalize system dynamics and utilizes a gradient-based matrix to monitor internal causal relationship breakdowns. By quantifying causal deviations of both dynamic evolution and relational topology, the CAAD is able to capture subtle causal shifts to achieve precise anomaly detection. Extensive experiments on real-world industrial datasets demonstrate that the CAAD achieves high-precision anomaly detection, outperforming most state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: CAAD reframes industrial anomaly detection as continuous verification of Granger causality consistency, modeling exogenous variables as residuals and using multi-scale alignment with gradient-based matrices to detect causal relationship breakdowns, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing anomaly detection methods focus narrowly on temporal similarity of representations, overlooking disruptions in internal causal relationships that characterize system failures and latent anomalies.
AI.method: CAAD framework models exogenous time-series variables as residuals, identifies anomalies as deviations from external interventions, employs multi-scale alignment to internalize system dynamics, and uses a gradient-based matrix to monitor internal causal relationship breakdowns. It quantifies causal deviations in both dynamic evolution and relational topology.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world industrial datasets show CAAD achieves high-precision anomaly detection and outperforms most state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: By reframing anomaly detection through the lens of Granger causality consistency, CAAD effectively captures subtle causal shifts, enabling precise detection of anomalies in complex industrial systems.

title: Steering Neural Network Training through Interpretable Constraints Based on Partial Dependence
summary: Over the last few years, there has been an increased interest in making machine learning models more interpretable. Although a great deal of effort goes into developing techniques for interpreting the interactions learned by a given model, fewer studies focus on assessing the quality of such explanations. Even fewer focus on how to adjust the model to produce explanations faithful to prior knowledge, a process known as explanation-guided learning. Furthermore, most approaches in this area focus on classification problems and usually assume prior knowledge about which input features or regions are most important. In this work, we introduce a new approach to steering neural networks based on partial dependence, such that their average response to certain features aligns with specific functional domain knowledge about the problem. We empirically demonstrate on a range of regression problems, including dynamical systems forecasting, that models whose training has been controlled using our method perform better than unconstrained models and are more data-efficient. Moreover, we highlight that interpretations obtained from the former actually align with the user-provided knowledge, whereas those obtained from the latter do not.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an explanation-guided learning method for regression that uses partial dependence to align neural network responses with domain knowledge, demonstrating improved performance and data efficiency.
AI.motivation: Most interpretability research focuses on post-hoc explanations for classification, with little work on (1) assessing explanation quality, (2) explanation-guided learning for regression, or (3) incorporating functional domain knowledge beyond simple feature importance. The authors aim to fill these gaps.
AI.method: A steering approach that constrains neural network training by enforcing that the model's partial dependence (average marginal effect) on specified features matches user-provided functional domain knowledge. This aligns the model's learned interactions with prior knowledge during training rather than post-hoc.
AI.result: On regression tasks including dynamical systems forecasting, the proposed method yields models that outperform unconstrained baselines, exhibit greater data efficiency, and produce explanations that faithfully align with user-provided knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Explanation-guided learning via partial dependence constraints is an effective way to inject functional domain knowledge into neural networks for regression, improving both predictive performance and interpretability fidelity.
